    Chapter 1

    Introduction and concepts

    1.1 · What REMOTIX is and what it promises

    REMOTIX is the Linux desktop in the browser, for several users at once. A server runs on the machine and serves one web page; the page and the server talk a protocol of their own, RCP/1 (Remotix Control Protocol), over WebTransport, that is HTTP/3 on QUIC. Nothing is installed on the device the user connects from: a browser with WebTransport and WebCodecs is the client. The user types the Linux user name and password of the machine, the server checks them with PAM, and the page shows that user's own desktop. This manual describes version 1.2.0 for Ubuntu 26.04 (“resolute”), built from the code of the folder ubuntu26.04/: one codebase and one package for the four flavours of that release, Ubuntu (GNOME), Kubuntu (KDE Plasma), Xubuntu (XFCE) and Lubuntu (LXQt). Each distribution that REMOTIX serves has its own manual with the same table of contents.

    What the product promises is written elsewhere and is not repeated here. docs/SPECS.md says what REMOTIX does and does not do, in the owner's terms; docs/RCP.md is the protocol, byte by byte, and is the referee between the page and the server; docs/DECISIONS.md and docs/DECISIONS-11.md give the reason and the date of every choice, quoted in this manual as “DECISIONS §n”. This manual says how the code keeps those promises: which file, which function, which number, and what has been checked.

    i
    Goals, not promises. SPECS §3 gives targets of image quality, frame rate and delay (a minimum of 480p at 25 fps, a desired 4K at 60 fps, a delay of at most 50 ms). Since 30 September 2026 they are design goals, not measured promises (owner's decision recorded in SPECS §3): performance depends on the hardware. The parameters the product really enforces (session cap, clocks, ban, minimum bandwidth) are configuration and hold as written.

    1.2 · What was verified and what was not

    Two kinds of statement are made in this manual and they are kept apart. What was verified was run on the owner's development server, in four virtual machines (one per desktop, with a graphics card passed through to the one being tested) with real browsers, by the checks in prove/ (ch. 17 “Testing”), and by the owner by hand on those machines and on the four live images on a real machine. What was not verified is said every time it matters, and collected in ch. 24 “Appendix C — Known issues and open points”.

    Browsers as SPECS §11.5 declares them. Chrome and the other Blink browsers on Linux and Windows: HEVC if the device decodes it, otherwise H.264. Chrome on Android: HEVC or H.264. Firefox on Linux: H.264 only. Firefox on Windows and Safari were never tested; Firefox on Android is outside the project (no WebCodecs). The technical minimum is WebTransport and WebCodecs.

    What REMOTIX deliberately does not do (SPECS §12): Windows as a server; any program to install on the client; X11 desktop sessions; redirection of disks, printers, serial ports or smart cards; file transfer; images or files in the clipboard; multi-monitor as a feature; stylus pressure and tilt; native multi-finger touch; recording a session; compatibility with RDP, VNC or SPICE clients.

    !
    Documents and code. The specification documents carry the history of the project and are not always rewritten when a decision changes. Where the code and a document disagree, this manual follows the code and records the difference (ch. 24 “Appendix C — Known issues and open points”). Two examples: SPECS §5.2-bis and §7.3-bis still describe the Ctrl+Alt+End logout shortcut and the Ctrl+Alt+Del button, removed in August 2026 (the checks were brought in line on 18 Nov 2026: page-cad-hidden and page-ctrl-alt-end-passes); and the documents cite files of the old repository (CODER.md, STUDIES.md, PHASES.md) that are not in this tree.

    1.3 · Basic vocabulary and the invariants

    A handful of words recur in every chapter. Their names in the code are in code spans, so that they can be searched for. Identifiers, options and log text are in English; a few source files and symbols keep Italian names (for example registro_dice(), the log function) and are quoted as they are.

    Seven invariants are quoted in code comments as I1…I7. Their full text is in CODER.md of the old repository, which is not in this tree; the table gives them as the code uses them.

    1.4 · The repository, folder by folder

    The repository holds the product, the package recipe, the build scripts, the checks that drive real browsers, the dev-server scripts and the specifications. Everything is in English except part of the older documents.

    i
    Working rules. The rules of the working copy are in CLAUDE.md: builds and tests only on the dev server (never on the tablet), and the old repository is a read-only reference. The title and the first lines of that file still name the Debian rewrite the branch started from: they are a leftover, not a description of this tree, and this manual does not rely on them.

    1.5 · The project in numbers

    How big REMOTIX is, part by part. The lines are counted from the sources every time the manual is generated: the files kept by git under src/, debian/, build/, prove/, boxes/ and server/, plus the manual's own sources; binary files are left out. The last row counts every file under manuals/sources/, which in this tree includes the chapters of the manual of the other distribution that was kept here.

    A large share of the C is comment: by the project's rules a non-obvious line carries the reason, the measurement or the decision behind it, often with the date. A comment is not always right: where a comment and the code disagree this manual follows the code (ch. 21 “Conventions”).

    Chapter 2

    Overall architecture

    2.1 · The roles of the server executable

    The server is one executable, /usr/libexec/remotix/remotix, that plays several roles. The role is chosen by the first argument, read at the top of main() in main.c before any option, certificate or socket is touched, so that each role starts from a fresh memory image: a child must not hold the server's TLS key, and the PAM dispatcher must not hold any password or secret. The package ships one more, very small program, /usr/libexec/remotix/remotix-local-login (local_login.c, libc only): it is not a role of the server but a hook that PAM runs at a local login (14.6 “The local-login hold”); the line that starts it is put into /etc/pam.d/common-session by pam-auth-update (the profile debian/remotix.pam-config), and the shell script /usr/libexec/remotix/remotix-pam-hook (src/remotix-pam-hook) checks at every start of the service that it is still there.

    The unit's command line is in debian/remotix.service: --address 0.0.0.0, --name %H (the certificate carries the machine's name), the port from REMOTIX_PORT (default 7447, debian/remotix.conf), --certificates and --ban-file in /var/lib/remotix/net, --page /usr/share/remotix/page.html, --split, --journal and then REMOTIX_OPTIONS from the administrator's drop-ins in /etc/remotix/remotix.conf.d/. The unit sets no User= and no hardening: whatever a unit restricts, every desktop born from it inherits (DECISIONS-11 §11.11), so the network side's restrictions are put on that one process by the program itself (2.4 “The network side and its walls”).

    i
    Single-process mode. The binary can still run as a single process, with no walls and no privilege separation: --no-split, or started as an ordinary user (main() logs “not started as root: ONE process”). The unit never uses it, and the cleaning inventory docs/INVENTARIO-non-debian.md lists it as code that stays for now. This manual describes the split server, which is the product. The single-process mode is not exercised by the checks in prove/.

    2.2 · Process tree and privileges at a glance

    The process layout answers one question: what can each part of the server do if it is taken over? The line is drawn between the code that talks to strangers (QUIC, TLS and RCP parsers, the page server) and the code that can do things to the machine (check passwords, become a user, signal a desktop).

    Two numbers keep the layout honest. The network side is never the parent of anything that matters: the children are forked by the root side and the network side receives only the child's socket end and a pidfd over SCM_RIGHTS. And the desktops are not behind the walls: they are started by the child, outside the unit, so that sudo apt install inside a remote desktop keeps working (walls.h).

    2.3 · The root side

    The root side is rootside_main() in rootside.c. It exists so that everything that needs root is done by a process that never parses a byte from the internet. It is single-threaded and uses no GLib or D-Bus: it forks children, and a fork of a multi-threaded process runs PAM and NSS in a copy whose locks may be held by a thread that is not there. For the same reason main() must call rootside_main() before anything that could start a GLib thread (rediscover.c opens a D-Bus connection).

    Startup order in rootside_main().

    Then it loops on poll() over the self-pipe, the channel to the network side, the PAM dispatcher and the inotify descriptor of the local-login requests, with a timeout of 1000 ms (100 ms while stopping or while a local login is being served). Each round it reads the channel (chan_read()), flushes queued answers, reaps children (reap_kids()) and the network side (reap_net()), checks the desktops found again (found_check(), found_pump()), repeats the card probe if needed (codec_retry()), sends overdue signals (kids_hurry()), serves the requests of a local login that is held in PAM (pl_step(), 14.6 “The local-login hold”), keeps its tables (tables_minute()) and sweeps the KDE compositor hosts (kdehost_sweep()).

    If the network side dies the root side reaps it, closes the channel, gives each of its children KIDS_EOF_GRACE_MS (5000 ms) to leave on the end-of-file, then sends SIGTERM and, KIDS_TERM_GRACE_MS (3000 ms) later, SIGKILL; only the children, never the desktops. It restarts the network side after a pause of 1 s, 2 s, 4 s … up to NET_RESTART_CAP_MS (30 s); a network side that lived at least NET_STABLE_MS (60 s) resets the count (reap_net()). Before each start it kills any process of the user remotix that is in the root side's own cgroup (net_leftovers_kill()), and it wipes the grants it had given to the previous network side (net_generation_reset()). It starts the new one only after listing the desktops found again, so that the list is ready when the network side asks (found_look()).

    If the root side dies the network side sees end-of-file on its channel, leaves its loop and exits (rootside_lost() in the loop of main()); systemd restarts the unit (Restart=on-failure, RestartSec=2). The desktops are outside the unit, so a crash does not end them by itself; the restarted root side ends every REMOTIX desktop that has no child, unless its user comes back first (3.7 “Desktops found again after a restart”).

    Stopping. On SIGTERM the root side sends SIGTERM to the network side and waits at most STOP_WAIT_MS (25 000 ms) for it and for the children, then SIGKILLs the network side. An orderly stop closes the remote desktops: the network side asks each child for the close of its desktop (at most STOP_CLOSE_WAIT_MS, 15 000 ms), and the root side ends what is still in a REMOTIX scope before it exits; KillMode=mixed takes anything left (3.11 “Stopping the service”).

    2.4 · The network side and its walls

    The network side is the same binary re-executed with --network-side as its first argument; the rest of main() is its code. It checks, before anything else, that it was born as intended (network_side_born_right()): not uid 0, PID 1 with parent 0 (its own PID namespace), PR_SET_PDEATHSIG set, and fd 3, 4 and 5 of the right socket types, with the peer of fd 3 being the root side (SO_PEERCRED). It then waits up to READY_WAIT_MS (30 s) for the root side's READY, which carries the codec probe's result, and exits if it does not come.

    What it holds: the TLS key and certificates, the QUIC secret, the ban table, the log secret, the RCP sessions and the attach slots, every WebTransport connection, the page server, and the table of the children's socket ends. What it asks the root side for goes over the closed list described next: a password check, the birth of a child, a signal to one of its own children, and the list of desktops found again.

    The walls are put up by the root side in the fork, as root, right before the execve(), by walls_apply() in walls.c. Any step that fails stops the start: there is no silent fallback to a network side without its walls.

    !
    AppArmor is not yet enforcing. The AppArmor profile is shipped with flags=(complain,attach_disconnected): it logs what it would refuse and refuses nothing, with one exception that matters: a deny line holds in complain mode too. On Ubuntu 26.04 (AppArmor on by default, a kernel that mediates Unix sockets) the first form of the abstract-socket rule, deny unix addr=@*, forbade every Unix socket, so that no sign-in worked on the first real machine (live Ubuntu 26.04.1, 19 Nov 2026: “the server could not open your session”, logind unreachable; REGISTRO C4). The containers of the first rounds did not show it, because AppArmor is not in force there. The profile now has two lines that name the operations: deny unix (bind, listen) addr=@** and deny unix (connect, send, receive) peer=(addr=@**), with two stars because one stops at a slash. Measured on the machine: the system bus and the journal reachable, abstract sockets still refused, the check of local sessions answering CONNECTED (also seen on the live Kubuntu). Known limit: autobind (a socket that asks the system for a random abstract name) is still allowed; it only lets a process be reached, and the Landlock scope of scope_abstract_sockets() remains. The same profile lists the XKB data of Ubuntu 26.04 (/usr/share/xkeyboard-config-2/, /etc/xkb/, /etc/X11/xkb/, with /usr/share/X11/xkb a symlink to the first) and ends with include if exists <local/remotix_network> for the administrator's additions. The header comment of the profile still describes the state of 17 Nov 2026 on another machine; the flags and the lines above are what is in force. Enforce mode was not tried, so the walls other than AppArmor are the ones exercised by every check in prove/, because the network side always runs behind them. The profile has no capability line of its own: the one that comes in, net_bind_service, is brought by the nameservice abstraction and is harmless against an empty bounding set.

    The network side keeps four threads (the main one, a pool spawner, gmain and gdbus, measured and noted next to WALLS_NPROC_MAX in walls.h); they are GLib's, started by the logind sentinel. It runs one ppoll() loop whose timeout is the smallest of the transport's next timer and the page's, at most one second (main()).

    2.5 · The closed list between the two sides

    Everything the network side may ask of the root side crosses one SOCK_SEQPACKET socket pair with SO_PASSCRED on both ends, made by the root side before the fork (fd 3 in the network side). The list is closed and is in rootside_proto.h; Appendix A has every message. The rules are in the header and in the validator rootside_check_packet():

    The structs are sent as they are, the two sides being the same binary; the sender zeroes the whole struct first so that no padding byte carries stack. The order of the desktops-found-again events is part of the protocol: RXR_READY, then N times RXR_FOUND_AGAIN, then one RXR_FOUND_END whose count is N, and only after it any RXR_FOUND_GONE; the network side treats any other order as a broken channel (rootside_found_step()). The login rules that sit behind this table are in ch. 13 “Login and its defences”.

    2.6 · The PAM helper

    Checking a password is the one thing the server needs root for besides changing user, and PAM can take one to two seconds (the delay is added by PAM's failure delay, measured on 11 August 2026). The PAM helper exists so that this wait is never in a loop that delivers frames, and so that PAM, which is not reliably reentrant, is never used twice in one process.

    A failure is a refusal. The only way to a yes is the byte 1 written by the check after both PAM steps succeeded; any other byte, a short answer, a silence, a dead dispatcher or a full queue is a no. The socket is SOCK_SEQPACKET so an answer can neither arrive halfway nor merge with another. The numbers are in helper.c: MAX_IN_FLIGHT = 16 requests in flight (an address not known to rcp.c gets MAX_IN_FLIGHT minus RESERVED_FOR_KNOWN = 14), EXPIRY_MS = 8000 ms before a request is called a no, GRANDCHILD_ALARM_S = 20 s after which a check kills itself. A dead dispatcher is started again after 1 s, 2 s, 4 s … up to RESTART_CAP_MS (60 s); a dispatcher that lived STABLE_MS (60 s) resets the count. While it is down, logins are refused and not counted towards the ban.

    The password's journey. It exists in the network side (the RCP buffer, zeroed after use), in one packet of the closed list (RXR_PASSWORD_MAX = 1025 bytes in struct rxr_auth), in the root side's request to the dispatcher and in the check. Each copy is zeroed as soon as it has served; the in-flight tables keep the name and address, never the password. A second net sits in rcp.c: a session still waiting for a verdict after VERDICT_CAP (12 000 ms) is refused, so that it cannot hang on a silence (ch. 13 “Login and its defences”).

    2.7 · The per-user child

    For every admitted user the root side forks one child that becomes that user. Two facts, measured on 12 August 2026, force the split: root does not connect to the user's session bus (no bus, no capture), and only root can check another user's password. The child is born by child_birth() in child.c, in this order:

    The new image runs child_alive(): it logs its identity, re-checks getresuid() (a mismatch exits 42, “I am not who I should be”), arms PR_SET_PDEATHSIG and the end-of-file on the socket as two independent ways to die with the server, introduces itself with MSG_INTRO and mounts the stage (take_stage()). The parent gives it SHOW_UP_DEADLINE_MS (15 s) to introduce itself; after that there is no deadline, because a stage that is silent because nobody asks it anything is doing its job (invariant I4). Every minute the parent asks “who are you” again (RECHECK_MS, MSG_CHI_SEI), and a child that has sent nothing for WHOAMI_DEADLINE_MS (600 s) after the question is killed. A child may also tell the parent that the graphical session is over before it dismantles its stage (session_over_early()); the parent then keeps it as “closing” for CLOSING_GRACE_MS (30 s) so that a login in the meantime is refused with the truth (3.10 “When the session ends before the stage is gone”).

    A stage the child refuses. MSG_STAGE ends with a fatal field (struct body_stage; a parent also accepts the older, shorter body, STAGE_MIN, and reads it as “not fatal”). Only the refusal for the screen scale (guard 2: on Mutter, the scale of the stage's monitor is not 1 and one temporary attempt to bring it back with mutter_scale_to_one() failed) sets it. The hook children_hook_stage_refused() then reaches stage_refused_by_child() in main.c, which sends 0x0E to the clients (wt_dismiss_user_session_over()), and the child closes the session (3.10 “When the session ends before the stage is gone”).

    The close-only child. A desktop found again may have no client and no password to start a child with. The root side then starts a child with --close-only (a RXR_CLOSE_ORPHAN birth): no stage, no frame, no input; it obeys only “end the session” and leaves after CLOSE_ONLY_LIFE_MS (30 s) if none comes (3.9 “Ending a graphical session”).

    +
    Why exec. The child is an execve() and not a bare fork() for three reasons: the parent's memory holds the TLS key (in the split server, the network side's; in the root side, the ban and grants), and /proc/self/mem belongs to the owner of the process; the environment is then composed variable by variable; and the child uses PipeWire and GLib threads, which a fresh image makes irrelevant to the fork.

    2.8 · The channel between the network side and a child

    The network side and a child talk over a SOCK_SEQPACKET pair created at the fork. The kernel keeps message boundaries and, with SO_PASSCRED, stamps every message with the sender's real pid, uid and gid (SCM_CREDENTIALS). SO_PEERCRED would be the wrong tool: on a socketpair() it holds the credentials of the process that created the pair, on both ends. Both ends check: the child discards a message not stamped with the network side's uid (--parent-uid), and the network side checks the stamp against the child's uid (child_credentials_ok()) and, where the kernel gives it, the pidfd the root side handed over (child_credentials_pidfd_ok()).

    The twenty message kinds are listed in Appendix A (ch. 22 “Appendix A — Data structures and messages”). Large payloads (frames, cursor images, clipboard text) travel in pieces of at most MAX_PIECE = 32 768 bytes with total, offset and piece length, and are reassembled on the other side; a table per kind, because the three arrive interleaved. A frame's input field is written by the child at capture time: only the child knows which input the compositor had received. If the socket is full an audio block is dropped, not waited for: late audio must not stop the capture.

    2.9 · The logind sentinel

    The sentinel answers questions for which logind is the authority, through the system bus, in sentinel.c. It is synchronous with a short wait because a thread and a mutex would cost more in a server that keeps one loop by choice.

    A local session is one with a seat. The obvious criterion (graphical type, not remote) would refuse REMOTIX itself: REMOTIX's own sessions are created without a seat, and a seat is what separates a real screen from a headless one. The numbers: the question at ATTACH, before a birth and before a logout (sentinel_local3()) waits at most FAIL_CLOSED_WAIT_MS (1000 ms) and is asked a second time before it answers “could not look”; the periodic one waits WAIT_MS (300 ms), and an answer older than ANSWER_MAX_AGE_MS (7000 ms) is not used. ATTACH_WAIT_MS (100 ms) and SILENT_BACKOFF_MS (30 s) belong to the two-valued sentinel_local(), which no caller uses any more. The periodic check asks logind once for all users, not once per user (the cost measured on 25 August 2026 grew with the number of tenants), and does not wait for the answer: it uses the previous round's.

    i
    Asked from the right place. The power-off check runs in the child, never in the root side: root is always answered yes because logind looks at CAP_SYS_BOOT before polkit.

    If logind does not answer, the periodic check dismisses nobody: “I do not know” must not close the session of a user who did nothing wrong (I1). If the system bus cannot be opened at startup, the periodic half is not connected and the log says so. The question asked at ATTACH, before a birth and before a logout is fail-closed and refuses when in doubt (ask_local_session() and local_three() in main.c): it protects the user's local desktop from a remote session and from a remote logout (ch. 14 “Security model”).

    2.10 · Event loops and threads

    Each process has its own loop. Only the network side and the child have threads, and they are the libraries' or narrow helpers.

    The encoder runs synchronously in the child's loop: capture, encode, send, then the next frame. Encoding frame N while capturing N+1 would raise the frame rate and add delay, and SPECS §3.2 forbids that trade.

    2.11 · Where state lives, owner by owner

    Each piece of state has one owner and one lifetime. Two of them are deliberately held on both sides of the channel, and the table says so.

    One number for the cap. RCP_SESSION_CAP (10) in rcp.h is the default, --session-cap N moves it at startup, and rcp_cap() is read once by every table that counts users: the attach slots of rcp.c, the children of child.c, the presence table of main.c, the root side's children and the budget's cells. The root side's children table is sized on the cap handed to it in struct rootside_options. The default of 10 is a technical value; the declared limit of the product (owner's decision, DECISIONS-11 §11.51, confirmed 18 Nov 2026) is 8 users at the same time.

    +
    Stages, not connections. the cap counts stages, not connections: a user who closed the browser still holds a stage until logout or abandonment. stage_count() adds the children and the desktops found again; a new user who finds them all taken is refused with 0x0E SESSION_UNSERVABLE before any process is forked.
    Chapter 3

    Startup and life cycle

    3.1 · Service startup, step by step

    The service starts in two stages: the root side (2.3 “The root side”) does its own work and forks the network side, and the network side then runs the rest of main(). Both write at startup what the machine can do and which values are in force, so that a missing piece is read in the log rather than discovered by the first user.

    Before the root side, systemd runs ExecStartPre=-/usr/libexec/remotix/remotix-pam-hook check (debian/remotix.service): it checks that the line of the local-login hook is in /etc/pam.d/common-session and, if it is not, puts it back with pam-auth-update --package; it writes one line in the log either way, and the dash means that it can never prevent the start (14.6 “The local-login hold” has the hook).

    In the root side, before the network side exists: the options are parsed; the network user is resolved once, as root (getpwnam() of remotix; if it is missing or is uid 0 the service exits with EXIT_CONFIG = 78, which the unit's RestartPreventExitStatus=78 does not retry); the certificate folder, the ban file and the page must lie where the network side can use them (inside --network-state-dir, and the page readable by remotix), or the service also exits with 78 and says which option to fix; the UDP and TCP port are bound; then rootside_main() makes sure the GNOME session's system dconf database is there (session_dconf_system_db_ensure(), 2.3 “The root side”), probes the card, sweeps the card ACLs of a previous run, starts the PAM dispatcher and the network side.

    In the network side, in the order of main():

    1. Born right. network_side_born_right() (2.4 “The network side and its walls”), then rootside_attach() waits up to READY_WAIT_MS (30 s) for RXR_READY.
    2. What is offered to the browser. The codecs of the HERE_I_AM are not measured here: READY carries the root side's probe (child_video_capabilities()). A machine with no card that encodes logs why, and every HELLO ends in NOTHING_IN_COMMON until a codec appears (3.2 “The card that arrives late”).
    3. The desktop. session_desktop_explain() says which desktop this machine will start and why; on KDE kwin_check_permission() checks that the .desktop file that lets KWin offer screen capture to this binary is there (the package ships debian/org.kde.remotix.desktop). On XFCE and LXQt the explanation also says whether labwc is installed: it is only a Recommends of the package, and without it the log says that labwc is NOT there and the desktop cannot start.
    4. The values in force. The three clocks, the ghost-eviction threshold, the session cap, the budget, the queue threshold, the rate regulator, the dead line, the decoder pace: each is written with its value, on or off, so that a one-hour clock is verified by reading and not by waiting.
    5. The log secret and the ban. rcp_log_secret_load() first (the ban file holds the HMAC of the names); then rcp_ban_load(). If the ban file cannot be read the service exits with 1 rather than forget who was banned; “zero bans” and “could not look” are different facts.
    6. The tables of helper_turn_on() (a proxy to the root side, in this process) and children_turn_on() (sized on the cap), the optional bench socket (command_open(), only with --command-socket; the unit never gives it), the PAM file check (look_pam_service()), the certificates (certificates_prepare(): reads valid ones, generates otherwise) and the two TLS contexts.
    7. The sockets. transport_open_fd() on fd 4 (UDP) and, after the next step, page_open_fd() on fd 5 (TCP): the network side never binds.
    8. The hooks that tie transport, RCP and children together (video, audio, input, canvas, layout, pace, terminate, clipboard, local sessions); the sentinel (sentinel_open()); and found_again_at_startup(), which asks the root side for the desktops found again (waiting at most FOUND_AGAIN_WAIT_MS, 3 s).
    9. Ready. The line “ready: https://name:port” is written and the loop starts. Every pass the loop reads the UDP socket, runs the abandonment clock, delivers PAM verdicts, moves the children, expires transport timers, moves the page sockets, sweeps local sessions every LOCAL_SWEEP_MS (2000 ms), and every 60 s checks whether the session certificate needs rotating (certificates_rotate_if_needed()).
    i
    Old words, current code. The first log line still reads “REMOTIX — phase 1, the bare wire”: it is the program's historical first line and the checks look for it. The comment at the top of main.c also still describes phase 1 (“no video”); the code is the whole server.

    3.2 · The card that arrives late

    A card whose render node appears only after the unit starts (late driver, firmware still loading, a GPU that comes up after boot) would otherwise leave the service refusing every HELLO for as long as it ran. When the startup probe finds no codec the root side keeps measuring (codec_retry() in rootside.c):

    On a machine with no card at all the package refuses a new installation (debian/remotix.preinst, no DRM render node; ch. 15 “The package”), so this case matters for a card that is present but late, or for an upgrade.

    3.3 · The systemd unit and its life-cycle settings

    The service is the system unit debian/remotix.service, installed by dh_installsystemd with --no-enable --no-start (debian/rules): the package puts the unit there but the administrator enables and starts it, and an upgrade restarts it only if it was already running (the postinst's debhelper part does a try-restart; the restart closes the remote desktops, see 3.11 “Stopping the service”). The settings that shape the life cycle:

    !
    Old comments in the unit. Some comments of the package's files are stale. The header of the unit mentions a build made with --without split (remotix.service, line 6) that this tree does not have; debian/remotix.conf, debian/remotix-no-suspend.conf and debian/remotix.tmpfiles still speak of “the engine”, a program that is not in this tree. The comment on KillMode in remotix.service (and similar sentences in debian/rules and debian/remotix.postinst) still says that the desktops survive the stop (SPECS §5.2): since the decision of 17 Nov 2026 (DECISIONS-11 §11.56) an orderly stop closes them. The settings in the table are those in force; the comments are to be corrected at the next build.

    3.4 · From password to admission

    A login crosses five processes. Only the order and the numbers are given here; the protocol is in ch. 5 “The RCP/1 protocol” and the defences in ch. 13 “Login and its defences”.

    1. Deadlines of the handshake (RCP.md §4.6, constants in rcp.c): HELLO within CAP_HELLO = 5000 ms of the control channel opening, CREDENTIALS within CAP_CREDENTIALS = 60 000 ms of HERE_I_AM (a person types), ATTACH within CAP_ATTACH = 10 000 ms of ADMITTED. While it waits for the credentials the server keeps the connection alive with transport PINGs, or the 30 s QUIC idle timeout would end it before the 60 s.
    2. The check. The network side sends RXR_AUTH; the root side applies its bounds, refuses names that are uid 0, listed or unknown, applies its three pauses, and only then asks the PAM dispatcher. The answer is a RXR_VERDICT with an outcome and, for a yes, a 16-byte grant valid RXR_GRANT_LIFE_MS (30 s) and the system's canonical spelling of the name.
    3. The answer is never early. FIXED_DELAY (1000 ms) after the credentials arrived for every answer; REJECT_FLOOR (2500 ms) for a refusal that goes out as 0x07, so that the time does not tell a name in the denied list, a wrong password and an unknown name apart. A verdict that has not arrived after VERDICT_CAP (12 000 ms) is a no; the helper's own expiry is EXPIRY_MS (8000 ms).
    4. Admission (delivery_verdict() in main.c), in this order, each a refusal that leaves no process behind: a local graphical session of that user, or logind not saying, before any birth (0x05 or 0x0E, fail-closed); the previous desktop of that user still closing (0x0E); the compositor not installed (session_missing_component(): XFCE or LXQt without labwc, 0x0E with the sentence “the desktop (…) cannot start: `labwc` is not installed on this server”, for a login that is not a resume; the log names the package; nothing is born); the stages of the server all in use (stage_count() not below rcp_cap(), 0x0E); the budget (has_capabilities(), 0x06 BUDGET_FULL); then the birth.
    5. The birth. children_ensure_from() sends RXR_SPAWN with the grant and waits up to SPAWN_WAIT_MS (15 s: at a user's first login the birth includes usermod, itself bounded to 5 s). The root side checks the grant, the name, that no child of that uid exists, the cap, and that the canvas is within 320×240 and 4096×2304 (else it uses its own 1920×1080), runs child_birth() and answers RXR_SPAWNED with the child's socket end and a pidfd. A refusal is an rxr_refusal code that the network side turns into a sentence.
    6. ADMITTED and ATTACH. Only now does ADMITTED go out. ATTACH, in the order of the code, reduces a canvas above RCP_CANVAS_MAX_W×RCP_CANVAS_MAX_H (4096×2304; the declared limit of the product is 3K) with a logged fallback, refuses one below RCP_CANVAS_MIN_W×RCP_CANVAS_MIN_H (320×240) or with an odd side with 0x0B PROTOCOL_ERROR, asks the sentinel once more for a local session (0x05, also when logind could not say), takes the attach slot (slot_take(); if another live client of that user holds it and is not evicted as a ghost, 0x0F ALREADY_ACTIVE_REMOTELY), asks the stage for that canvas (the canvas granted can differ from the one asked for: the stage may already have another size, RCP.md §4.5), and answers SESSION with state 1 (NEW) or 2 (RESUMED, the stage was already there).

    Who is told when a session ends. The farewell of a session that is over (0x10, or 0x0E for a refused stage) does not go to every connection that carries the user's name: wt_dismiss_user_session_over() in webtransport.c tells the connections that are logged in at once; a connection that was ADMITTED but is still inside the fixed second (rcp_admitted_waiting()) gets the same farewell held until that second has passed, in the place of ADMITTED; a connection still waiting for PAM, or whose refusal is being held, is skipped, because it was never attached to that session and must learn nothing about the account (RCP.md §4.4). Before 19 Nov 2026 all three kinds were told at once, and a login refused with 0x0E “still closing” received a false 0x10.

    +
    Refuse before forking. None of the admission checks forks a process: a user refused for a local session, a full cap or the budget costs no child. A desktop found again of a user who then opens a local session is not closed by the network side (it is user remotix, and only the root side may end a logind session): it leaves the list (found_again_close_for_local() says so in the log, “the root side ends its scope by itself”), and the root side ends its scope within about 10 s; the local-login hook does it before the local desktop starts (14.6 “The local-login hold”).

    3.5 · Birth of a graphical session

    The child is born before it knows the window's size, and it must not start the desktop at the wrong size: on Wayland a resize completes only when the compositor delivers a frame, and a freshly started desktop that does not move never does. So the child waits for the client's canvas before making anything be born, with a ceiling.

    1. Introduction. child_alive() sends MSG_INTRO (who it is: uids, gids, pid, open descriptors, the runtime folder, whether the session bus socket exists) and the network side checks it against the kernel's stamp. A non-answer within SHOW_UP_DEADLINE_MS (15 s) kills the child.
    2. Waiting for the canvas. take_stage() answers “waiting for the client's canvas” (a MSG_STAGE with an unread session state) for up to CANVAS_WAIT_MS (1200 ms) while the client's ATTACH carries its window size to the child as CHILDREN_INPUT_RECANVAS. If none comes, the child starts at the fallback canvas and says so.
    3. The desktop. session_ensure() (or the non-blocking session_spawn()) asks whether the session exists and has the right monitor. If the session is dead it starts one with setsid --fork sh -c: the desktop is detached from the child's process group, which is why it survives the child. An orderly stop of the service closes it (3.11 “Stopping the service”). Its output goes to ~/.local/state/remotix/session.log (the user's state folder). The start command is the desktop's own. GNOME: the Exec line of the GNOME session the machine offers, chosen by the rule D8 (DECISIONS §10.20): the only gnome-session session found in wayland-sessions, else the one bearing the distribution's name (ID of /etc/os-release), else gnome; on Ubuntu that is ubuntu, with XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP=ubuntu:GNOME taken from the session's file. The Shell's unit is overridden to start headless (below). KDE: startplasma-wayland, with a drop-in on plasma-kwin_wayland.service whose ExecStart is remotix --kwin-nested W H node -- kwin_wayland_wrapper --xwayland --width W --height H --no-lockscreen. XFCE and LXQt: xfce4-session or lxqt-session on the distribution's own labwc (ch. 12 “The four desktops”). The PATH of the session is the one pam_env gave the child (2.7 “The per-user child”). On GNOME 50 one more guard applies: gnome-session refuses to start while graphical-session.target of the user manager is still active, so inactive_unit() counts it, with the session manager's unit and the D-Bus restart unit, among the things that must have ended: a birth too close to the end of the previous session says no, and the child's retry loop asks again a moment later.
    4. Retries. If the stage is not there yet the child retries every STAGE_BIRTH_RETRY_MS (200 ms) inside a window of BIRTH_REIN_MS (12 s) after asking for the session's birth, then at STAGE_RETRY_MIN_MS (1000 ms) doubling to STAGE_RETRY_MAX_MS (30 s); a blocking session_ensure() waits at most WAIT_STARTUP_MS (40 s). The child does not exit when there is no stage: §8.3 of SPECS forbids disconnecting; it logs a heartbeat once a second.
    5. The stage. The virtual monitor, the capture stream, the input device (libei on Mutter and KWin, virtual devices on labwc), the clipboard and the audio sink are mounted by take_stage(); the child reports the result in MSG_STAGE and, once the first frame is seen at the right size, MSG_CANVAS.

    The logind session. Before dropping privileges the child opens a PAM session (service remotix, type wayland, class user, no seat) and calls pam_end() without closing it. Since logind 258 the session is held by the pidfd of its leader, which is the child (the process that opened it, with the same pid after the execve()), so nothing is carried across the execve() and the logind session lives exactly as long as the child (Ubuntu 26.04 has 259.9; an older logind is not supported). A desktop's processes are in that session's scope. A session without a seat is headless, which on GNOME is the only form in which the screen locker does not revoke the capture (sentinel_without_seat() verifies it after startup). 2.7 “The per-user child” has the details of the fork.

    i
    GNOME 50. On GNOME 50 the Shell is the template unit org.gnome.Shell@.service (SESSION_UNIT_SHELL_MODEL in session.h; its own ExecStart is gnome-shell --mode=%i, read in the 26.04 package, studio/1-gnome50-avvio.md). The instance is the one the chosen session asks for: ubuntu gives org.gnome.Shell@ubuntu.service, gnome gives org.gnome.Shell@user.service. unit_shell() reads it from the Requires of gnome-session@<session>.target, asking the user manager. The drop-in that removes the monitors of the Shell's own is written at every birth into the folder of the instance (its ExecStart is gnome-shell --headless --no-x11 --mode=%i, so the mode that carries Ubuntu's dock and colours is kept), never into that of the template (a drop-in on org.gnome.Shell@.service.d/ would also apply to the Shell of the login screen), and is verified, because a line that can be lost is not a protection (invariant I7).

    3.6 · Detach and reattach

    Detaching is the normal end of a connection, and it ends nothing else: the slot frees and the stage stays (invariant I4). Three things can detach a client, and the farewell differs:

    When the last client detaches, the network side asks the child to turn the video and audio off (codec 0, MSG_VIDEO, MSG_AUDIO): the capture stops, the virtual monitor and the audio sink stay. Reattaching is a normal login: the user is checked again, a child already exists for that uid (so no birth), the attach asks for the new window's canvas, the child resizes the desktop and starts a keyframe, and SESSION says RESUMED. The page returns to the same windows and text. prove/check-lifecycle.py verifies it three ways on each desktop (clean close, a browser killed with -9, and a smaller window on return), and prove/check-resilience.py verifies a network drop longer than the silence clock.

    !
    Two clocks look like one. The silence clock is 30 s in the code and in SPECS §5.3, but the dead line (on by default since 24 August 2026) can end a connection earlier: after WT_LM_SILENCE_S (10 s) of client silence while the server has something to send. The stage is not touched either way. prove/check-resilience.py names both numbers (“spec 30 s; code 10 s dead-line”).

    3.7 · Desktops found again after a restart

    Only a fall of the service (a crash, a SIGKILL) or of the network side leaves a desktop with no process that watches it. The root side ends such a desktop within about 10 s (it must be seen in two scans of LX_EVERY_MS = 5 s in a row: “no orphan desktops”); a user who comes back before that finds it again (RESUMED), and after that the next login is NEW. An orderly stop closes every desktop (3.11 “Stopping the service”), so there is nothing to find after it. The mechanism below (rediscover.c, FOUND_*) still runs at every start of the network side, but it now describes a window of a few seconds, not a normal outcome. Until 17 Nov 2026 (DECISIONS-11 §11.56) a stop left the desktops alive for the reattach; the owner decided that they are closed because an orphan desktop breaks the local login of the same user on GNOME's login screen.

    The criterion (rediscover.h), the same for all desktops: a logind session with Service=remotix, in any state (it is “closing” as soon as its leader, the child, is gone, which is the case after a fall of the service; the comment in rediscover.h still describes the behaviour before 17 November 2026, when it was “closing” a moment after birth), that contains a process of the user which is leader of its own process session (pid equals sid) and whose parent is not in the same scope. That is the signature of setsid --fork: gnome-session-binary, startplasma-wayland or labwc. A terminal opened inside the desktop does not match, because its parent is in the scope.

    If the search cannot look (the sessions directory or /proc unreadable) the outcome is RXR_FOUND_UNKNOWN and the network side counts nothing, and says so: found desktops then count for neither cap, budget nor clock. If more desktops are found than the cap allows, no new user gets in until they leave, but each of those users gets back into their own. A restarted network side alone is told the table as the root side still has it.

    i
    Split server. The network side's repeated search (the whole question every 10 s, FOUND_AGAIN_SWEEP_MS in main.c) is the single-process mode's; in the split server found_again_sweep() returns at once and RXR_FOUND_GONE says when one dies.

    3.8 · The clocks, each one cited from its constant

    Clocks run on scales from milliseconds to an hour. Each one is listed with the constant that holds it, the file, and what it ends. Values are those of the code today; options move some of them, and the value in force is written in the log at startup.

    How the abandonment clock is fed. By the five real input gestures of RCP §7.3 (pointer, button, wheel, letter, key by position), recorded by presence_mark() per user in a table sized on the cap. Not by the release sent at detach (it arrives exactly when the user leaves), not by the canvas change that starts on its own at reattach, not by the request to log out. Resetting the clock at reattach was considered and discarded. abandon_round() runs every pass of the loop, because an expiry that waits for an event never fires. If the root side finds a found-again desktop not yet abandoned by its own clock (which counts from its own start, or from the last child's exit) it refuses with RXR_REF_TOO_SOON and the time to wait; the network side asks again, at most ABANDON_TOO_SOON_RETRIES (3) times.

    !
    Verified by mechanism. The 30-minute and 60-minute clocks were verified only by mechanism at short values (prove/check-resilience.py, check “clocks”: --inactivity-s 30 and --abandon-s 90, then a new login is NEW). Their defaults are read from the startup line, not waited for, by design (owner's decision of 16 August 2026).

    3.9 · Ending a graphical session

    The user ends their session; the server ends it itself when it is abandoned, when the service stops, when a local login of the same user is held, and when no child holds it (the root side's rule “no orphan desktops”). Whatever the cause, the reason is sent to whoever is watching before the desktop dies (RCP.md §8.1, finding B-7: a silence would read as “network error”).

    The close itself (session_terminate() in session.c) asks the desktop's own manager to exit and waits WAIT_EXIT_MS (10 s) for the session to be gone, then forces: GNOME Logout(1) then Logout(2); Plasma org.kde.Shutdown.logout then a forced stop of the unit, with a rescue described below; XFCE org.xfce.Session.Manager.Logout then SIGTERM to labwc; LXQt org.lxqt.session.logout then the same. When the close is the one for a local login held in PAM (14.6 “The local-login hold”), the orderly step on Plasma waits KDE_PRELOCAL_ORDERLY_MS (5 s) and not 10: a program that asks “save?” would keep the local login waiting for nobody. Then session_clear_out_scope() removes what a desktop that detached itself left in the child's logind scope (SIGTERM, a pause, SIGKILL), and the user manager's variables and drop-ins carrying REMOTIX's mark are restored. If the close fails the log says the two truths do not match (the client has its farewell, the desktop is still there).

    Plasma: a logout that stops halfway (session_kde_logout_watch() in session.c, Kubuntu 26.04, Plasma 6.6, 18 Nov 2026; REGISTRO D). “Log Out” starts plasma-shutdown, which asks systemd to stop graphical-session.target and exits without repeating the request. If a service (usually the portal) is still starting, systemd refuses, and the desktop stays up with the client never told. The older rescue waited for a unit to stop, which on Plasma 6.6 never happens. The rescue now notices that plasma-shutdown has finished (it owns the bus name org.kde.Shutdown while it runs), asks ksmserver whether a logout is really in progress (isShuttingDown), and only if the answer is yes waits KDE_LOGOUT_GRACE_MS (4 s) and repeats the stop of the target every KDE_LOGOUT_RETRY_MS (3 s): KDE_LOGOUT_TRIES (10) times in mode “fail”, then as many in mode “replace”, which also passes a queued start job. If the stop is still refused after about a minute the function returns true and the child closes the session by the product's own road (log: “closing the graphical session by force”). If ksmserver does not answer, or says no (a cancelled logout, an application asking to save), nothing is forced: unsaved work is worth more than a lost logout. Known limits: a power-off or reboot asked from the desktop does not release the bus name, so a refusal in the first seconds would stay lost (REMOTIX removes those menu entries); a restart of KWin during the wait resets the request.

    The light close (local_light_close()) is used when the user has a local session or logind could not say. Since 19 Nov 2026 the child sends MSG_LOCAL_FOUND to the parent before it starts the close (the close dismantles the stage, which can wait for PipeWire), so the clients get their 0x04 at once. The close dismounts the stage, releases the suspend inhibition, neutralises the session's dconf profile, closes what is left in the child's own seatless scope only if logind confirms it has no seat, stops REMOTIX's own KDE compositor service only if its processes carry REMOTIX's mark, and restores the manager's marked variables. It never calls the session manager's logout, which is shared with the local desktop. Decisions: docs/DECISIONS-11.md.

    i
    TERMINATE_SESSION has no trigger. The page contains the confirmation dialog and run_logout(), which sends TERMINATE_SESSION, but nothing in page.html opens the dialog: the Ctrl+Alt+End shortcut that did was removed on 17 August 2026. The message is served but has no way in from the page today. Log Out from the desktop's own menu is the only way for a user (SPECS §5.2-bis still describes the shortcut).

    What was verified. prove/check-lifecycle.py check 4 (“logout”) runs each desktop's own Log Out (xfce4-session-logout --logout, the LXQt and GNOME and KDE D-Bus calls): the client is told, nothing of the user is left in the box, and a new login gives a NEW session. login-after-other-logout in prove/check-resilience.py checks that a second user is untouched. Two corrections of 17 November 2026 are recorded for the work on Debian (17 Nov 2026; DECISIONS-11 §11.55-§11.56): the logind session now lasts for the whole life of the desktop and Log Out really closes it on all four desktops (child.c), and on KDE a Log Out succeeds even if systemd refuses the stop (session.c; the rescue above is its form on Plasma 6.6). XFCE ignores a Log Out asked while the desktop is still starting; that is the desktop's behaviour. On Ubuntu 26.04 the lifecycle/logout line passed on the GNOME virtual machine (19 Nov 2026) and, after the 18 Nov correction of the early Log Out, in the KDE container round (studio/giro2-kde.md); whether the rescue was exercised on the live Kubuntu is not recorded (not verified).

    3.10 · When the session ends before the stage is gone

    When a graphical session ends, the page must be told at once. For the first versions the child told its parent only after it had dismantled its stage (capture, input, clipboard). On Ubuntu 26.04 that order was wrong: the dismantling waits for PipeWire, and on a machine where RealtimeKit is installed but cannot start (containers, hardened machines) PipeWire's real-time module can sit in a D-Bus call to it for up to 25 s. In a measurement of 18 Nov 2026 on the 26.04 box the page stayed on the last image, without a word, for 17 s after a Log Out. Since 19 Nov 2026 the farewell does not depend on the dismantling. Measured afterwards in the containers (docs/STORIA-ubuntu-26.04.md): the page is told in about 6 s instead of 17-20 s, and on XFCE in 0.25 s instead of 1.3 s.

    The rule (session_over_early() in child.c). The child sends MSG_SESSION_FINISHED to the parent first, and dismantles the stage afterwards. Four conditions hold together, and each exists because the farewell cannot be taken back:

    Unknown is not dead. At a logout the user's session bus itself goes away for a moment, so the answer can be “unknown” exactly when the session has just ended. When the compositor closes the input channel and the answer is unknown, the child asks again after one second, up to EIS_UNKNOWN_ROUNDS (3) rounds, before it falls back to the old road (dismantle, no early farewell). The settings preparation at the child's start uses the same three answers (REGISTRO C5, 19 Nov 2026): alive, it writes the session's runtime dconf profile at once; dead, it neutralises a file of ours left behind and writes at the birth; unknown, it touches nothing and the birth writes the file if it is missing. The branch “unknown” at the child's start was not exercised on a machine (REGISTRO C5).

    What the parent does. It counts the child as closing from the moment it receives the message (closing_asked_ms, for at most CLOSING_GRACE_MS, 30 s). A login in the meantime is refused with the true 0x0E “still closing” and is never given a desktop that is going away (3.4 “From password to admission”). The clients that were logged in get 0x10 at once through wt_dismiss_user_session_over() (3.4 “From password to admission”). After the early message the child cannot find the session again in any branch of its loop except one: a compositor that takes its name back before the remount reads it (about a second; nothing of REMOTIX does that, and the Shell's unit is not restarted). Otherwise the remount reads “dead” with the session seen alive, takes the §7.6 road, and ends the child with SIGTERM. In that one case the clients are already gone and the parent keeps the child “closing” for the grace period.

    The stage refused for the scale. If the user has a screen scale other than 1 (their own settings, or Settings → Displays saved in monitors.xml) the pointer would go elsewhere, and guard 2 (DECISIONS §5.0-sexies) refuses to serve it. Since 19 Nov 2026 the child first makes one temporary attempt to bring its own monitor back to 1 (mutter_scale_to_one(): nothing persistent, the user's files untouched). If the scale re-read is 1 the stage goes on. If not, MSG_STAGE goes to the parent with fatal set, the clients get 0x0E (stage_refused_by_child() in main.c) instead of a black page, and the child closes the graphical session by the road of the user's Logout (the check for a local session first, which turns it into the light close), retried every 10 s if it fails; once the session is gone the child leaves, so nothing stays alive. The cause upstream is cured in the session's dconf rules, where scaling-factor is locked to 1 (a key of the table DCONF_KEYS added on 19 Nov 2026, with the user's own file never touched); the refusal is the net under it, and its log line lists the likely causes: a scale saved from Settings, a mandatory dconf profile of the administrator, or the fallback without dconf compile, where the lock does not hold.

    i
    Same window, two cures. The early farewell and the Plasma rescue have the same origin, a window in which the desktop is over and the clients do not know: the first closes it on every desktop but KDE, the second (3.9 “Ending a graphical session”) on Plasma. The records are in the comments of session_over_early() and session_kde_logout_watch(), and in docs/REGISTRO-problemi.md (D).

    3.11 · Stopping the service

    When systemd stops the unit (systemctl stop or restart, a package upgrade that restarts the service, a shutdown), every remote desktop is closed, as at a reboot. Until 17 Nov 2026 the desktops stayed for the new service to find; the owner's decision of that night (DECISIONS-11 §11.56) reversed it, because a desktop left without anyone to watch it breaks the local login of the same user (14.6 “The local-login hold”).

    1. Signal. SIGTERM reaches the root side, which sends SIGTERM to the network side and waits STOP_WAIT_MS (25 s, rootside.c) for it and for the children; the log says “the network side is asked to stop (SIGTERM), 25 s at most”.
    2. Farewell. The network side leaves its loop and calls transport_dismiss_all() with RCP_SERVER_CLOSING (0x0C), “the server is shutting down”, polling the socket for at most 4000 ms until every session is closed, then 50 more rounds of 10 ms so that the closing capsule really leaves; if some sessions did not finish it says so.
    3. The desktops are asked to close. For every child that is alive the network side sends the request to close its desktop and waits at most STOP_CLOSE_WAIT_MS (15 s, main.c). A user with no local session gets the full close (the desktop's own logout); a user who has a local session, or for whom logind could not be asked, gets the light close, never the session manager's logout (the log says “its desktop gets the LIGHT close, not the Logout”). Desktops found again that have no child here are left to the root side. If the root side is already gone no request is sent: the children see the end-of-file and leave, and the next root side ends the desktops.
    4. Tidy. helper_turn_off(), sentinel_close(), page_close(), transport_close(), then children_turn_off(): each child's socket is closed (the end-of-file is the second net, beside PR_SET_PDEATHSIG), the child gets SIGTERM and TURN_OFF_WAIT_MS (1500 ms) to be reported gone by the root side. A child on SIGTERM dismounts its stage (capture, virtual monitor) and exits.
    5. The root side ends what is left. Once the network side is gone (or at the deadline) the root side ends whatever is still in a REMOTIX scope: SIGTERM to that scope's processes, SIGKILL LX_TERM_MS (3 s) later, the clean-up of what REMOTIX put in the user manager (up to LX_CLEAN_MS, 15 s), all bounded by the root side itself; it waits for these endings (21 s at most) before it exits. If nothing was left at its scan it says “⭐ no orphan desktops: no REMOTIX session is left with processes — the service stops clean”; if it had to end something, the lines are the per-session “⛔ no orphan desktops: the REMOTIX session N of «user» (uid N) is still there while the service stops — it must not stay: SIGTERM …”; if something is still there at the ceiling it says “⛔ no orphan desktops: the service stops and N REMOTIX session(s) still have processes (…): the next start of the service ends them”. KillMode=mixed takes anything left of the unit.

    The stop takes a few seconds when the desktops close by themselves. The code states these bounds and no other total: 25 s for the network side and the children, 15 s of those for the close of the desktops, and the root side's own endings after that (SIGTERM, SIGKILL after 3 s, clean-up up to 15 s). A user with a client open is sent away with 0x0C; a new login gives a NEW session, and the programs of the old desktop, with their unsaved work, are gone. In the journal, area startup, the lines are “stopping: N desktops asked to close (waiting at most 15 s for them)” and “stopping: N desktops closed, M still alive after 15 s”; a request that did not leave says “the request to close the desktop of … did NOT leave towards its child”. Area rootside has the “no orphan desktops” lines.

    A restart of the network side alone (a crash, or the root side's decision after a malformed packet) closes the clients' connections without a farewell, since the process is gone; the root side then restarts it. The children see the end-of-file, and a desktop left without a child is listed as found again for the new network side and ended by the root side within about 10 s, unless its user logs in first (3.7 “Desktops found again after a restart”). After a restart of the whole service, prove/check-resilience.py (“service-restart”) checks that the client is told or returns to the form (within 45 s), that no REMOTIX session of the user and no process of the old window are left, that the root side's journal says “the service stops clean”, and that a new login is a NEW session with a working desktop.

    +
    Upgrades close the desktops. Restarting the unit to install a new package closes the remote desktops: the postinst's debhelper part restarts the service if it was running, and the restart is a stop followed by a start. The prerm does not close sessions on an upgrade, but the stop does. Warn the users of a busy server before upgrading; they log in again and get a new session. On Ubuntu the package also installs /etc/needrestart/conf.d/remotix.conf (debian/needrestart/remotix.conf), which sets $nrconf{override_rc}{qr(^remotix\.service$)} = 0: needrestart (and so unattended upgrades) no longer restarts the service by itself after an update of a library it uses (libc, OpenSSL, PAM), which would close every remote desktop. The service is then only listed under “Services to be restarted manually”, and the administrator restarts it when no remote desktop is open; until then the old library stays loaded.

    3.12 · The log line that marks each step

    A defect in this chain rarely names its cause: the user sees “black”, “slow” or “nothing happens”. The log line that marks each step is the map. The first token after the time is the area (rootside, child, session, startup…); the log chapter has the format (ch. 16 “Logging and diagnostics”).

    The priority marks of the journal (a leading ⛔ is an error, a leading ⚠ a warning, anything else information) were reviewed on 17 November 2026: of 33 message patterns seen at error priority, 29 routine ones were lowered to information or warning and 4 were kept as errors (docs/REGISTRO-priorita.md).

    Chapter 4

    Transport

    4.1 · The transport stack and the network side

    REMOTIX has no client program: the client is the browser. A web page cannot open a bare QUIC connection, but WebTransport over HTTP/3 gives it the building blocks the protocol needs: independent unidirectional streams, the abandonment of a stream with RESET_STREAM, unreliable datagrams and connection migration. The server therefore speaks QUIC version 1 with mandatory TLS 1.3, HTTP/3 and WebTransport on UDP, and serves the page itself on TCP. There is no clear-text mode, and RCP never runs on TCP.

    Both listeners belong to the network side, the unprivileged process that the root side forks (see ch. 2 “Overall architecture” and ch. 3 “Startup and life cycle”). The root side binds the two sockets before the fork and hands them over as descriptors 4 (UDP) and 5 (TCP) (ROOTSIDE_FD_UDP, ROOTSIDE_FD_TCP); the network side then calls transport_open_fd() and page_open_fd() on them. In the single-process mode (--no-split) transport_open() and page_open() bind and open in one step. Either way QUIC, HTTP/3, WebTransport, RCP and the page server share one thread and one poll loop. Whatever could block that loop lives in other processes: PAM in the helper (helper.c) and everything that touches a user's desktop in the per-user child. The transport only moves bytes between the network and those processes.

    i
    Libraries. the QUIC and HTTP/3 libraries are linked statically. build/quic-static.sh builds ngtcp2 v1.25.0 and nghttp3 v1.18.0 from source (the NGTCP2_VER and NGHTTP3_VER defaults) and debian/control records them in Static-Built-Using, together with the labwc (0.9.3) and wlroots (0.19.2) of the package's own labwc. They are built from source because the 26.04 packages of ngtcp2 (1.16) and nghttp3 (1.12) are older than the versions the code needs (studio/8-pacchetto-e-prove.md). OpenSSL is the system library (libssl-dev 3.5 or later at build time; 3.5.5 on 26.04) used through ngtcp2_crypto_ossl, which carries the native QUIC API of OpenSSL 3.5. The reasons for choosing ngtcp2 over the other QUIC libraries are in DECISIONS.md §6.4.

    4.2 · The WebTransport announcement and the SETTINGS rewrite

    No QUIC library considered for REMOTIX implements WebTransport on the server side, so webtransport.c adds it on top of ngtcp2 and nghttp3. The price is declared in webtransport.h: nghttp3 has no API to put an arbitrary setting on the HTTP/3 control stream, so the server rewrites the SETTINGS frame while nghttp3 is writing it, in rewrite_settings().

    The rewrite depends on the shape of the bytes nghttp3 produces, not on a promise of its API, and must be re-tested at every nghttp3 upgrade. The guard is loud. rewrite_settings() first checks that the bytes handed over fit its 512-byte buffer, that the control stream starts with stream type 0x00, that the first frame is SETTINGS (type 0x04) and that its length covers exactly those bytes. If any check fails nothing is rewritten, the log says which one, and the server has no WebTransport; it never emits a misaligned control stream.

    i
    Provenance. the benches that compared the QUIC libraries and measured the WebTransport handshake against real browsers are not part of this tree. This manual repeats their result from code comments, not from a re-run. What was verified for this version is in 4.15 “What was verified for the transport”.

    4.3 · Listeners, sockets and port 7447

    The server listens on port 7447 twice: UDP for HTTP/3 and WebTransport, TCP for the first load of the page. The user types https://address:7447, accepts the certificate warning once per device, and types user and password into the page.

    The two are independent. WebTransport does not use Alt-Svc: a WebTransport session opens its own HTTP/3 connection to the address it is given, so there is no fallback from UDP to TCP to make. RCP.md §2.4 carries a note that corrects the earlier requirement of an Alt-Svc header.

    !
    No SO_REUSEADDR on UDP. the UDP socket is bound without SO_REUSEADDR. With that option two unicast UDP sockets can share the port and the kernel hands each packet to only one of them, which looks like «the server is on and the page does not connect» with two processes both convinced they are listening. On TCP the option stays: there the kernel refuses a second listener anyway, and the option only avoids TIME_WAIT after a restart.

    Address and port in the package. debian/remotix.service starts the binary with --address 0.0.0.0, --name %H and --port taken from REMOTIX_PORT. The binary's own default for --address is also 0.0.0.0, an IPv4 wildcard, so the packaged server does not listen on IPv6. The code supports IPv6 sockets (transport_bind() resolves with AF_UNSPEC and pktinfo.h handles IPV6_PKTINFO), but nothing in the package asks for them and no check in prove/ exercised IPv6. The port is REMOTIX_PORT, 7447 in remotix.conf (installed as /usr/share/remotix/remotix.conf), overridable by files in /etc/remotix/remotix.conf.d/. Extra options go in REMOTIX_OPTIONS. The compiled-in default is DEFAULT_PORT in main.c.

    !
    TCP and UDP, and nobody opens them. both protocols of the port must be reachable: TCP loads the page and UDP carries the session. With only TCP open the page loads and the desktop never arrives, because there is no fallback. The package ships a ufw application profile (debian/remotix.ufw, installed as /etc/ufw/applications.d/remotix, 7447/tcp and 7447/udp) but only defines it: ufw app list shows it. On Ubuntu 26.04 ufw is a recommended package of ubuntu-standard and is off by default (ENABLED=no in /etc/ufw/ufw.conf), so on a stock install the port is reachable anyway. Nothing opens a firewall that is on, and this tree has no installer to do it, so the administrator must run ufw allow REMOTIX or the equivalent for another firewall. A firewall outside the machine (a provider's) needs the same two rules.

    4.4 · QUIC transport parameters

    Every connection gets the same transport parameters, set in accept_conn() just before ngtcp2_conn_server_new. With a browser as client the server cannot dictate the client's parameters: what is normative is what the server announces.

    • No UDP GSO. write_connection() asks ngtcp2 for an aggregate sized to ngtcp2's send quantum (never less than one full-size packet, never more than its 64 KiB buffer), splits it and sends one packet per sendmsg through send_on(). ngtcp2's pacing is honoured.
    • MAX_PACKETS_PER_ROUND (64) limits reading: transport_read() takes at most that many datagrams per pass of the loop, then transport_write() runs.
    • A datagram shorter than 21 bytes is dropped before ngtcp2 sees it (transport_read()).
    • The congestion controller was never chosen: ngtcp2_settings_default() leaves cc_algo at ngtcp2's default (CUBIC). The comment above wt_adaptive_rate() records the choice of a controller as an experiment still to be made.

    4.5 · Admission of new connections, Retry and Stateless Reset

    A stranger gets no connection state. read_packet_1() in transport.c is the function to read; the figure shows the order in which a packet whose destination connection id is not in the map is treated.

    The «address» of every cap is computed by address_key(): an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address and a NAT64 address become the IPv4 address inside, ::1 is kept whole, any other IPv6 address becomes its /64, and the /48 is the second key. The login ban applies the same rule through rcp_key_address() in rcp.c. A connection is charged to its birth address even if it migrates (birth_key). pick_victim() never evicts a connection in wait-verdict (PAM is judging it) or a logged-in one; it prefers a finished connection, then one from the place that holds the most pending connections, so a flood evicts itself. The page opens the QUIC connection only after the password has been typed, so nobody is evicted while typing.

    Connection ids that carry a proof. Every id the server issues is CID_NONCE = 10 random bytes plus CID_TAG = 8 bytes of HMAC-SHA256, 18 bytes in all (CID_LEN, SCIDLEN). The HMAC key is derived from the static secret with the domain string REMOTIX CID v2, and for a normal id the tag also covers the epoch (CID_EPOCH_S = one hour of UTC clock); an id counts as signed for the current and the previous epoch. The tag does not decide whether a packet finds its connection, because the map is always searched. It decides which Reset budget a packet for an unknown id may use, so a flood of forged ids cannot use up the Resets that real clients need after a restart. Retry ids carry a different label and never count as signed. The residual limit is declared in cid.h: about 100 collected ids can still use up the signed budget.

    The static secret. secret_load() reads or creates quic-secret (32 bytes, mode 0600, owned by the running user, written through a temporary file with fsync and rename) in the certificates directory. Retry tokens, Stateless Reset tokens and the connection-id key all derive from it, so it must survive a restart: otherwise a client holding an old id would not recognise the Reset. If the file cannot be read or written the secret of the run is used and the log says so.

    The source address of a reply. The UDP socket is bound to the wildcard, so with a plain sendto the kernel would choose the source address, and a client drops a reply that does not come from the address it wrote to. pktinfo_cmsg() builds the IP_PKTINFO or IPV6_PKTINFO control message that fixes the source, and pktinfo_sendmsg() retries once without it when the kernel refuses that source (pktinfo_refusal(): EINVAL, EADDRNOTAVAIL, ENETUNREACH, ENODEV), so a temporary address that just expired does not leave a connection mute. The destination address of an incoming datagram is read from the same control message in transport_read() and becomes the local end of the ngtcp2 path.

    i
    Refusals do not flood the log. every refusal and eviction is counted and summed in one log line per 10 s (REFUSAL_LOG_S) instead of one line each. The same budgeting protects the «new connection» lines (BIRTH_LINES), the «packet not sent» lines (SEND_FAIL_LINES) and the lines a stranger can provoke before any login. The reply to a refusal is sent only to an Initial whose Retry token proved the address, so a forged source is not reflected.

    4.6 · TLS contexts and the two certificates

    Two TLS contexts are built by tls.c from the two certificates, and they never share one. Both come from a single common() function: TLS_server_method(), minimum version TLS 1.3, server cipher preference, SSL_OP_NO_ANTI_REPLAY and the key-exchange groups X25519MLKEM768:X25519:P-256:P-384 (TLS_GROUPS). If the installed OpenSSL does not know the ML-KEM group, the list without it (TLS_GROUPS_CLASSIC) is set and the log says so. The server never starts on OpenSSL's default list, because a client could then offer only an expensive group and the single loop that also serves the video would pay for each handshake.

    There are two certificates, kept apart down to their file names. The page certificate is the one on which the user grants the browser exception, so it must change as rarely as possible. The session certificate is checked by fingerprint, and browsers accept that only for certificates valid less than 14 days, so it rotates on its own.

    The directory is the value of --certificates. The binary's own default is /var/lib/remotix/certificates, or the folder certificates under --network-state-dir when the server runs split (main.c); the unit passes /var/lib/remotix/net/certificates explicitly. debian/remotix.tmpfiles creates /var/lib/remotix/net with mode 0700 for the system user remotix and keeps the modes of what is inside; the directory itself is created 0700 by certificates_prepare(). It also holds quic-secret and the log secret. certificates_prepare() runs at start-up in the network side.

    • Key type. ECDSA P-256 only (EVP_EC_gen), never Ed25519 or RSA: P-256 is the key type that keeps serverCertificateHashes open.
    • The private key is born 0600 (write_pem() opens it with mode 0600), not chmod-ed afterwards, so there is no window in which it is readable.
    • Contents. X.509 version 3, a random 128-bit serial, notBefore one hour in the past, signed with SHA-256, basic constraints critical,CA:FALSE, subject CN equal to the name, and a subjectAltName that san_di() writes as IP: or DNS: according to the form of the name. The name is --name (the unit passes %H, the host name); main.c refuses to start with 0.0.0.0 or :: as the name. A user who connects by IP address declares it with REMOTIX_OPTIONS=--name 192.0.2.10.
    • The administrator's certificate is never touched. Every certificate REMOTIX writes has a .ours marker next to it. A page.pem with its key but without the marker belongs to someone else and is used as it is and never regenerated, even when it expires. The test is «did we write it?», not «is it self-signed?». The session certificate has no such exemption: certificates_rotate_if_needed() regenerates it whatever the marker says.
    • The two must differ. At start certificates_prepare() compares the two fingerprints and refuses to start if they are equal, because one certificate for both listeners would bring the browser warning back every two weeks.
    • Fingerprint. SHA-256 over the DER bytes of the session certificate, not over the public key and not over the PEM text (fingerprint_of(), X509_digest). It is kept in base64 for the page and in hexadecimal for logs; rotations counts the generations since start (the first generation counts as one).
    !
    A changed name is not noticed. certificates_prepare() never compares the name inside an existing certificate with the current --name. If the host name or the option changes, the page certificate keeps its old subject alternative name until it expires or is removed, and the browser shows a name-mismatch warning. The session certificate follows the new name at its next rotation, but pinned connections do not depend on the name. Nothing in the package removes the old page certificate.

    4.7 · Certificate pinning and the fingerprint endpoint

    The page carries the fingerprint of the session certificate, and the browser accepts the WebTransport connection without a warning when the certificate matches it. The exception the user grants on the page certificate does not extend to WebTransport, so the fingerprint is the normal road, not a safety net (RCP.md §4.1-bis).

    1. The server writes the current fingerprint into the page: page.c replaces __FINGERPRINT__ in page.html on every request for /.
    2. Before every connection the page fetches /fingerprint with cache: "no-store" (page.html). A tab left open for two weeks holds the fingerprint of a certificate that has since rotated, and without the fresh fetch the browser would refuse the reconnection without saying why. The fetch does not go through RCP, because there is no session yet. If it fails the page falls back to the fingerprint it was served with and says so.
    3. The page opens new WebTransport("https://" + location.host + "/rcp/1", …) with allowPooling: false and serverCertificateHashes: [{ algorithm: "sha-256", value: … }].

    Whether this works on a given browser was measured, not assumed: the driving checks in prove/ run Chrome and Firefox against the server and open the session through this very mechanism (4.15 “What was verified for the transport”). Safari and iOS were never tested, and nothing here claims they work. A rotation of the certificate while a client is connected was not exercised by any check.

    i
    Accepted risk. the first connection on each device is open to a man in the middle, who would not merely read the page but could rewrite it. The risk is accepted for the intended scenario, an own server on an own network or a VPN, and a certificate from a real authority removes the warning (SPECS.md §4.1, DECISIONS.md §1.7).

    4.8 · The page server on TCP

    page.c is a small HTTPS/1.1 server: one request per connection, Connection: close, non-blocking sockets inside the same poll loop. It reads page.html from --page (the package installs it as /usr/share/remotix/page.html) and treats the request line only for its path: the method is logged, not judged, and the query string is cut off before the path is compared.

    Every response carries Cache-Control: no-store, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, the three cross-origin isolation headers (Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin, Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp, Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin, the macro ISOLATION) and the macro PAGE_SECURITY: a Content-Security-Policy with default-src 'self', frame-ancestors 'none', connect-src 'self' and the directives the page really needs, Referrer-Policy: no-referrer, and a Permissions-Policy that leaves the clipboard to the page itself and switches off camera, microphone, location and the other device features. Isolation gives the page full-resolution timers and shared memory (SPECS.md §11.5). The third isolation header is not optional: with require-corp the browser refuses any sub-resource that does not declare it, and the symptom does not mention isolation. The reasons for each CSP directive are in the comment above PAGE_SECURITY.

    When the table is full, fair_victim() evicts by groups: clients that never sent a byte first, then clients without a whole request, then slow writers, then fresh writers, at random among equals; the newcomer is refused only if its own group would then be larger than the largest. Expired and evicted clients are closed with a reset (SO_LINGER zero) so the kernel does not hold their data. The price is declared in the code: a crowd behind one address, a CGNAT or a carrier /48, is one group.

    The banned address still gets the page. The ban is not checked at accept.
