The picture, a moving counter, bursts that stop and the frame rate are measured by prove/check-media.py; the capture is exercised through them but no check isolates the capture alone (ch. 17 “Testing”).
    • The owner's hand tests: the four virtual machines and the four live images 26.04.1 on a real machine (27 Nov 2026) found everything regular.
    • Not verified on Ubuntu: the nested KWin without our labwc (--virtual fallback) beyond a first check on the Kubuntu box; the shape probe and the encoded theme by eye; NVIDIA with GNOME on this tree (the modifier path of capture_modifiers_card(); measured on Ubuntu 26.04 on 6 Oct 2026 with an earlier version of the code); a canvas of 4096×2304 end to end (the test browser's decoder stops at 3840×2160); the lost-frame cure on a real machine beyond the hand tests.
    Chapter 7

    Video encoding

    7.1 · Encoding at a glance: one front, two GPU routes

    REMOTIX encodes every frame on the graphics card, in H.264 or HEVC, into Annex-B that the browser's WebCodecs VideoDecoder decodes. encoder.c is the front: it chooses the route by capability, Vulkan Video if the card encodes that codec through Vulkan and VA-API otherwise, and it keeps everything that works on the bytes (shape checks, keyframes, the 16 MiB ceiling, quality steps, the level check) in one place for both routes. There is no software encoder and no libavcodec: a server without a capable GPU says so at startup and offers no video codec. On Ubuntu 26.04 the package also contains a GPL-2.0 program, the labwc that hosts KWin on Kubuntu (ch. 6 “Screen capture”); it is a separate executable and is not linked into the encoder, so «no GPL encoder library» remains true.

    The licensing consequence is stated in debian/control and THIRD-PARTY-LICENSES: the product binary links libva (MIT), the Vulkan loader (Apache-2.0), libgbm and PipeWire, and no GPL encoder library.

    7.2 · Codecs and their negotiation

    RCP/1 numbers the video codecs in the frame header: 1 = HEVC, 2 = AV1, 3 = H.264. The enum CodecVideo (encoder.h) uses the same values so that no conversion table can drift. AV1 is never negotiated and nothing in the product encodes it, but its number stays reserved, and encoder.c still carries a reader for AV1 sequence headers that no route can reach (see ch. 24 “Appendix C — Known issues and open points”).

    What the server offers is measured, not written. At startup the codec probe opens each codec through the same encoder_of() a session uses and encodes a PROBE_SIDE = 256 pixel synthetic frame until bytes come out (at most PROBE_ROUNDS = 8 attempts). The probe runs in a short-lived process, because a driver that crashes must not take the server down before it has opened its port. In the default two-process server the root side runs it (rootside.c, child_video_probe_begin() and child_video_probe_step()), since the network side runs as the user remotix and does not open the card, and hands the result to the network side. The result reaches rcp_video_codec_set() as hevc,h264, hevc, h264 or empty. With an empty list every HELLO ends in NOTHING_IN_COMMON and the startup log says why, with the remedy. A browser must never be offered a codec the server cannot keep.

    The measure is repeated when the card arrives late. If the card's node does not exist at startup (at boot it can appear after the unit starts), codec_retry() in rootside.c measures again in a probe process collected without blocking the loop: after 2 s (codec_every_ms starts at 2000), doubling up to 60 s. When something is found it logs «the card arrived N s after startup», tells the network side, and video.codec is offered from the next HERE_I_AM. If the node opens but nothing encodes (a driver still loading its firmware), child_video_retry_worthwhile() allows five more tries at the same pace and then one line and stop: not a matter of time. The single-process server (--no-split) has the same loop in main.c.

    The codec string handed to VideoDecoder.configure() is built in the page by codec_strings(): for H.264 avc1.6400 plus the level in hexadecimal (5.1 gives avc1.640033, decimal would give the invalid avc1.100051), for HEVC hev1. with profile, level and L93 as second choice. The server composes its own string from the SPS it produced (codec_string in the confession), and the profile and level bytes are what decoders use. The browser-side logic is in ch. 9 “The browser page”.

    i
    Depth. H.264 is High, 8 bit only. profile_va() returns VAProfileNone for H.264 at 10 bits instead of trying, and the Vulkan route refuses it in vulkan_fit(). HEVC is Main or Main 10. The capture is 8 bits per channel on every desktop (ch. 6 “Screen capture”), so a 10-bit stream is 8 bits promoted; the confession declares it (promotion_8_to_10).

    7.3 · Choosing the GPU route

    The encoder is asked for by name, and the name says how the route is chosen. A name that is not one of these six is refused by codificatore_nuovo() with the reason: there is no silent fallback to another component, profile or depth.

    child.c builds the name from the codec and the route in force (component_of()); the route is card unless the server was started with --encoding-route card|vulkan|vaapi, which the parent repeats on every child's command line (the child is an exec, a static of the parent would not reach it). The component actually opened is what encoder_name() and the log report, with the node, the vendor string and the VA-API entry point.

    The VA-API entry point is a declared rule, ENCODER_POWER_DECLARED (RENDER_POWER in child.c): low-power EncSliceLP if the driver declares it for the profile, full EncSlice otherwise, failure if neither. The pair (profile, entry point) is read with vaQueryConfigEntrypoints() before opening, with three outcomes: present, absent, could not look. The maximum size is read with vaGetConfigAttributes() at every opening, because another card may declare less.

    When opening fails the child does not retry at every frame: the wait doubles from ENC_RETRY_MIN_MS = 500 ms to ENC_RETRY_MAX_MS = 10 s and the log says the next attempt time. A second guard, enc_death_wait_ms() in encbackoff.h, covers an encoder that opens fine and then dies at the first quality change: the count of deaths is kept apart from the count of failed openings (a successful creation resets the latter), doubles the wait up to the maximum, and goes back to zero only after a frame was really sent. A full card is not a missing codec: when vkCreateVideoSessionKHR returns VK_ERROR_TOO_MANY_OBJECTS the log says the card has run out of encode slots, and the session gets its first frame by itself when one frees.

    7.4 · Choosing the card and granting access to it

    Two different cards matter. The desktop is drawn by the compositor on its card, and the encoder must open the same card, or every frame is a cross-card import that fails or goes through memory. REMOTIX therefore chooses the desktop's card itself and then makes the encoder follow the compositor.

    The choice is made once per session, logged once with the PCI address, the driver and the vendor:device pair (render_node_describe()), and latched (render_node_latched) so that it does not move under an open encoder. render_node_is_drm() refuses a --render-node that is not a character device with major RENDER_NODE_DRM_MAJOR = 226 under /dev/dri/, and render_node_same() compares two names by st_rdev. When the card is a service or BMC card (card_pick_service_driver(): ast, mgag200, hibmc) the child logs one warning that the desktop probably draws in software; behaviour is not changed. If no card can create a buffer, session.c passes WLR_RENDERER=pixman and says so.

    Access to the card: groups and the render grant

    A session has no physical seat, so logind gives it no ACL on the render node, and the user must be in the group that owns /dev/dri/renderD*. At the first connection, after PAM said yes and before the child is forked, the parent adds a user who is not in the group with usermod -aG (only the group of the render nodes, read from /dev/dri, not video) and records the enrolment in /var/lib/remotix/group-enrollments.jsonl (child.c; the policy side is in ch. 13 “Login and its defences”). If the user is not in the group the log says that the session will be born blind.

    A group is read when a process is born. If the user already has a systemd --user manager (SSH, lingering) it keeps the old list, and so does gnome-shell or KWin started by it: the desktop would draw in software. render_grant.c bridges that without closing anything: for GNOME and KDE only (child.c tests desktop_session()), render_grant_needed() reads the manager's groups from /proc and /sys/fs/cgroup, and if it cannot open the node render_grant_add() writes an ACL entry for the user's primary group on every renderD* (the system.posix_acl_access attribute, written directly, so no setfacl is needed) and records it in /var/lib/remotix/render-grants. XFCE and LXQt need nothing: labwc is born from the child with fresh groups.

    • Group, not user: logind rewrites the named-user entries of those ACLs when the person in front of the machine changes; named-group entries it leaves alone.
    • Only a provably private group: an ACL for a group shared by several accounts would give the card to all of them. group_is_private() reads /etc/group and /etc/passwd only, and anything it cannot judge (a line over MAX_LINE, a NUL byte, a NIS compat line starting with +, a read error) counts as not private. A network account gets no grant, and its desktop is born in software.
    • Lifetime: the grant lives as long as the child, not the desktop. It is removed when the child ends (render_grant_remove()), by the start-up sweep (render_grant_sweep()) after a crash, and by remotix --drop-render-grants (render_grant_drop_all()) at package removal (debian/remotix.prerm). The nodes live in devtmpfs, so a reboot clears every ACL.
    • Declared limits: a device recreated while the desktop lives (driver reload, hotplug) loses the grant; removing the grant does not close descriptors already open.
    i
    NVIDIA device files. NVIDIA's proprietary driver opens the card through /dev/nvidia* devices with group and mode set by module parameters, not through /dev/dri alone. The code of this tree does not handle that case, and DECISIONS-11.md §11.38 records it as a known limit, not measured on a real NVIDIA machine for the device files (the rest of the NVIDIA route was measured on Ubuntu 26.04, 5–6 Oct 2026, with an earlier version of the code).

    7.5 · The encoding test: remotix --encoding-test

    The package asks the product itself whether the machine encodes a frame on the GPU. remotix --encoding-test [h264|hevc] [--node /dev/dri/…] [--encoding-route vaapi|vulkan|card] (child_test_encoding(), dispatched from main.c) goes through encoder_of() with H.264, 8 bits, no level ceiling and BGRx, encodes a 256×256 frame until bytes come out, and prints one JSON line on stdout (the log goes to stderr):

    The probe's answer (shape; keys as printed by test_exits() in child.c)
    {"outcome":"hardware","encoder":"h264_vaapi","route":"vaapi","node":"/dev/dri/renderD128",
 "reason":"…","codec":"h264","offered":"hevc,h264","hevc":"hardware","h264":"hardware",
 "hevc_route":"vaapi","h264_route":"vaapi"}

    outcome is hardware or none; encoder is the component opened; route the route that encoded; node the render node; reason the reason in words; offered what the server would offer the browser with the same arguments; hevc and h264 with hevc_route and h264_route give the same answer per codec.

    «hardware» is said only if the component accepts GPU surfaces (codificatore_in_hardware()), a frame came out with bytes, and the bytes were read back (read_from_stream). The frames of the test are shared with the startup probe and with the per-session test of node_of_codec() (probe_frames()): one test, not two that drift. Permissions matter: without the node's group a user sees none where root would see hardware, so the probe must run with the identity in question.

    Where the package uses it. debian/remotix.preinst refuses a new installation when the kernel lists no DRM render node (/sys/class/drm/renderD*), and debian/remotix.postinst runs remotix --encoding-test h264 under a 30 s timeout at the first configuration (with MESA_SHADER_CACHE_DISABLE=true, so that no shader cache is written in root's folders) and, if it does not exit 0, prints that the card did not encode a test frame and what to check (the message names va-driver-all for Intel and AMD, or NVIDIA's own driver). It never makes apt fail, because the driver may arrive with the Recommends configured after the package. On Ubuntu 26.04 va-driver-all is in universe and pulls only the Intel drivers; the VA-API driver for AMD comes with Mesa (mesa-libgallium, in main, which provides va-driver), so the package Recommends va-driver-all alone, without the alternative, or apt would take the Recommends as satisfied by Mesa and an Intel card would encode nothing (comment of debian/control, checked in clean containers on 18 Nov 2026). The package is described in ch. 15 “The package”.

    i
    Comment against code. the comment above test_exits() in child.c (around line 7055) still lists the per-codec keys as hevc_strada and h264_strada, but the code prints hevc_route and h264_route. The manual follows the code.

    7.6 · VA-API without libavcodec

    vadirect.c talks to libva (MIT) directly and does the four things a media library would: configure the driver, fill the sequence, picture and slice parameters, write the stream headers, and run begin/render/end for each frame. Its governing rule, from the file's comments, is to produce the same kind of stream as the library it replaced, field by field, so that the browser receives what it was tested with.

    Headers are passed to the driver as packed headers; VaDirectDeclaration records the mask the driver declares and the one in force, the surface alignment (16 for H.264, the CTB for HEVC), whether HEVC P frames are coded as generalised-B slices (p_come_b, iHD) and the input fourcc (NV12 or P010).

    i
    The AMD driver rewrites the headers. the comments record that on Mesa radeonsi the driver reads REMOTIX's packed headers and regenerates them, and that the cropping window Mesa does not write is fixed afterwards on the bytes (7.10 “Bytes, levels and the confession”). The comment dates from Mesa 25.0.7; whether it still holds with Mesa 26.0.8 is not verified, and on the Radeon of the virtual machines the encoder takes the Vulkan route, so this code path was not exercised there.

    The padding past the canvas. The card encodes a picture a little larger than the screen (the sides are rounded up, H.264 to 16, HEVC to the coding block; a 1080-row screen goes out as 1088 rows) and the decoder is told to hide the extra strip. The hidden strip still takes part in the compression, so what is in it can leak into the last visible row or column. convert_on_gpu() adds, in the same GPU step that turns RGB into the encoder's YUV, up to three layers that copy the last row, the last column and the corner pixel into the hidden strip. REMOTIX_VPP_PADDING set to 0 switches this off (read in encoder.c); the layers are also dropped for the rest of the encoder's life if the driver refuses them once. The comments record that with more than one layer AMD changes conversion engine (a shader instead of the encoder) at a small per-frame cost, and Intel is unchanged; those figures were taken on earlier builds (Mesa 25.0.7 on the AMD side, ffmpeg as the reference) and were never taken again on Ubuntu 26.04, which has libva 2.23 and Mesa 26.0.8. A canvas already aligned has no layers.

    7.7 · The Vulkan Video encoder

    vulkanvideo.c uses VK_KHR_video_encode_queue with the H.264 and H.265 encode extensions, the Vulkan loader and the system driver, and nothing else. It is the route for cards whose driver does not encode through VA-API, and every vendor that encodes in Vulkan gets the same code.

    i
    Which route the card takes. on the same machine, which card is used decides which route is taken: the virtual machines with the Radeon take Vulkan Video, the real machine with Intel graphics takes VA-API. Both routes have been seen working on Ubuntu 26.04, but on different benches; no machine with an AMD card was run through VA-API on Ubuntu 26.04 (forced with --encoding-route vaapi): not verified. At startup of the virtual machines the service writes «THIS SERVER CANNOT ENCODE VIDEO … /dev/dri/renderD128 does not open» and about 2 s later «the card arrived 2 s after startup … HEVC: yes via vulkan · H.264: yes via vulkan»: the card's driver is still loading, and the retry described in 7.2 “Codecs and their negotiation” closes it by itself.

    Cards that refuse linear buffers. vulkanvideo_card_rejects_linear() asks whether the card's GBM can create a LINEAR|RENDERING buffer; if not, vulkanvideo_modifiers() lists the non-linear modifiers the card can import and sample, and the capture offers them (ch. 6 “Screen capture”). Intel and Radeon never take this branch.

    The bench switch. REMOTIX_VULKAN_CONVERSION set to copy forces the shader to write into an intermediate image that is then copied, even where it could write the encoder's input directly. It exists to measure that branch; the product's choice is the one read from the driver. The shader's SPIR-V is a generated header, and the script that regenerates it (cited in the Makefile and in the shader's comment as benches/19-vulkan/19-shader.sh) is not part of this tree.

    7.8 · BT.709 colour conversion

    The capture delivers RGB and the encoders want YUV 4:2:0. The conversion is always BT.709, from full-range RGB to limited-range YUV (Y 16 to 235, Cb and Cr 16 to 240; at 10 bits 64 to 940 and 64 to 960), and the stream's VUI says so. Who converts depends on the route.

    The arithmetic (colors709.c and the shader): coefficients in fixed point with SCALE = 15 fractional bits so each fits an int16 for pmaddwd; luma (YR 5983, YG 20127, YB 2032) sums to 28142 = 219/255 · 32768, so white gives 235 and black 16; Cb (−3298, −11094, 14392) and Cr (14392, −13072, −1320) each sum to 0, so every grey is exactly 128. Chroma is the sum of each horizontal pair, filtered vertically with a 1-3-3-1 tent over four rows, rounded to nearest. At 10 bits the matrix is computed at 10 bits and P010 stores the ten bits high in sixteen. x86-64 always has SSE2, so there is no runtime dispatch (COLORS709_SSE2); other architectures run the same arithmetic in plain C with the same bytes.

    !
    The 1088-row scaling. leaving the VPP regions NULL means «the whole surface», and the destination surface is aligned (1920×1088 on iHD for 1080p): the VPP would then scale 1080 rows to 1088, a slightly blurred, slightly stretched desktop with no log line. Both regions are the canvas, and the source is the canvas size (comment in encoder.c).
    i
    Radeon VPP. the comments record that the Radeon's VPP loses on chroma against the CPU reference; with Vulkan on AMD the shader does the conversion instead.
    i
    Gamma 2.2 on GNOME 50. the stream of Mutter 50 declares colorPrimaries = BT709 and transferFunction = GAMMA22 and Mutter composes SDR with gamma 2.2 (read in the source, 6.6 “PipeWire negotiation, resize and wake-up”). colors709.c and the shader use the BT.709 matrix and ignore the transfer tag, as before. Whether the result differs visibly from Debian was not compared: not verified.

    7.9 · Writing the bitstream headers

    bit_writer.c knows no codec: it knows bits, Exp-Golomb and the 00 00 03 rule. Which fields to write and in which order is in vadirect.c, with the standard's clause beside each line. It is the mirror of the BitReader in encoder.c, which reads back what was produced.

    A field that does not fit sets overflowed and whoever closes the NAL sees it: a truncated header looks like a header.

    The cropping window rewrite

    The comments record that on a Radeon with Mesa radeonsi, HEVC at 2544×1344 produced a stream declaring 2560×1344: the card codes the multiple of its 64-pixel block and does not write the conformance window. The byte check rightly refuses a stream whose size differs from the canvas, so the session would stay black. border_in_place() decides on the first SPS of each encoder context: if the stream is larger than the canvas by less than 64 pixels on each side and by even amounts, the window is written. rewrite_sps_with_crop() re-reads the SPS up to the cropping flag, rewrites the head identically, sets the flag with the four offsets (in chroma units), copies the tail bit by bit to the stop bit, and puts the NAL back with its emulation bytes. Only keyframes carry an SPS, so only they are touched; any other mismatch remains an error.

    7.10 · Bytes, levels and the confession

    Pure Annex-B and no description. Every keyframe carries its parameter sets in front (H.264: SPS, PPS, IDR; HEVC: VPS, SPS, PPS, IDR), so a client that attaches late decodes from the first key it sees. The stream is described in ch. 5 “The RCP/1 protocol”.

    Before any byte leaves, bitstream_ok() checks it, because a decoder fed the wrong shape does not complain: it paints black, or at the old size.

    • the frame starts with a start code (not a length prefix);
    • a keyframe has its parameter sets before the IDR;
    • the SPS is read with the bit reader (read_h264_sps(), read_hevc_sps()), and the depth and the displayed size in the bytes must equal what was requested; the size coded and the size displayed are kept apart (encoded_width and stream_width: on radeonsi 1080p is coded as 1088 and cropped);
    • a frame larger than FRAME_CAP (16 MiB) is never sent.

    The confession. codificatore_confessione() returns what the encoder actually did, from two independent witnesses: the context (component opened, route, vendor, entry point verified, size limits, rate-control mask and mode read back, working point, maximum rate, VBV) and the bytes (depth, profile, level, tier, sizes, chroma format, codec_string). If they disagree the component disobeyed: has_obeyed becomes false (the reason is in why_no) and nothing is sent.

    The level is imposed, then verified. RCP/1 says the server must not emit a level above the client's video.level, and the browser does not enforce it, so the check is the server's. imposed_level() translates the ceiling into the codec's alphabet, the encoder writes it, and the child logs the level read from the bytes in decimal next to the client's. The declared cost: a level's frame-rate limit can be exceeded, because the encoder keeps running at MOTION_FPS = 60; halving the rate would change what the user sees and is not done. The largest canvas, 4096×2304, is exactly the MaxFS of H.264 levels 5.1 and 5.2 (36864 macroblocks); for HEVC it is above the picture size of level 5.1 in the encoder's own table (8 912 896 samples), and the imposed level is written all the same.

    A change of negotiated depth, level ceiling or capture channel order (BGRx and RGBx) between two clients of the same session rebuilds the encoder, because these are fixed at opening; the next frame is a key.

    7.11 · Keyframes on demand

    The GOP is infinite (chiavi_ogni = 0): periodic keyframes are bandwidth spent on an insurance the protocol already buys, and on a bad line keys sent by the clock are the spiral RCP/1 forbids. A keyframe is produced exactly when one is owed.

    A keyframe on a still desktop has nothing to encode, because the compositor sends nothing: the child wakes the stream so a frame arrives (ch. 6 “Screen capture”).

    7.12 · Resizing the encoder and the frame ceiling

    codificatore_ridimensiona() reopens the encoder at the new size; the first frame after is a true key. The size it receives has already been checked by rcp_size_allowed(): at least RCP_CANVAS_MIN_W×RCP_CANVAS_MIN_H (320×240), at most RCP_CANVAS_MAX_W×RCP_CANVAS_MAX_H (4096×2304; the declared limit of the product is 3K), even sides; a larger request is reduced (the side that overflows goes to the maximum, the other stays), a smaller one is refused. The driver's own maximum is still read at every opening (max_size_w, max_size_h), and vulkan_fit() compares the canvas with the card's limits.

    The frame ceiling. FRAME_CAP is 16 × 1024 × 1024 bytes. A frame that exceeds it is re-encoded at lower quality and never sent; the ladder (lower_quality(), CRF_STEP = 9, MAX_REENCODES = 3) and its way back are in ch. 8 “Quality, degradation and budget”.

    Encoding at a size that is not a multiple of the block: H.264 writes the cropping window itself; HEVC relies on the driver and, where the driver does not write it, on the rewrite of the previous section. With Vulkan the capture slabs on labwc stay at the maximum canvas across resizes (ch. 6 “Screen capture”).

    7.13 · Encoder timings, constants and verification status

    Every encoded frame carries its costs separately, so that a drop in frame rate can be attributed. They are logged for the first frame and summarised afterwards; performance figures with their hardware are in ch. 19 “Performance and capacity”.

    +
    Diagnosis. the log area of the encoder is video; the line that starts with opened: names the codec, depth, component, node, vendor and (on VA-API) the entry point actually in force. remotix --encoding-test with --encoding-route vulkan or --encoding-route vaapi reproduces one route in isolation.

    What was verified, and what was not

    • Verified (Ubuntu 26.04): the four desktops with real browsers through prove/all.sh, and in particular prove/check-media.py «codec» (the line media/codec is green in the round of 26-27 Nov 2026 on the four virtual machines; Chrome 156 and Firefox 153.7 negotiate H.264 avc1.640033 at 8 bits on the test machines), which reads from the journal which codec, level and GPU node the server negotiated and that the picture is sharp at the default quality; on the virtual machines with the Radeon, the opened: lines of the encoding test for HEVC and H.264 via Vulkan Video; on the real Kubuntu live image with Intel graphics, HEVC via VA-API; installation, remove and purge in the test machines (the package check check-package.py does not run in the virtual-machine bench, which skips it).
    • Known behaviour without a card: on the virtual machines, at service start, the card's driver is still loading and the log says the server cannot encode video; about 2 s later the retry of rootside.c finds the card (7.2 “Codecs and their negotiation”). A machine with no card at all was not run on Ubuntu; the Debian notes recorded the error repeating every 2 s, which loop writes it was not traced.
    • Not verified: NVIDIA on this tree (measured on Ubuntu 26.04 on 5–6 Oct 2026, with an earlier version of the code); the VA-API route on an AMD card on Ubuntu; a virtual machine with no video card at all (the refusal at installation is in the package scripts, not exercised on Ubuntu here); a canvas at 4096×2304 end to end (the test browser's decoder stops at 3840×2160); AV1 (not offered); the padding layers' effect by eye on AMD in this build; the render group and ACL grant on machines with lingering users on Ubuntu.
    Chapter 8

    Quality, degradation and budget

    8.1 · The quality contract

    REMOTIX does not chase a bitrate or a quality score. It follows a short contract written by the owner in SPECS.md and in DECISIONS.md: what may be spent when there is not enough, in which order, and what must never be spent. Every mechanism of this chapter exists to keep one line of that contract, and each one writes in the log, at startup, whether it is on and with which number.

    The numbers of SPECS.md §3 (a minimum image of 480p, 25 frames/s, 24 bit; a desired image of 4K, 60 frames/s, 10 bit per channel; 50 ms for the server's own piece of the latency; a network floor of 30 Mbit/s) are design goals, not measured promises. What the code really uses are the constants named in this chapter. The shipped stream is H.264 or HEVC, 8 bit (ch. 7 “Video encoding”), and the capture asks for MOTION_FPS = 60 frames/s. Bandwidth is a premise; the harder case the mechanisms react to is a line that loses, reorders and jitters, and most of them therefore watch queues and not Mbit/s.

    8.2 · Where quality is decided

    Quality is not decided in one place. The encoder lives in the per-user child process; the budget and the admission live in the server's main loop (main.c; in the default two-process server that is the network side, ch. 2 “Overall architecture”); the line-facing regulators live in the WebTransport layer; and the last word, what reaches the screen, is the page's. Each piece decides only on what it can measure locally.

    Three of these live in the child, which is a separate program started with execve and a freshly composed environment: they cannot travel as environment variables. children_phase9() stores them and the child's command line carries --quality-recovery, --bandwidth-cap-mbit and --no-audio-silence when it is built. Every switch writes its value in force at startup, on and off: «switched off» and «never had to act» must not look the same in the log. Extra server options go in REMOTIX_OPTIONS of a drop-in under /etc/remotix/remotix.conf.d/ (debian/remotix.conf, debian/remotix.service); there is no other road to a value.

    Switching on the budget (the numbers are an example, not a recommendation)
    # /etc/remotix/remotix.conf.d/capacity.conf
REMOTIX_OPTIONS=--budget-mpixel-s 480 --reserve 0.5 --session-cap 8

    8.3 · Encoder rate control

    By default the encoder runs at a constant QP of 26 (QP_HARDWARE in child.c, mode CODIFICATORE_QUALITA_QP), with no bitrate, no buffer and no rate controller. With --bandwidth-cap-mbit N it switches to a rate controller with a ceiling: QVBR on VA-API, VBR on Vulkan Video, which has no QVBR.

    Constant QP is the direct translation of I1 and of «never coarsen»: the quantiser is fixed, so the image of a quiet desktop never gets worse, and the bandwidth is simply what comes out. The comments of encoder.c record measurements on the earlier test machine (2560×1080, Intel iHD, QP 26): the real desktop moving at full screen cost 0.204 Mbit/s and a film with grain at full screen cost 58.7 Mbit/s, which is why a cap that bit on ordinary content would be the wrong default and the cap is for the hard case only. Those numbers were not re-measured for this tree.

    The three numbers of the cap are derived from the floor given on the command line, never written by hand:

    The mode is asked for by name (wanted_bitrate_mode()) and checked against the mask the driver declares: on VA-API the declared rate-control bits are read with vaGetConfigAttributes and printed in clear, and a mode the driver does not declare makes the encoder fail loudly instead of falling back to a mode nobody chose. cap_in_three_numbers() refuses a working point not below the wire and a non-positive buffer, and reservoir_within_50_ms() refuses a buffer longer than 50 ms. On Vulkan the cap becomes VBR with the requested QP as the floor of the controller (open_vulkan_card()); without the cap the card must declare CQP (vulkan_fit()). Every 10 s (BANDWIDTH_WINDOW_US) the encoder also writes a «video bandwidth» line from the bytes it produced: the third witness that the ceiling is obeyed.

    !
    Which floor. the value passed is a floor, not a ceiling, and the comments of encoder.c still describe the cap with 20 Mbit/s while main.c and SPECS.md name 30 Mbit/s. The three quota constants make the derivation independent of which one the operator passes.

    Not settled: the cap and the quality rise are off by default and have not been judged on a real desktop since this tree began; max_frame_size, which QVBR would accept, is deliberately not used.

    8.4 · The 16 MiB frame cap and the quality ladder

    RCP/1 forbids a video frame larger than 16 MiB: the sender must re-encode it at a lower quality and log it, never send it. That rule is the only thing that moves the QP of a running encoder.

    When a frame comes out of the card above FRAME_CAP (16 × 1024 × 1024 bytes), compress_common() logs it, records the rung on which the cap bit (failed_quality), and lower_quality() raises the QP by CRF_STEP = 9, capped at 51. Changing quality closes and reopens the card context (change_quality()), so the next frame is always a keyframe. The ladder from the default is 26, 35, 44, 51. A lossless request leaves at EMERGENCY_CRF = 24.

    The comments record why the step is 9: with a step of 6, a 7680×4320 keyframe of almost incompressible content measured 16.654 MiB at QP 38, over the cap, and 11.056 MiB at QP 44. The canvas has since been limited to 4096×2304 (RCP_CANVAS_MAX_W, RCP_CANVAS_MAX_H), and the ladder is a safety net for exceptional frames, not a working mechanism. At startup the encoder writes the ladder it will walk, with the values in force, by simulating lower_quality() instead of printing a hand-written copy: two drafts of one rule would diverge on the day someone retunes the step. Every descent is declared in the log (area video) with the frame size and its percentage of the cap.

    8.5 · Quality recovery after the cap

    Without a way back the QP is a ratchet: one exceptional frame would leave the session at the bottom of the ladder for hours, with a quiet desktop permanently coarse. --quality-recovery (encoder_quality_rises()) adds the climb; it is off by default because it changes what the user sees.

    raise_quality() runs at the entry of the next frame, never with a packet in hand (closing the context frees its bytes). It climbs one step at a time and never above the quality the caller requested. A relapse right after a climb doubles the wait (recently_risen). If the context does not reopen at the new value, it falls back to the old one: climbing is optional, and a cure that kills the session when it fails is worse than the defect.

    Not settled: the three numbers are declared sufficient, not right.

    8.6 · The video queue threshold

    Each video frame travels on its own unidirectional QUIC stream (ch. 4 “Transport”). When a newer frame is produced while an older delta still has bytes in our send queue, RCP.md §5.1 allows (it does not require) a RESET_STREAM of the old one. video_clear_out() decides when to use that permission: an older delta is abandoned only if the video queue cannot drain within WT_CLEAR_THRESHOLD_MS = 100 ms.

    The decision of video_clear_out()
    wait_ms = video_queue_bytes * smoothed_rtt / cwnd       (from ngtcp2; queue_drain_ms())
        = video_queue_bytes / WT_FLOOR_BYTE_MS          (fallback: no rtt or cwnd yet, 3750 bytes/ms = 30 Mbit/s)
wait <= threshold            -> keep every delta (counted, one log line per state change)
wait >  threshold            -> abandon the live deltas still in our queue
wait >  threshold, a KEY in queue -> keep the deltas behind it

    Only bytes still in our own queue are considered; what has already been handed to ngtcp2 is not taken back. The last rule exists because a large keyframe in the queue pushes the wait above the threshold by itself, abandoning the deltas behind it does not shorten it but opens a gap, which requests another large keyframe: abandons would climb by one per keyframe until the dead line fired (the keyframe spiral that RCP.md §5.2 names). Behind a keyframe the deltas are kept, and braking production is left to the rate regulator. --clear-threshold-ms 0 restores abandonment at every newer frame. The comments record a price of up to 160 ms of drift on a bad line and zero on a healthy one.

    8.7 · The rate regulator

    The rate regulator is the mechanism that lowers the frame rate on a local fact: backlog, the number of live, non-key deltas that still have bytes in our send queue, read when a new frame arrives and before video_clear_out().

    rate_brake() returns «do not send» when backlog reaches WT_RATE_SLOTS = 2: one frame of overlap is allowed, two left behind are not. Nothing comes from outside, no loss rate, reordering or client silence can distort it, and there is no state to climb back: the quantity is re-read at every frame, so the episode ends by itself when the queue empties. Keyframes never pass through it; they have their own pacing.

    The congestion algorithm was never chosen: transport.c keeps ngtcp2's default. On Wi-Fi a loss-based algorithm reads radio loss as congestion, which can manufacture the backlog this regulator measures (ch. 4 “Transport”). Not settled: WT_RATE_SLOTS = 2 is declared, not calibrated, and the proper fix of the cost (stop encoding instead of dropping after encoding) would need the decision to reach the child.

    8.8 · Keyframe request pacing

    A keyframe is about ten times a delta. Asking for one at every sign of trouble is the spiral RCP.md §5.2 names, so both ends pace their requests.

    key_interval_ms() first looks at a fact: if the previous keyframe still has bytes in our queue, the answer is the 2-second ceiling. Otherwise it computes from ngtcp2's own cwnd and smoothed RTT how long a keyframe of the last size needs to leave, applies the margin, and never goes below 150 ms or above 2 s. Where there is bandwidth the cure declares itself inert; on a narrow line the image stays broken longer after a loss, which is the price, and in exchange the audio datagrams are not starved by keyframes asked faster than they can leave.

    8.9 · The dead line

    This cure does not decide how well the desktop is seen but whether the connection still exists. The owner's decision is that a line losing in bursts is not a slow line but a broken one: the wire drops and the user signs in again. It is on by default and switched off with --no-dead-line.

    dead_line_judge() evaluates both from monotonic local counters and ngtcp2's received-packet counter. When either fires, dead_line_fires() writes one line starting with dead-line that carries every number of the decision, and the transport, the only owner of the QUIC connection, closes it. The page then returns to the login form (ch. 9 “The browser page”). The comments record that the stall threshold sits 5.0 times above the longest empty second of a line that holds and 2.9 times below the freeze of a line that serves nobody (measured on emulated lines on the earlier test machine); a wrong value would throw out someone who is working, so whoever changes WT_LM_STALL_MS must measure those two margins again.

    The line that says why a connection closed. When a QUIC connection is reaped, close_why() in transport.c adds the reason to the log line «connection with … closed (N left) — …»: who closed it (the peer or the server), the QUIC error or, for a close by silence, «idle timeout (silence)»; for a CRYPTO error the TLS alert is named (42 bad_certificate, 45 certificate_expired, 46 certificate_unknown, 48 unknown_ca and others) and the line ends with «TLS handshake COMPLETED» or «NOT completed». The reason text sent by the peer is cut to printable ASCII and 60 characters. The function decides nothing and changes no behaviour (4.14 “Why a connection closed”).

    !
    Loss is not a cause. DECISIONS.md also lists «copious loss within 1–2 s» as a cause, and the code does not use it: the comments record that the loss fraction was refuted by its own bench, because on a reordering line pkt_lost over pkt_sent measures reordering, not loss. The fraction stays in the log line as permille=, a witness rather than a judge.

    8.10 · Ghost eviction and audio silence

    Two of the line-facing cures change nothing the user sees, and are on by default.

    The eviction removes a false sentence rather than adding one: the old refusal claimed the user was connected from another device when it was usually their own dead session.

    8.11 · The composition budget

    Without a budget the server accepts everyone and starves everyone together: the header of budget.h records that on a saturated scene the eleventh user entered with zero refusals and the first session fell from 39.60 to 0.96 frames/s. budget.c computes, before a desktop is started, whether the machine can afford one more. It is off by default and does not tune itself.

    The currency is the composed pixel, not the encoded one. The header records, for the Intel UHD 770 of the earlier test machine, that the encoder alone held 1.86 Gpixel/s in H.264 while composition (the render engine, saturated by gnome-shell) held 0.97: the neck is upstream of REMOTIX, and the budget can only count composition. The figures are from GNOME on that one machine.

    The admission rule of budget.c (budget_count_inside() and budget_count_verdict())
    fits(inside, new)  <=>  sum of demand(inside) + worst(new)  <=  C * (1 + BUDGET_TOLERANCE)
                         AND  no tenant's median delay > BUDGET_STRAIN_DELAY_MS

demand(t)   = worst(t)                              if t never delivered, or has no delay sample
            = max(delivered(t), F * worst(t))       otherwise
worst(t)    = canvas_width * canvas_height * BUDGET_MAX_FPS / 1e6    Mpixel/s

    The accumulator. deposit_frame() in main.c already receives every frame of every child with width, height and capture instant, so no new channel is needed: budget_deposit() is called there before the frame is broadcast, without an «is someone watching» guard. That is deliberate: a session whose client has left keeps encoding until its seat expires (a ghost) and costs the GPU as much as the others. The delay is capture to server, an upper bound of the compositor's hold time.

    The reserve. An idle session does not cost zero: it costs F times its worst case, because idle sessions wake up together. The header tabulates, for the climb it was calibrated on, F = 0 as blind to wake-up, F = 0.5 as the chosen value (cap 6 saturated, 10 idle), F = 1 with one false no. Unknown is not zero: a tenant that has not yet delivered a full 2-second window, or has no delay sample, is counted at its worst case. The newcomer is counted at the smaller of the stage canvas (CANVAS_W × CANVAS_H = 1920×1080 in main.c) and its video.max_size (wt_max_size_of()), because the real canvas is decided later, at SESSION. A missing monotonic clock gives BUDGET_UNKNOWN, which admits and logs: a budget that refused for having failed to measure would make the user pay for the server's fault.

    A canvas that grows. recanvas_fits_budget() asks the same question again for a new FIT_CANVAS that exceeds the stage canvas: the session's own stage is left out of the sum and the new size is judged as a newcomer's, and if it does not fit the client is answered NOT_NOW and keeps the canvas it has (the canvas_fits hook, wt_canvas_fits_hook()). With the budget off it passes.

    !
    Off, and not self-tuning. the budget never calibrates itself. Before the machine has given way once, the highest capacity read is a lower bound, not a ceiling. Whoever types --budget-mpixel-s N declares that N Mpixel/s of composition were measured at saturation on that machine. Passing the encoder's number instead would admit about 22 sessions where six fit on the measuring machine.

    8.12 · Admission: the session cap and the budget

    A refusal decided after the desktop has started is not a refusal: it is a login followed by an eviction. Both limits are therefore checked in delivery_verdict() before children_ensure_from() starts the child.

    The two refusals are deliberately different: two different facts may not share an outcome. A child that cannot be born for another reason (a name NSS does not resolve, uid 0, fork failing) also ends in 0x0E, with the cause in the log. On Ubuntu 26.04 the code has more roads to 0x0E: the page's own comment (REASON_TEXT in page.html) counts six: an unknown layout, a full slot register, a canvas that cannot be granted, memory exhausted on the control channel, all stages busy, and «the desktop's compositor is not installed» (XFCE or LXQt without labwc: session_missing_component() is tested in main.c before the child is spawned, so no process and no logind session exist). Four more uses are outside that count (as in ch. 5 “The RCP/1 protocol”): the previous desktop of the user still closing (delivery_verdict()), logind not able to say whether a local session exists, a failed birth, and the stage refused because the user's scale is not 1 and the repair failed: stage_refused_by_child() sends 0x0E to the clients of that user and the graphical session is closed (ch. 6 “Screen capture”). The farewell of a session that ended is sent with wt_dismiss_user_session_over(): a login of the same name still waiting for PAM, or whose «no» is being kept for the fixed second, is skipped, so it is not given a false 0x10 in place of its true 0x0E; a login already admitted onto the ended session gets the farewell when its fixed second ends. The refusals of this section use wt_dismiss_user(). Neither limit is checked on a resume: a user whose stage already exists is already inside both counts, and refusing their reattach would be a false no. The refusal is sent after transport_verdict(), through wt_dismiss_user(): that order lets the admitted verdict reset the failed-password counter of that user on that address (login_resolve() in rcp.c; the counters of the address itself and of the /48 are not reset), and the client never sees ADMITTED, only the farewell. The body of the FAREWELL carries the figures for the log; the page shows its own phrase (ch. 5 “The RCP/1 protocol”). The phrase for 0x06 promises only what is true at the gate: at that point the only canvas number is video.max_size, the decoder's ceiling, so shrinking the window would get the same refusal.

    --session-cap N sizes the four tables that count a user (the attached seats in rcp.c, the children in child.c, the presence table in main.c, the stages in webtransport.c). MAX_IN_FLIGHT in helper.c stays separate on purpose: it counts PAM verifications in flight, not sessions. The count of refusals is written even with the budget off, because reading zero there is the fact that proves the product behaves as before.

    8.13 · Rate and size guards: hsrate, msgrate, linebudget, dimcheck

    Four small headers, each with no dependency and no clock of its own (the caller passes the time), bound the work an unauthenticated or authenticated peer can ask of the single-threaded main loop, so that one noisy source cannot take frame rate away from everybody else. They are written so that a unit test can include each alone. The unit benches the comments name are not part of this repository.

    encbackoff.h belongs to the same family: enc_death_wait_ms() returns the wait before an encoder is made again after it died, doubling from ENC_RETRY_MIN_MS = 500 ms to ENC_RETRY_MAX_MS = 10 s, and the count of deaths goes back to zero only after a frame was really sent (ch. 7 “Video encoding”). The handshake limits are part of ch. 13 “Login and its defences” as well.

    8.14 · Frames that are not encoded, and what is adapted

    Two producers of unnecessary frames are cut before they reach the encoder, and one consumer-side limit is exposed to the client.

    • Empty damage. When the compositor declares that nothing changed (SPA_META_VideoDamage present and empty), damage_classify() counts the frame in empty_damage and the buffer goes back to PipeWire without being encoded (ch. 6 “Screen capture”).
    • Frames asked again, not dropped. On KDE the opposite case is also handled: when KWin's buffer numbers show a hole, the next frame goes out as «all changed» and, if no picture follows, a poke makes KWin draw one (6.5 “The lost frame (KWin)”). It adds at most one frame request every 200 ms and only after a hole, never on a still desktop.
    • The «unchanged» filter (unchanged.h, KDE only). A frame whose damaged rectangles hold the same bytes as the last frame that went out is not encoded. The filter measures its own cost: the mean cost of a look over a window (the first window of UC_COST_FIRST = 30 looks, then every UC_COST_EVERY = 300) switches it off if it exceeds UC_COST_HARD_US = 10 000 µs whatever it holds back, or UC_COST_MAX_US = 3000 µs when it held back fewer than one look in UC_YIELD_DIV = 4; a switch-off for cost re-arms after UC_REARM_MS = 5000 ms, and after UC_STRIKES_MAX = 3 strikes it is off for the capture. A held-back frame goes out after UC_REFRESH_MS = 250 ms at most. The full table of limits is in ch. 6 “Screen capture”.
    • Decoder pace. With --decoder-pace the server declares video.pace; a client whose decoder queue stays behind may send PACE (0x0012) with a ceiling clamped to RCP_PACE_FLOOR_FPS = 5 to RCP_PACE_TOP_FPS − 1 = 59 frames/s, and the child then takes fewer frames from the capture before encoding (pace_set()), so no frame is thrown away and no keyframe is owed. A keyframe owed is never held back. It is off by default and RCP.md §13 marks it as proposed.

    What the product adapts, and what it does not

    Capacity numbers for this tree, per card and desktop, are in ch. 19 “Performance and capacity”.

    What was verified, and what was not

    • Verified on Ubuntu 26.04: with the budget off (the default), prove/check-media.py «two-sessions-budget» has two users animating at the same time and requires that neither goes below 25 frames/s and that the first does not lose more than 30 % of what it had alone; the checks of prove/all.sh were green on the four desktops in the round of 26-27 Nov 2026 on the virtual machines (GNOME 125 PASS and the accepted desktop/users-shell-and-environment, KDE, XFCE and LXQt 126 PASS); the dead line and the reconnection after a network drop are among the resilience lines of that round. The figures of the budget's own measurements quoted above are from the earlier test machine.
    • Not verified on Ubuntu: the budget switched on (the figures above are from the earlier test machine); the bandwidth cap and the quality rise on a real desktop; the decoder pace; a keyframe cap actually biting at 4096×2304; any of these on NVIDIA.
    Chapter 9

    The browser page

    9.1 · How the page is served

    The whole client is one file, src/page.html: the login page, the RCP/1 client, video decoding and drawing, audio, clipboard, keyboard, pointer and touch. Nothing is installed on the user's device and nothing else is downloaded: the page is the product's only client. The package installs it as /usr/share/remotix/page.html and the service starts with --page pointing at it (debian/rules, debian/remotix.service).

    Cross-origin isolation is a product requirement (SPECS.md §11.5), not a tuning option: without it Firefox and Safari round the page's timers to 1 ms, against a latency cap of 50 ms, and shared memory does not exist. With require-corp every sub-resource would have to declare its own policy; the simplest cure is to have none, which is why everything is inline. The isolation is inherited by the optional video worker, born from a Blob (measured 13 Aug 2026: crossOriginIsolated true inside the worker, timer grain 0.005 ms).

    page_open_fd() in page.c refuses to start if any marker is missing from the file, or if data-banned=" or data-remaining-ms=" occur more than once (a reader that searches the document for the first occurrence would read the wrong one). The fingerprint is the only server text that enters a JavaScript string, and it is base64 written by REMOTIX; the ban sentence never enters the script. A banned visitor is served the page anyway: the ban is not checked at accept, because the person must read the reason (SPECS.md §4.2). The TLS side, the certificates and the ban are described in ch. 4 “Transport”, ch. 13 “Login and its defences” and ch. 14 “Security model”.

    9.2 · Structure of page.html

    The file is about 14 000 lines and 0.9 MB (14 258 lines and 937 399 bytes on the Ubuntu tree), most of it comments that carry the reason and the measurement behind each rule, plus the embedded Opus decoder and the probe keyframes. The code is organised in blocks, and the three input blocks are “anchors”, each written inside its own markers.

    The page defines one main global, window.REMOTIX, an object to be read by checks and diagnostics (viewer the screen object, probing the probe results, stretches() the latency stretches, round_trip, video, declarations, logbook(), shortcuts, read_one_stream…): nothing in it changes what the page does. The input anchors meet through REMOTIX_INPUT (the input stream, set after SESSION), REMOTIX_CLASSIC, REMOTIX_POINTER and REMOTIX_SHORTCUTS.

    i
    Test switches, not settings. the switches exist so that a comparison changes one variable inside the same page; they are not per-browser or per-compositor options, and the product has one behaviour without them (the one exception, the video worker on desktop Firefox, is a documented default, not a switch). The fragment form (#…) never reaches the server, so it also works on a page served by any static server.

    9.3 · Layouts and the states of the document

    The page has one document and two input layouts, classic (mouse and physical keyboard, the desktop use) and touch (a finger as a trackpad, the phone use). The chapter ch. 10 “Input” describes what each layout sends; this section lists what the page itself changes in the document, because the style sheet is where the layout in force is read.

    The login page itself is a two-panel grid: a story panel, and a card with #username, #password and #signin-button and a footer line that the page fills with location.hostname (the server does not need to know under what name it is reached). Under 860 CSS px the two panels stack into one column and the story text and the list of points are hidden (only the logo and one line stay); under 420 px the padding shrinks. All text the user reads is in English (DECISIONS.md §10.32). The canvas #viewer exists from the start as a 16×16 element that is not displayed.

    Desktop dress is undone as carefully as it is put on. Whoever puts the desktop dress on must hide what the desktop replaces, and whoever switches a state on must know how to switch it off. back_to_form() (9.15 “End of session in the page”) removes data-viewer, releases pointer lock and full screen, returns the canvas to 16×16 and gives the focus back to the user name.

    Under body:not(.diagnostics) the log, the footnote .note and the shortcuts bar are not displayed, even though their text keeps accumulating. A visitor who has not asked for them sees no bar at the bottom of the desktop: 10.7 “Shortcuts the browser keeps” explains what that means for the one on-screen button the page has.

    9.4 · The connection sequence

    The login form has two fields and a button — #username, #password, #signin-button — plus #outcome for the outcome, #warning for the ban and #declaration for what the page declares about codecs and video. The ids are stable: the checks of prove/ find elements by id, not by text.

    1. Submit. The button is disabled, the outcome cleared; connect() runs. Whatever happens, the password field is emptied at the end: it is never kept, and never logged.
    2. WebTransport present? If not, the page says so and stops.
    3. Fingerprint. fingerprint() fetches /fingerprint before every attempt, because a tab left open for two weeks holds the fingerprint of a certificate already rotated. A 503 (server busy) is asked again up to twice, 1 s apart. If the fetch is rejected by the network (TypeError: nobody listens), it is tried once more after 1 s and then the page says that the server does not answer and does not open WebTransport (Firefox would otherwise wait the 30 s of its QUIC handshake). Any other failure falls back to the fingerprint served with the page, and says so in the log.
    4. WebTransport to https://<host>/rcp/1 with allowPooling: false and serverCertificateHashes: the browser checks the fingerprint, not a certificate chain — the only mechanism browsers offer to a server without a domain (RCP.md §4.1-bis).
    5. Listen first. Video streams, audio datagrams and clipboard streams are listened to before the handshake ends: a server that opened one before SESSION violates RCP §2.5, and the violation is only visible to someone already listening.
    6. HELLO with the capabilities (9.5 “Capabilities declared by the page”), after waiting for the codec probes. HERE_I_AM: a version other than 1 is refused with INCOMPATIBLE_VERSION before the password leaves.
    7. CREDENTIALS. REJECTED shows the reason and stops (a second attempt needs a new connection); a FAREWELL shows its reason and stops; ADMITTED continues.
    8. ATTACH carries the canvas to ask for (canvas_to_request()), the view (view_size()) and the keyboard layout (layout(), the value of the sign-in menu). SESSION says new or resumed, the granted canvas and the desktop name. A granted canvas different from the requested one is declared to the user (RCP §4.5 allows it).
    9. After SESSION: the single input stream is opened, the video is negotiated with the decoder, the first-frame watch starts, the control channel is read in a loop (listen_control()), and FIT_CANVAS is sent once for the window size.

    The keyboard layout is the value of the Keyboard menu of the sign-in form (select#keyboard, with the hint line #keyboard-hint). The menu lists the 33 layouts of the KEYBOARDS table (code and English name, sorted by name; the menu shows the names), exactly the codes that layout_from_browser() can return. layout_from_browser() (the former layout()) guesses a layout from navigator.language (en → us, except en-GB → gb and en-IE → ie; about thirty languages whose XKB name equals the ISO code pass through, a few are mapped, such as sv → se and da → dk; the rest falls back to us) and only presets the menu. A manual choice is stored in localStorage["remotix.keyboard"] (per browser and device) and, if the stored code is still in the table, presets the menu at the next load; storage that is blocked or holds junk means “not remembered”, without an error. layout() returns the menu's value if it is in the table and otherwise layout_from_browser(). ATTACH, the wire format and the server are unchanged; the menu is read once, at sign-in, so changing keyboard means signing out and in again. A page cannot know the physical keyboard, and the negotiation is described in 10.12 “Keyboard layout negotiation”. The input stream coalesces pointer moves: when the writer's desiredSize is at or below zero, a POINTER is held aside and replaced by the next one, and any key or button pushes it out first (measured from Samsung DeX on 14 Aug 2026: median round trip 135 ms but worst 2161 ms, a queue rather than a slow network). Keys and buttons are never dropped.

    Why a connection closed. When a QUIC connection ends, the server writes in its log who closed it and why (close_why() in transport.c; see ch. 8 “Quality, degradation and budget”): the peer or the server, the QUIC error, «idle timeout (silence)» for a silent line, and for a CRYPTO error the name of the TLS alert (42 bad_certificate, 45 certificate_expired, 46 certificate_unknown, 48 unknown_ca) with «TLS handshake COMPLETED» or «NOT completed».

    !
    The client's clock. the certificate the server makes for the session is valid from one hour before it was made (notBefore = now − 3600 s, certificates.c). The browser checks it against the clock of its own device: a device whose clock is more than an hour behind the server's gets «Opening handshake failed» and nothing else. The cure is to set the clock of the device; the log line above should then name a TLS alert (45, 46 or 42). The user manual lists the clock among the requirements.

    The page does not store the user name, the password or any session token: the only thing that persists after the tab closes is the keyboard choice (9.14 “What the page stores and what it declares”).

    9.5 · Capabilities declared by the page

    The HELLO capabilities say what this browser can do, measured where possible. An empty value is a protocol error (RCP §4.3), so a capability with nothing to say is omitted, and the omission is logged.

    Declaring something the browser cannot do does not give an error; it gives a black canvas or silence, because the server must choose within the intersection following the client's order. Declaring opus on an engine that cannot decode it makes the server send fifty datagrams a second into a decoder that cannot read them — and the PCM fallback, which exists to be Opus's positive control, never comes into play.

    9.6 · Choosing the codec on the pixel

    The codec is not chosen by asking the browser's APIs. It is chosen by decoding a real keyframe and reading the pixels back.

    Measured on 12 August 2026 on Firefox 140 ESR (the Debian browser; the Ubuntu rounds ran Firefox 153.7.0 and Chrome 156.0.8078.79 and did not repeat this measurement), for all seven HEVC strings: navigator.mediaCapabilities.decodingInfo() said supported, smooth and power-efficient; canPlayType() said “probably”; VideoDecoder.isConfigSupported() said false; and no pixel arrived. Three witnesses, two of them false and agreeing with each other. The page never uses the first two to choose a codec (decodingInfo() is called once at load, only to write the diagnostic MARK no-webcodecs log line about MSE; canPlayType() is not called at all). isConfigSupported is used as a filter only — when it says no the pixel never arrives, when it says yes it proves nothing (Chrome accepts a level-3.0 declaration on a 5.1 stream and paints anyway).

    The preference is PREFERENCE = ["hevc", "h264"]: HEVC where it paints, H.264 as the universal fallback; the server makes the final choice within the intersection. AV1 is not offered (DECISIONS.md §1.13-ter): Firefox for Android had neither HEVC nor AV1, H.264 is the only codec in hardware at both ends, and Firefox's AV1 decoder painted rectangular blocks where Chrome and dav1d were clean on the same bytes. Its RCP number, 2, stays reserved forever (CODEC_RCP): reusing it would make an old client paint garbage without an error. The H.264 string is avc1.640033 (High, level 5.1), the same the server derives from the SPS; level 5.0 (avc1.640032) cannot reach 3840×2160.

    If no codec reaches the pixel, video.codec is omitted and the server answers NOTHING_IN_COMMON; the page writes its own explanation first, because only the page knows which probe failed and why, and the password does not leave. Whether decoding happens in hardware is not observable from JavaScript, and the page never claims it. The server side of the choice is in ch. 7 “Video encoding”.

    9.7 · Measuring the decoder ceiling

    video.max_size is the largest frame the browser's decoder can bring to the pixel. It is not the screen size: a phone's decoder has limits its screen does not declare, and a desktop screen can be smaller than what its browser decodes.

    The screen size goes where it belongs, in the view of ATTACH. Putting the screen size in video.max_size produced a failure that no test page showed: on a screen 1010 pixels tall the server granted a 1794×1010 canvas while the stage captured 1920×1080, frames of the wrong size were refused, and the user saw nothing.

    If a codec paints at 64×48 but not even at 320×240, the page declares 320×240 and tells the user the image may not arrive at all. The cost of the ladder is logged on every load (probing.size.ms).

    The ceiling also limits what the page asks for. The result is kept as canvas_cap and canvas_to_request() brings the side that overflows it down to the ceiling (a phone 412×915 CSS at ratio 2.625 asks for 1072×2160, not 1072×2304), so that the server has nothing to reduce. With the ladder as it is, a browser that decodes the whole ladder declares 3840x2160 and cannot be granted the 4096×2304 maximum of 9.8 “Canvas and view”: the largest canvas a page can ask for through canvas_to_request() is the ladder's last rung, 3840×2160.

    !
    Open point. whether the ladder should stop at 3840×2160 or reach the protocol maximum of 4096×2304 has not been decided: the last rung was chosen to stay inside the declared level 5.1 (4096×2176 is its width limit), and the run of prove/all.sh of 17 Nov 2026 (Debian) showed the 3840×2160 ceiling of the test browser as the reason a check of the maximum size was not green; a canvas of 4096×2304 end to end has not been verified on Ubuntu (ch. 24 “Appendix C — Known issues and open points”).

    9.8 · Canvas and view

    Two sizes must never be confused. The canvas (canvas in the code) is the remote desktop's size: it belongs to the session, is fixed at attach and reattach, and is what the frames carry. The view (view) is how much the page has to draw in: it belongs to the connection and changes with the window.

    The canvas takes the size of the client's window at attach (DECISIONS.md §5.0-sexies). Scale 1 makes the coordinate conversion the identity, removes the black bands and the interpolated text, and the request at attach restarts the capture stream, which makes Mutter deliver a frame at once instead of after a long wait on a still scene. The canvas never changes while the session lives (§5.1-bis): resizing the window only rescales the image. Resizing an output live could not be done on every compositor and, where it works, it rearranges the user's windows; the owner did not want a product that behaves differently depending on the compositor. A new size is taken by reconnecting: the page asks for its window's size at every attach, and a resumed session takes it too. On KDE the compositor (KWin) runs nested inside a screenless labwc that REMOTIX starts, and at reattach REMOTIX resizes labwc's output, which KWin follows (§10.40, ch. 12 “The four desktops”). If the host cannot be resized the session keeps the canvas it was born with, the page rescales it, centred between black bands, and the server log says so.

    The maximum 4096×2304 is a protocol constant (RCP_CANVAS_MAX_W and its siblings in src/rcp.h): H.264 on the Intel card stops at 4096 per side and Firefox on Linux receives only H.264; 2304 is 16:9 at 4096 and the MaxFS of level 5.1. A larger window gets the maximum on the side that overflows (5120×2880 → 4096×2304, 5120×1440 → 4096×1440), shown at scale 1 with bands; the server applies the same rule in rcp_size_allowed(). Whether a 4096×2304 canvas is actually granted and shown has not been verified: the decoder ceiling of the browser used in prove/ is 3840×2160 (9.7 “Measuring the decoder ceiling”). Both are technical bounds: the declared limit of the product is 3K (the size actually used depends on the client).

    The canvas the server grants is checked. The page does not take the canvas of SESSION and CANVAS as it comes (a u32 per side): a width or height of zero, or above 4096×2304 (CANVAS_MAX_W × CANVAS_MAX_H), closes the session with PROTOCOL_ERROR, the same way the cursor's check does. RCP.md §4.5 and §7.1 never grant such a size, so the server that does is wrong or hostile, and a canvas of billions of pixels would only bring down the tab.

    html { overflow-y: scroll } keeps the vertical scrollbar always present, so turning the canvas on never changes clientWidth. The canvas has tabindex="-1", without which its focus() calls do nothing and the keyboard stays in the password field.

    i
    Not settled yet. a change of devicePixelRatio with the window still (page zoom, a window dragged to a screen with another scale) is not handled: the emulated test delivered no event at all, and a cure needs a measurement with real zoom. The VIEW message is never sent after a resize either: no server component reads it in RCP/1.

    9.9 · Asking for the canvas with FIT_CANVAS

    The canvas is requested once per session, at attach, with FIT_CANVAS. The server answers with CANVAS: adopted, or refused with a reason.

    The control channel and the video streams are independent QUIC streams, so a frame at the new size can arrive before the CANVAS that announces it. While an FIT_CANVAS is unanswered (canvas_waits, the pending canvas requests, > 0), a frame at an unannounced size is held (Viewer.hold()) and judged again when the answer arrives. With no request in flight, such a frame is PROTOCOL_ERROR at once: the condition is a request in flight, not a number of frames. The page compares a new request with the size it is going to, not the one in force (ask_canvas()): the rule was written when a window resize still sent a request, and today it serves the attach and the single NOT_NOW retry.

    9.10 · Receiving video frames

    Each video frame arrives on its own unidirectional stream, opened by the server in frame order. start_video() reads the incoming streams and read_one_stream() collects each one. The wire format is in ch. 5 “The RCP/1 protocol”; this is the page's side.

    The 28-byte video header (RCP.md §6.2), big-endian, read by Viewer.read_header()
    offset  size  field
 0      u16   type      0x0301 keyframe, 0x0302 delta
 2      u16   codec     1 hevc, 3 h264 (2 reserved: av1)
 4      u32   width
 8      u32   height
12      u32   number    frame number, 0 reserved, wraps to 1
16      u64   instant   server monotonic clock, microseconds
24      u32   input     last input id applied when captured (0 = none)
28      ...   Annex B data

    The reader of these 28 bytes is written from the protocol table, independently of the server's writer: two implementations of the same bytes are part of the referee, and a disagreement is a gift. Viewer.deliver() then applies the rules in a fixed order:

    1. type must be key or delta; codec must be the negotiated one; otherwise PROTOCOL_ERROR;
    2. the input field closes an input round trip (9.13 “Measurements and the diagnostics mode”);
    3. number 0 is a protocol error;
    4. order before size: a number not after the last delivered one (mod 2³²) is dropped without looking at its size — otherwise the keyframe that closes a tolerance window, overtaking older frames, would close the session;
    5. size: the canvas in force or a tolerated one; an unannounced size is held if an FIT_CANVAS is pending, a size that was in force and no longer is closes the session;
    6. a jump in numbers is a hole: one REQUEST_KEY with the last delivered number, repeated at most once a second while the hole stays open (Viewer.hole()); the last good image stays on screen, deltas are not even given to the decoder until a keyframe arrives (RCP §5.2) — a delta referencing a missing frame does not error, it just decays;
    7. a frame whose size differs from the decoder's configuration is decoded only if it is a keyframe at the canvas in force (then the decoder is reconfigured); otherwise it is dropped and treated as a hole;
    8. decode, with the server's instant as timestamp.

    9.11 · Decoding with WebCodecs

    Decoding uses one VideoDecoder per session, configured with the string the probe saw paint, the frame size and optimizeForLatency: true. Painting happens inside the decoder's output callback, not on requestAnimationFrame: an extra animation frame would add up to one display interval to a latency budget measured in tens of milliseconds.

    Viewer.reconfigure() creates the decoder lazily and recreates it if an error closed it: after an error a VideoDecoder is closed and every configure() throws, which would make a session unrecoverable in silence. A decoder error is treated as a hole and asks for a keyframe.

    The decoder-queue skip. Measured 14 Aug 2026 with a scene at 58 draws/s: the server sent 39.6 frames/s, the page drew 34.7, nobody dropped the excess, and the delay between decode() and the callback grew by about 108 ms every second. The cause was a 34 ms drawImage of the 2D path. The cure skips the drawing, never the decoding, so the delta chain is intact and no key is needed. The rule is weighted by the measured drawing cost:

    Viewer.paint(): when a decoded frame is not drawn
    skip this frame  if  decodeQueueSize > 2  and  decodeQueueSize * draw_cost() > 16 ms
draw_cost()       = median time the callback holds the main thread
                    (+ median transfer-to-glass on the bitmaprenderer path)

    With a 34 ms drawing cost the rule fires at the old threshold; with WebGL2 at 0.26 ms it practically never fires, because skipping a 0.26 ms draw gains nothing — when the decoder itself is behind, the cure is the server's rate regulator. Every skipped frame is counted (queue_skipped): a rate that falls without a count would hide the cause.

    The counters close, within a session: delivered = exited + inside the decoder and exited = queue_skipped + painted + late + in_bmp + bmp_failed. They were added after a Firefox session showed 8 952 delivered and 6 929 drawn, with 2 007 frames that no counter named.

    9.12 · Drawing paths: WebGL2, bitmaprenderer, 2D canvas

    The decoded VideoFrame reaches the screen by one of three paths, chosen once when Viewer is built: a canvas takes only one context, so the choice cannot change during a session.

    The blocks. In August 2026 the owner saw rectangular blocks of 64×192 pixels in still areas. They were hunted suspect by suspect, with a measurement each: the capture was clean, the encoder was clean (0 damaged superblocks out of 600 through ffmpeg), VideoFrame.copyTo was clean, and getImageData after the draw found 0 wrong pixels out of 180 000 — while a phone photo of the same canvas showed the rectangles. The pixels entered the 2D canvas correctly and broke on the way to the screen, in a stretch no API can read: getImageData reads the backing store, not what the compositor shows. Firefox and Chrome behaved alike, and a <video> on the same GPU was clean. The bitmaprenderer context has no 2D backing store, and the owner's verdict on it was “no artefacts”.

    WebGL2. On Firefox the bitmaprenderer path reads every frame back from the GPU synchronously — about 34 ms at 4K — and the page skipped 11–62 % of frames. WebGL2's texImage2D has a fast path in Firefox (DMA-BUF and a GPU blit, YUV→RGB without read-back) when level 0, offset 0, RGBA/UNSIGNED_BYTE, no unpack skip, default colour space and visible rectangle equal to the coded one. Measured 26 Sep 2026 on Firefox at 4K: drawing 34 ms → 0.26 ms, skipped frames 60 % → 12 %. The multiple-of-16 canvas keeps the visible rectangle equal to the coded one; the log says once whether the fast path is possible.

    The last row of the picture. Chrome converts the VideoFrame to RGB before the shader sees it, and builds the last visible row from part of the padding chroma row below, which is zero: that row came out tinted (the check that caught it in the old test bench was called chroma_bleed; DECISIONS-11.md §11.41). The page therefore looks at the frame: when its codedHeight is greater than the visible rectangle it sets the uniform trim and the shader repeats the row above for the last visible one. Firefox, with no rows below the visible ones, is untouched; the price is one row of detail at the bottom edge on Chrome. Verified on 24 October 2026 on gnome and xfce, Chrome and Firefox: on Chrome row 2063 equals row 2062.

    On every path the buffer is set to the frame size only when it changes (writing canvas.width clears it), explicitly: Chrome, unlike Firefox, does not resize a bitmaprenderer canvas on transfer, and a 16×16 buffer stretched by CSS would send every click to the top-left corner. In the classic layout the pointer is not painted on the canvas; it is a CSS cursor or a separate element (10.4 “Mouse and pointer in the classic layout”).

    i
    A stale label. when Viewer is built on the WebGL2 path, it still writes a log line describing the path as a candidate “requested with ?canvas=gl”, “not the default”, and the context-loss lines advise reloading without ?canvas=gl. Those texts predate WebGL2 becoming the default and are stale; REMOTIX.stretches().route reports webgl2-requested for the same reason. The behaviour is the default one: the code decides, the texts are wrong.

    9.13 · Measurements and the diagnostics mode

    The page measures its own share of the latency and exposes it, so that checks read the path really in use instead of a copy of it. Everything it writes goes to one in-memory list, shown only in diagnostics mode.

    REMOTIX.round_trip is the full input round trip: each input message records when it left, and the input field of a later frame closes it. It is a lower bound — it stops when the frame arrives, not when it is drawn. SCENE samples the age of the image at every pointer move, which distinguishes “the desktop is frozen” from “the hand moved over the wallpaper and nothing changed”. voff_ms() (glass time minus the frame's server instant) is the video half of the audio/video distance; with the audio's aoff_ms(), the unknown clock offset cancels out (ch. 11 “Audio and clipboard”).

    The log does not contain what the user types: lines say “a character” or “key pressed”, and codes are written only for modifiers and mouse buttons (DECISIONS.md §9.2). The shortcuts bar is the one place where diagnostics hide something a user may want, which is why 10.7 “Shortcuts the browser keeps” states it.

    9.14 · What the page stores and what it declares

    The page keeps on the device only the choice of keyboard, and declares what it does and does not do.

    What the page declares to the user. DECLARATIONS (also REMOTIX.declarations) holds the sentences shown in #declaration: the codec situation (9.6 “Choosing the codec on the pixel”; the field DECLARATIONS.codec), and the video situation (DECLARATIONS.video: the desktop is on its way, no frame arrived within the wait, the server granted a canvas different from the one requested, the desktop cannot change size). The rule behind them is that what cannot be done is declared, never faked: a capability the page cannot back is omitted from HELLO, and the user reads why.

    What the page declares to the server. The HELLO capabilities (9.5 “Capabilities declared by the page”), the keyboard layout and the view in ATTACH, and a FAREWELL when the page goes away. The page sends nothing about the user's computer beyond that: the user agent and system lines written by note() stay in the in-memory log and are not transmitted (the /diary endpoint no longer exists, see the comment in page.c).

    9.15 · End of session in the page

    A session ends for one of four reasons — a FAREWELL from the server, the transport closing without one, the page closing it, or the tab going away — and in each case the page must say what it knows and go back to a usable login form.

    back_to_form() undoes everything the session turned on: the audio context is closed, Viewer.close() closes the decoder and bumps the epoch (frames still in flight from before the farewell would otherwise put the desktop dress back on), the data-viewer dress is removed, pointer lock and full screen are released, the canvas returns to 16×16, the logout dialog is hidden, and focus goes to the user name.

    The first-frame watch. After SESSION the page says at once that the desktop is on its way — after a logout or a reboot the graphical session is born from scratch. Measured on Ubuntu 26.04 (round 1, 18 Nov 2026): on GNOME, when the new login finds the previous session still closing and waits for it, the client was admitted 1.2 s after the click and the first picture was painted 27.3 s after the click, with a blank screen and no message in between; on Kubuntu a new user shows only the wallpaper after 10 s and the panel and icons after 40 s (round 2).
