The two Debian figures of the earlier text (9 s and about 32 s) are not carried over. Whatever the time, after FIRST_FRAME_WAIT_S = 6 s without a frame it explains with numbers: if the granted canvas differs from the requested one, that is the likely cause; otherwise the server log has it.

    When the server ends the session. The FAREWELL 0x10 (TERMINATED, «the graphical session has ended») is sent by the parent when its child reports MSG_SESSION_FINISHED. Since 19 Nov 2026 the child sends that message before it dismantles the stage (session_over_early() in child.c), not at the next remount: dismantling the stage waits for PipeWire, and PipeWire's real-time module can stay in a D-Bus call to RealtimeKit for up to 25 s where rtkit-daemon is installed but does not start. Before the change the page stood on its last image, with no word, for up to 17 s (measured on the Ubuntu 26.04 test machine, 18 Nov 2026). The early farewell is sent only on a certain death, session_life() = dead (the session bus answered and the compositor's name has no owner), never on «unknown»; KDE is excluded, because a KWin restarted by systemd leaves its name without an owner for a moment, and waits for a proof on a real machine. The parent then counts the child as closing, so a login in the meantime gets the true 0x0E «still closing». A login of the same name that is still waiting for PAM, or whose refusal is being kept for the fixed second, does not receive the farewell (wt_dismiss_user_session_over()), so it is never told «the session has ended» in place of its own answer. The roads and the other reasons are in 3.10 “When the session ends before the stage is gone” and ch. 5 “The RCP/1 protocol”. On KDE with a local login the close of the remote desktop is forced through graphical-session.target after at most KDE_PRELOCAL_ORDERLY_MS = 5000 ms of waiting (that is the root side, 3.10 “When the session ends before the stage is gone”; the page sees only the farewell). Time to the client after Log Out, measured: 11 s on Kubuntu (lifecycle/logout, round 2); 0.17 to 0.29 s on GNOME in the first checks of the work on that desktop (docs/STORIA-ubuntu-26.04.md).

    The page's sentence for 0x0E stays generic. The code of the page counts six roads to that reason (an unknown layout, a full slot register, a canvas that cannot be granted under video.max_size, memory exhausted on the control channel, all stages busy, and, since 18 Nov 2026, «the desktop's compositor is not installed»). Four more uses of 0x0E are not in that count: the previous desktop still closing, logind unable to say whether a local session exists, a failed birth, and the refusal for a scale that is not 1 (ch. 6 “Screen capture”); see 8.12 “Admission: the session cap and the budget”.

    Logging out. The page keeps no key combination for itself: every combination reaches the remote desktop, and the user leaves from the desktop's own menu, which REMOTIX keeps available (ch. 12 “The four desktops”). There was once an exit shortcut, Ctrl+Alt+End, and it was removed because the local desktop of the user's computer takes that combination before the browser: it closed the PC's session, not the remote one. TERMINATE_SESSION remains in the protocol and the confirmation dialog (#confirm) remains in the page, but no gesture opens it today.

    9.16 · The video worker and the MSE path

    Two other ways of drawing exist in the file. The video worker is the default on desktop Firefox and an option elsewhere; the MSE path is off and kept because it is measurable.

    i
    Comment behind the code. the comment above VIDEO_ASKED in page.html still calls the Firefox worker default “PROPOSAL … NOT decided, NOT on main”, and a log line says “default: desktop Firefox (§11.36 D, proposal)”. The code enables it, and DECISIONS-11.md §11.36 is marked DECIDED D; the manual follows the code. A live browser proof of the worker default is noted as still to do in the same decision file; the final run of prove/all.sh (Firefox included) does not isolate it.

    9.17 · Browsers supported and untested

    The technical minimum is WebTransport and WebCodecs. The table separates what was exercised by the checks of prove/ (Chrome and Firefox on Linux, real browsers driven by DevTools and WebDriver) from what the owner has tried by hand and what has never been tried.

    The rule behind the list: a page runs on three engines written by three teams who do not know REMOTIX — Blink, Gecko, WebKit — and testing on at least two of them gives back part of the external referee lost with native clients. Where two agree and the third does not, the defect names itself.

    !
    DeX and the pointer. on Samsung DeX, Chrome delivers mouse moves with no button pressed only around a click (the known noVNC issue #1727, also seen in KasmVNC #222 and in the native moonlight-android #573); it is not a REMOTIX defect. The page copes in two ways: since the canvas equals the window every event carries its own position, so pointing and clicking hit correctly even without hover; and the first click on the canvas takes Pointer Lock where hover does not arrive (DECISIONS.md §10.29). Details are in 10.4 “Mouse and pointer in the classic layout”.
    • The owner's hand tests on the four virtual machines and the four real live images (19 Nov 2026) used the browsers of his own devices (Windows, Linux, Android); their versions are not recorded in the tree.
    • Not verified: a real phone with the on-screen keyboard. prove/check-phone.py is an emulation (Chrome device emulation with touch events), and its header says what only a real phone can show.
    • Not verified: Safari on macOS and iOS, and Firefox on Windows, have never been opened against REMOTIX.
    • Not verified: Android's coming desktop mode, which may change the pointer behaviour; the capture rule looks at behaviour, not at the system, so it should adapt by itself.
    Chapter 10

    Input

    10.1 · Input at a glance

    Input travels the opposite way to video: from the browser page to the desktop of the remote session. The page turns mouse, keyboard and fingers into five RCP messages on a single unidirectional stream; the parent process validates them and passes them to the per-user child; the child injects them into the compositor through libei (GNOME and KDE) or through the Wayland virtual keyboard and pointer protocols (labwc, that is XFCE and LXQt). On KDE, KWin runs nested inside a screenless labwc that REMOTIX starts only to host it; input still goes to KWin through libei, never to that labwc. What was verified with real browsers is listed in 10.17 “What was verified for input and what was not”.

    10.2 · The input messages

    Input uses five message types on the input channel, all big-endian, defined in RCP §7.3 and decoded by rcp_receive_input(). The client opens exactly one unidirectional stream for them, after SESSION, and keeps it open; a second input stream is a protocol error.

    Every message starts with the same two fields: u32 id and u64 instant (a timestamp). The id grows by at least one on every message of the channel, whatever its type, and never takes the value 0, which means “no input”. It is the number that comes back in the input field of every video frame header (RCP §6.2): the child sets that field to the last id injected before the capture, not the last received, so a message refused by the compositor or a letter the layout cannot produce never claims an effect that the frame does not show. The instant is the client's monotonic clock in microseconds; no rule consumes it, it is kept for diagnosis.

    Frequency ceilings. After login the parent applies a token bucket per client and per kind of message (msgrate.h, msg_class_rate()): POINTER 2000 a second with a burst of 4000, BUTTON and WHEEL 1000 with a burst of 2000, LETTER and KEY_POSITION 2000 with a burst of 4000. The rates are far above what a hand or a password manager's automatic typing can do. A message over its rate is consumed without effect and counted, and one line per 10 s window says how many were dropped. The id of an input only has to grow, so a gap is legitimate. The wheel amounts are bounded to ±WHEEL_MAX_UNITS units (100 notches) by wheel_clamp() in wheelclamp.h before any negation, because a negated INT32_MIN would overflow, and the server refuses key and button codes at or above 0x300 (MAX_KEY, MAX_BUTTON) because Mutter would drop them silently.

    Codes are those of evdev (the kernel header linux/input-event-codes.h) because libei and the Wayland virtual devices both speak evdev: any other convention would add a translation table that fails silently. Coordinates outside the canvas close the session with PROTOCOL_ERROR, except during the one-second grace after a CANVAS(FITTED) reply, where coordinates still valid on the previous canvas are saturated (RCP §7.1, CANVAS_GRACE = 1000 ms); the page saturates them anyway, three times over, because a closed session for a rounding error is the worst possible answer.

    Two control-channel messages belong to input as well: the keyboard layout declared in ATTACH (RCP §4.5) and LAYOUT (0x0009), which changes it while the session is open (10.12 “Keyboard layout negotiation”).

    i
    Clock grain. the page writes instant as Math.round(ms) * 1000 (cl_instant_us(), touch_instant_us()), that is whole milliseconds. RCP §7.3 was corrected on 14 Aug 2026 to say that the client should write the real microseconds it has (5 µs grain on an isolated page in Chrome 151); the page code still rounds, and no rule on the server uses the value.

    10.3 · Classic and touch layouts in the page

    The page has two input layouts and chooses between them by itself, from what the device has and what the user is using, never from the user-agent string: DeX is Android with a real mouse, a laptop is Linux with a touch screen.

    A change of any media query re-reads the context but does not discard the last observation (since 26 Oct 2026: Android desktop mode fires such changes while the mouse is in use); the observation wins until a pointer of another type is used: pick up the mouse and the page goes classic, touch the screen and it goes back to touch. The layout in force is written in body[data-layout] so that the checks read it from the document. Leaving the touch layout resets the pinch zoom (with the mouse there is no panning, and part of the desktop would be unreachable: measured on DeX on 14 Aug 2026) and releases the button held by a tap-and-a-half; leaving the classic layout releases every key and button it pressed.

    Both layouts send through the same interface, window.REMOTIX_INPUT (next_id() and send()), created right after SESSION together with the input stream, with a single writer so that messages leave in the order the user produced them. If the stream cannot be opened the session continues view-only, and the page says so. When the stream is congested (desiredSize at or below zero) a POINTER is not queued: it is held aside and replaced by the next one, and the held position is always flushed before any key or button, so a click never travels with an old position. Measured from DeX on 14 Aug 2026: median input-to-frame loop 135 ms but worst case 2161 ms, which was a queue of stale pointer moves in front of a keystroke.

    10.4 · Mouse and pointer in the classic layout

    In the classic layout (cl_* functions, for “classic”, in page.html) the mouse is the primary path, including on DeX, which is the main Android use.

    One visible pointer. The page has three pointer modes (REMOTIX_POINTER.mode()): system (the default since 14 Aug 2026), where the browser's own cursor takes the remote cursor shape through a CSS cursor: url(...) x y, default rule, the way Xpra does; drawn, where the browser cursor is hidden and the page draws its arrow; and both, both arrows overlaid, kept for comparison. In the touch layout the drawn arrow stays, because a finger has no cursor to restyle. A zero-by-zero shape (RCP §5.5) means “hidden” and is applied in both modes. The cursor shape itself comes from the capture (ch. 6 “Screen capture”).

    Mutter and the first movement. The comment of input.c records that on Mutter 51 (Fedora 45 GNOME, measured on 23 Nov 2026, with one user and with a phone) the first absolute movement after the pointer device starts or restarts reaches the windows with one of its two coordinates at 0 and the other right, so a click made at once, such as the tap of a phone, lands on the edge of the screen. The movements that follow are exact, and so is the same position sent a second time right after the first. The cure is in input.c: the field pointer_primed is cleared at every DEVICE_RESUMED of the pointer, and the first absolute movement is sent twice. It touches only the libei path (GNOME), not the wlroots one, the comment in the code says it is to be removed when Mutter is fixed, and the repeat is harmless on compositors that do not need it. The Ubuntu 26.04 GNOME is Mutter 50.1: the defect was not measured there, and the repeat runs all the same.

    Pointer Lock only where hover is missing. The lock is requested at the first click (the gesture it requires) only if, before that click, no move with buttons up arrived, or the last one is CL_JUMP_PX = 8 px or more from the click point. On a computer the last move falls on the click and the lock never fires; on DeX moves with buttons up arrive only around clicks, and with the lock the borders of windows can be grabbed (user test, S23, Android 16, Chrome 154, 3 Oct 2026). The lock asks for unadjustedMovement (the client applies acceleration, CL_GAIN = 1.0); the first movement after the lock is dropped if longer than 100 CSS px (CL_FAKE_JUMP: Chrome reports the jump of the system cursor); pushing 160 CSS px (CL_EXIT_PUSH) beyond an edge releases the lock, so that the DeX bar and the browser tabs stay reachable, while a pointer resting on the edge still triggers GNOME's hot corner.

    The lock can also be switched by hand: the diagnostics panel (9.13 “Measurements and the diagnostics mode”) has a “Pointer capture” button that calls cl_hook(), and Esc leaves it. The button exists only when the panel is open.

    !
    A limit that is not ours. on Samsung devices (DeX included) Chrome does not deliver mouse moves with buttons up (noVNC #1727, open since 2022; the same on moonlight-android #573, a native app). Pointing, clicking and dragging land correctly; what is missing is the preview: the resize arrow on window borders, buttons lighting up, tooltips. The automatic Pointer Lock above reduces it.
    i
    Comment behind the code. a comment in cl_on_mousedown() still says that the lock is only manual and switchable through REMOTIX.classic_input.hook(). The code requests it automatically (cl_hover_missing()) and REMOTIX.classic_input exposes no such function; the manual button of the diagnostics panel is the manual road. The code wins.

    10.5 · Wheel and scrolling

    The wheel has one sign convention on the wire and three on the way out; the sign is inverted exactly twice, once in the page and once in the server, and nowhere else.

    The sign was measured on 10 Aug 2026 on Mutter (libmutter 48.7, libei 1.3.901, Firefox 140, all Debian versions; Ubuntu 26.04 has Mutter 50.1 and libei 1.5.0, and the sign was not measured again on them, only the check mouse-wheel passes on GNOME in the round of 18 Nov 2026): ei_device_scroll_discrete(0, +120) scrolled the page 114 px towards its end. Hence the server inversion. The horizontal axis of the touch gesture mirrors the vertical one and has not been judged. The wheel event also carries a position, and the page sends it first, for the same reason as a click.

    10.6 · Keyboard: letters and positions

    The keyboard sends letters when the user writes text and positions when the user gives a command. cl_command() decides: a key is a command when Ctrl, Meta or Alt (without AltGr) is down.

    The table CL_POSITION maps KeyboardEvent.code to evdev by hand from the kernel table; positions are physical, so KeyZ is the key where Z sits on a US board, which writes Y on a German one. That is exactly why shortcuts travel as positions.

    Modifier resynchronisation. Because Shift alone is not sent, the page sends it at the moment a position key arrives while getModifierState("Shift") (or AltGr) is true but the page has not pressed it. Since 24 Sep 2026 this happens for every position key, not only for commands: before, Shift+← arrived as a bare arrow and did not select text on any of the four desktops. Conversely, before a LETTER the page releases the Shift or AltGr it holds, because the server presses and releases its own Shift to produce the letter and on labwc that release would leave the page and the server disagreeing.

    Ctrl+V is the one command the page does not cancel. Calling preventDefault() on it would stop the browser paste, and with it the paste event that is the only free way to read the local clipboard on Firefox; the canvas is not editable, so the browser paste writes nowhere. When the clipboard is on, the V is also held back until the page has read the local clipboard and announced it, at most PASTE_HOLD_MS = 400 ms, with every key typed meanwhile queued behind it (11.11 “Clipboard in the browser”).

    Release on focus loss. On blur, on visibilitychange to hidden and on pagehide the page releases every key and button it pressed (cl_release_all()). The Keyboard Lock switches itself off precisely when the page loses focus, which is when a modifier is likely to be held; the session does not detach in that case, so the server-side release at detach would not help.

    i
    Privacy of keystrokes. by decision of 26 Sep 2026 (DECISIONS.md §9.2) the log never contains what the user types: neither characters nor key codes. Lines say “a character” or “key pressed”; codes are written only for modifiers and mouse buttons (on the server, log_speakable_key() in log.c: whether a key code may be named in the log). It applies to unproducible characters too: the log says that one occurred, not which.

    10.7 · Shortcuts the browser keeps

    Some combinations never reach the page, and some reach it while the browser also runs its own command. The page declares them per engine and per screen state instead of pretending they work.

    The catalogue SC_CATALOG holds, per engine family (blink, blink-app for an installed app, gecko) and per screen state (window, whole full screen, whole+lock full screen with Keyboard Lock, F11), what is lost; it was measured on 14 Aug 2026 on GNOME/Wayland by injecting from a real keyboard path (org.gnome.Mutter.RemoteDesktop), with Chrome 151 and Firefox 140 ESR. The catalogue has not been re-measured with the browsers of the current checks. Safari, Chrome on Android/DeX and Firefox 151 or later are listed as not tested (SC_NOT_TRIED), and an untested engine is never deduced from the others.

    On-screen buttons. SC_BUTTONS lists five combinations that no browser lets through; only Ctrl+Alt+Del is marked active: true, because without it a locked session cannot be entered at all. It is sent as positions 29, 56, 111 down and up in reverse. Ctrl+W, Ctrl+T, Alt+F4 and Super are present but off: switching one on is active: true. Off means not drawn, not drawn and inert.

    !
    Hidden by design, not yet reconciled with the specification. the Ctrl+Alt+Del button is not visible to a normal user. It lives in the shortcuts bar, which is opened by the small ⌨ button at the bottom-left corner, and both are hidden by the style sheet unless the page is in diagnostics mode (body:not(.diagnostics), 9.13 “Measurements and the diagnostics mode”): the bar was covering the bottom of the desktop and the corner button was pressed by mistake while aiming at the desktop's own controls. The consequence, and the sentence that SPECS.md §7.3-bis would require (“the page declares which shortcuts it cannot deliver”), is that the notice is written in the page log at session start and is visible only with ?logbook. A user whose own computer keeps Ctrl+Alt+Del and who has no way to open the bar cannot send it. The button is hidden by decision (DECISIONS-11.md §11.54), and the checks follow it since 18 Nov 2026 (register entry B3): page-cad-hidden passes when, outside diagnostics, the page shows neither the bar nor the button (check-input.py), and page-ctrl-alt-end-passes passes when Ctrl+Alt+End reaches the desktop like any other combination. The old names page-cad-button and page-ctrl-alt-end are gone. The text of SPECS.md §7.3-bis is still to be aligned (ch. 24 “Appendix C — Known issues and open points”).

    Ctrl+Alt+Del on KDE. On Plasma 6.4 and later the shortcut did not open the logout screen: kglobalaccel emitted the signal but ksmserver never opened the prompt (measured on Kubuntu, 18 Nov 2026), because the prompt first asks org.freedesktop.ScreenSaver.GetActive and nobody owned that name. The cure is the sidecar of kwin.c described in 6.4 “KDE: the KWin screencast protocol and the nested KWin”. It was measured with a stand-in (the prompt appears within 1 s), and page-cad-chain is green on Kubuntu in both browsers in the 1.2.0 round.

    There is no page-side exit shortcut: Ctrl+Alt+End was removed because the user's own desktop takes it before the browser, so every key combination the browser lets through reaches the remote desktop, and the way out is the desktop's own Log Out… (which session.c keeps available, see ch. 12 “The four desktops”). The page says so in its log at the start of each session.

    10.8 · Touch gestures

    The touch layout turns the phone screen into a trackpad: the finger pushes a pointer drawn by the page, and clicks happen where the pointer is, not where the finger lands.

    The thresholds are a declared starting point, judged by using them. Four design points are not thresholds, and each came from a failing run of a gesture bench (gestures, 14 Aug 2026; the bench is not part of this repository):

    • Tap-and-a-half and double click are the same gesture. At the second contact the two have produced the same events, so the button is pressed at contact and released at lift: a quick lift is the second click of a double click, a drag is a drag. Waiting to decide would delay every double click.
    • Two fingers make a two-finger gesture if they are down together for at least one sample. Two non-overlapping taps are two one-finger taps, so a badly timed right click comes out as a left double click; the only cure would delay every click by 300 ms, above the 50 ms budget.
    • A tap is short if every contact is short, not the whole gesture: three fingers never land and lift together.
    • When the set of fingers changes, the two-finger reference is rebuilt and nothing is decided in that sample: three fingers lifting one by one move the centre by tens of pixels without any movement, which used to be read as a wheel.

    Wheel and pinch are both “two moving fingers”: the page compares the change of distance with the movement of the centre, takes the larger once, and keeps that decision for the whole gesture. The pointer is moved on every touch sample, without coalescing and without requestAnimationFrame (which never ran on the Xvfb bench). Times come from event.timeStamp when plausible (within 5 s of performance.now()), otherwise from the handler time, declared.

    10.9 · The touch pointer is announced to the server

    In the touch layout the pointer is drawn by the page and the server only moves where it is told, so the server's pointer has to be put under the drawn arrow before the first tap. touch_announce_pointer() does that: once the session has a canvas, an input channel and a painted frame (the compositor takes input only when its stage is open, just before the first frame, so a POINTER sent at SESSION is dropped), the arrow is placed inside the canvas (its centre if it was never placed or fell outside), drawn, and sent through the same touch_send() as every drag. It is sent again when the session is another one (a reattach brings a new input channel) or the canvas or frame size changed, and it is called from the geometry paths of the viewer and when the layout switches to touch inside a live session. Nothing is sent without a session, and the classic layout never runs it.

    !
    Not settled yet. a residual case is not proven: in one test out of thirteen on GNOME the first tap after login landed at the initial point, probably because the pointer position arrived before Mutter was ready for input. GNOME is born in the Activities overview, which holds touches, so most failures of the emulated phone check were the check's own; the one that remains has low priority (ch. 24 “Appendix C — Known issues and open points”).

    10.10 · The on-screen keyboard on a phone

    With the phone in hand the system keyboard opens only on request (DECISIONS.md §10.28, 2 Oct 2026), through a small ⌨ button at the top right that exists only in the touch layout.

    1. Why. The hidden paste field is always focused, and on Android a focused text field opens the keyboard, which covered half the desktop for 60 % of a test and typed nothing (measured on an S23+ with Chrome 154).
    2. The field. In the touch layout it carries inputmode="none" and virtualkeyboardpolicy="manual" (and no autocapitalisation or autocorrection); in the classic layout none of these attributes is present, so paste and keys are unchanged.
    3. The button. keyboard_toggle() switches inputmode to text, re-focuses the field inside the user's touch, and calls navigator.virtualKeyboard.show() where it exists. The button never takes focus. It sits at the top because the open keyboard covers the bottom.
    4. What is typed. keyboard_on_input() compares the field with what was already sent: the common prefix stays, every vanished character becomes Backspace (position 14), every new one a LETTER; newline and tab become Enter and Tab positions. Autocorrection works by rewriting the word. Outside composition the field is emptied.
    5. Real keys (Enter and Backspace on an empty field, a Bluetooth keyboard without a mouse) are handled in keyboard_on_keydown(); if code is empty, as can happen on Android, the key name is used.
    6. Closing. The button again, or Android's back gesture, recognised when the visual viewport grows back above 85 % of the window height.

    10.11 · From a letter to key positions

    keyboard.c (keyboard) solves the reverse problem of a keyboard: given a character, which keys must be pressed on the session's layout to make the compositor produce it. It works on the keymap the session itself handed over, compiled with xkbcommon.

    input_letter() presses the modifiers first and the key last, releases in reverse order, and if a press fails halfway it releases what it already pressed. It returns 0 when sent, 1 when the character is not producible (the log line is written by keyboard_positions_for(), which knows the layout name), −1 on a fault; values outside the Unicode scalar range are protocol errors, not “unproducible”. xkbcommon's own log is redirected so that a layout that does not compile says why, and the layout name always includes what the compiled keymap calls itself (“it [Italian]”), so a silent fallback would read “it [English (US)]”.

    10.12 · Keyboard layout negotiation

    The layout is negotiated at every attach, like the canvas, for two reasons: to make characters reachable and to make shortcut positions match. The client proposes, the server asks the session, and the session's real keymap is always the one in force.

    1. The page proposes a layout in ATTACH: the value of the sign-in form's Keyboard menu (layout(); a choice kept in localStorage, see 9.14 “What the page stores and what it declares”), which is preset from navigator.language (layout_from_browser()) when nothing was chosen: en becomes us (or gb/ie by region), sv → se, da → dk, cs → cz, el → gr, he → il, ja → jp, ko → kr, uk → ua, thirty languages whose XKB name equals the ISO code pass unchanged, everything else becomes us. Until 10 Aug 2026 the page sent en, which is not an XKB name, and the server rightly refused the session of every English-language browser.
    2. The server checks the form (layout_well_formed()): at most 64 characters in all, a name of [A-Za-z0-9_-] optionally followed by a non-empty variant of the same characters in parentheses. Dots, slashes and commas are refused because the string ends up in XKB's include machinery, which opens files by name. A bad form is PROTOCOL_ERROR.
    3. The server checks existence by compiling it with xkbcommon (hook_layout_exists() → keyboard_open_for()). At attach an unknown layout is SESSION_UNSERVABLE; a fixed list of layouts from the first phase is only a declared fallback when the hook is missing or cannot answer. The list alone would refuse layouts that are installed, such as hu, tr, gr and ua.
    4. The child asks the session (input_layout()), after releasing everything pressed, unless the current keymap already does the same thing as the requested layout (compared key by key, keyboard_is_this()): a needless change costs Mutter the destruction of the keyboard device.
    5. The keymap confirms. The compositor recreates the keyboard device with the new keymap; read_keymap() reads it, fingerprints it (size plus hash, since Mutter names every keymap (unnamed)) and writes KEYMAP CHANGED. If the session layout differs from the requested one, keyboard.c writes DECLARED FALLBACK and uses the session's.
    i
    Mutter 50 and the keymap. Mutter 50 has a new method, RemoteDesktop.Session.SetKeymap (read in its source, studio 4 §2.4), and the comment of input.c saying that Mutter offers no lever on the D-Bus is false for Mutter 50; it is true for Mutter 48. The product stays on dconf, which was tried on Ubuntu, because a second road would be a second code path for one distribution; the method is not used. The key input-sources is read by the Shell (gnome-shell 50.1, js/ui/status/keyboard.js), not by gsd-keyboard as the same comment says. The schema and the keys current, sources and mru-sources exist unchanged in GNOME 50.

    While the session is open, LAYOUT (0x0009) changes the layout: a well-formed unknown layout does not close the session (the previous keyboard still works, and “never detach” applies); the same layout as the current one asks nothing; there is no reply on the wire. The page does not send this message today (the menu is read only at sign-in).

    i
    Limits: a page cannot know the physical layout of the keyboard in front of it; navigator.language is only the preset of the menu. Since 1.0.1 the user chooses, once per browser; what is still missing is a change without signing out, and variants such as “US international”.

    10.13 · Injection through libei

    On GNOME and KDE the child is a libei sender on a socket that the compositor hands over: ConnectToEIS on the Mutter RemoteDesktop session (asked before Start, see mutter_open()) or connectToEIS on org.kde.KWin.EIS.RemoteDesktop with the capability mask 7 (keyboard, pointer, touch) and a token. On KDE that KWin is the nested one: the labwc that hosts it is written by REMOTIX with no key or mouse binding that acts (HOST_RC in kwin.c: one key and one mouse binding whose only action is None, because a file with none would make labwc load its defaults), so nothing typed into the session is taken by the host.

    The nested KWin host. On KDE the compositor is the user unit plasma-kwin_wayland.service, whose ExecStart the drop-in zz-remotix-monitor.conf (written by write_dropin() in session.c) replaces with remotix --kwin-nested: REMOTIX starts the screenless labwc and becomes the KWin wrapper; the labwc is REMOTIX's own (6.4 “KDE: the KWin screencast protocol and the nested KWin”). A user unit lives outside the logind scope of the session, so it would outlive a remote session. kdehost.h (header only, shared by the root side, the single-process server and the child) stops it when the session is over, only if a process of the unit's own cgroup is recognised as ours: its command line carries the folder remotix-kwin-host or the option --kwin-nested (KDEHOST_MARK, KDEHOST_OPTION). A service with the same name and no mark is a local desktop's, and is said in the log and never touched. The process is recognised from /proc and its cgroup, never by name and never with kill; the stop is systemctl --user stop run as the user. In split mode the root side does the periodic sweep (kdehost_sweep() in rootside.c), since the network-facing user can do neither. When a local login is held back, the child waits up to KDE_PRELOCAL_ORDERLY_MS = 5000 ms for the orderly close of the KDE session and then forces it by stopping graphical-session.target (StopUnit in session.c), which takes with it the nested KWin, plasmashell and the rest of the desktop (3.10 “When the session ends before the stage is gone”).

    !
    The handshake that must not be interrupted. until 25 Aug 2026 input_close() called ei_disconnect() and ei_unref() unconditionally, and a channel opened 33 ms earlier killed the child with SIGSEGV before the first frame. In libei 1.3.901 (Debian's version), a context whose handshake was requested but not answered has a NULL connection that ei_disconnect() dereferences, and ei_unref() calls it first. The cure (D4): EI_EVENT_CONNECT marks the handshake; whether the defect still exists in libei 1.5.0 (Ubuntu) was not checked; the cure stays in input.c. Without the handshake the context is abandoned (its descriptors closed, the memory lost, the count kept in input_abandons()), and input_run() checks with a zero-timeout poll() whether the compositor hung up before dispatching a context whose handshake is incomplete.

    10.14 · Pressed keys: counting, releasing, healing

    Input keeps a ledger of everything pressed (RCP §11), because a modifier or a button left down in a session that outlives its client makes the desktop unusable, and nobody connects the two.

    Why orphans exist. Measured on 16 and 21 Aug 2026 with a Wayland test client inside the session: hold BTN_LEFT, let Mutter recreate the absolute pointer (canvas change, or simply a capture wake-up on a still desktop), then release. The release never arrives, and from then on no click arrives at all, while the keyboard keeps working. The chain is in Mutter: remove_viewport_devices removes the device without drop_device(); the new device silently swallows a release it never saw pressed; and the seat counts presses across devices, so it stays at one forever. A press-release on the new device makes the count go 1 → 2 → 1. Only the drop of the EIS client resets it, and it is the ei_disconnect() message, not the closing of the descriptor, that triggers it (both verified with injected faults). Releasing before a resize and cure A close the doors that REMOTIX controls; cure C repairs the doors it does not control (monitors-changed, keymap changes, and whatever GNOME adds: meta_eis_viewport_notify_changed() is new in GNOME 48.5). All of this was measured on Mutter 48.7 (Debian). In the source of Mutter 50.1 drop_device() and handle_button() are unchanged and the EIS client code has only clean-ups, but cure C was not measured again on Ubuntu: the bench that measured it is not in this tree.

    Healing for the other desktops. input_dropped() says whether the compositor has hung up the input channel. For libei it reads the flag of the channel; since 19 Nov 2026 it also answers for wlroots (it asks wlr_input_dropped() on the virtual keyboard and pointer). Before, it always said no there, and the child of an XFCE session did not notice the Log Out. The child looks at it at most once a second, and only for GNOME and the wlroots desktops (KDE has its own check of the connection to KWin), together with session_life(), which answers alive, dead or unknown: the stage is dismantled at dead, and at unknown (the user's bus itself disappears for a moment at a logout) the child asks again after a second, up to EIS_UNKNOWN_ROUNDS = 3 rounds, before taking the old road. A dead answer also sets off the early farewell (9.15 “End of session in the page”).

    Keyboard devices are not recreated by geometry changes (measured: zero keyboard swaps out of fifteen pointer swaps) but they are by keymap changes, which is why every layout change starts with input_release_all().

    10.15 · Virtual keyboard and pointer on labwc

    labwc has no libei. wlr_input.c creates our own virtual keyboard (zwp_virtual_keyboard_manager_v1) and pointer (zwlr_virtual_pointer_manager_v1) on the user's Wayland socket; input.c keeps the same contract on top of it, branching at the top of every public function, so the GNOME and KDE paths are untouched.

    Measured on 21 Sep 2026 on the laptop, with a private headless labwc 0.8.3 (Debian's version) and a small Wayland test client (the “witness”, not part of this repository), not on the test server nor in a full XFCE session: Shift arrives as a modifier before the letter; CapsLock pressed three times locks once; +120 from the client is one notch up and two halves of 60 are one notch; absolute positions are exact and saturated; a double press with one release gives one pair; switching to de puts Z on key 21; closing with Ctrl and left button down releases both. Ubuntu 26.04 has labwc 0.9.3-1 and wlr-randr 0.4.1 (both in universe). These measurements were not repeated with 0.9.3 on their own: the XFCE and LXQt rounds of 18 Nov 2026 (126/128 and 124/124 lines green) contain all the input checks. The version-sensitive points (the form of <keybind> in rc.xml, SESSION_LABWC_*, cursor names) were not re-examined one by one.

    !
    Shortcuts belong to labwc. labwc applies its own keybindings to virtual keys too. Measured on 21 Sep 2026 (laptop, headless labwc): Alt+F4 from our channel closes the test client's window, which sees Alt and never F4. It is the desktop's behaviour, and on XFCE what the user expects.

    Bringing windows back inside. On labwc a shrinking output leaves large windows partly outside the right and bottom edges. After every resize the child calls input_bring_back_inside(), which releases everything and types the unused shortcut SESSION_LABWC_KEY (the labwc session key, W-C-A-S-F12, i.e. Super+Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F12) that REMOTIX writes into labwc's configuration, then puts the pointer back where the user had it. On GNOME and KDE the function does nothing, because the compositor already does it. The shortcut itself is described in ch. 12 “The four desktops”.

    10.16 · Input decisions

    The main decisions of the input subsystem, with the reason that made each one.

    10.17 · What was verified for input and what was not

    What the checks of prove/ exercise for input, and what they cannot. They run on the development server, one virtual machine per desktop (Ubuntu, Kubuntu, Xubuntu, Lubuntu) with the Radeon passed through to one of them at a time (ch. 17 “Testing”), with real browsers: Chrome through DevTools, Firefox through WebDriver, real mouse and key events. Lines that need a real login screen or several network addresses are skipped on a machine where they cannot run, with the reason (prelocal/real-greeter, ban/other-addresses, package). The desktop side is a window inside the user's session (window-input.py) that logs every event it receives, so the verdicts are built on what the application got, never on what the browser was told to send.

    The automatic round of the 1.2.0 release gave GNOME 125 lines PASS and one known FAIL (desktop/users-shell-and-environment, pkexec with an empty SHELL, accepted), and KDE, XFCE and LXQt 126 PASS each. The owner's hand tests of 27 Nov 2026, on the four virtual machines and on a real machine with the four 26.04.1 live images, found the input regular. Not verified: a real phone, the Android on-screen keyboard, Safari, labwc's own shortcuts inside a full XFCE session, and the layout change on every compositor with a physical non-US keyboard (the check uses the Italian layout through navigator.language and sends AltGr characters as the characters themselves, because DevTools and WebDriver cannot press AltGr).

    Chapter 11

    Audio and clipboard

    11.1 · Audio at a glance

    The session's sound is the mix of every application in it: REMOTIX creates a virtual sink in the session's PipeWire, captures its monitor, encodes 48 kHz stereo blocks and sends one per QUIC datagram. The page decodes Opus with its own WebAssembly decoder and schedules each block at the time the server stamped on it.

    i
    Volume and microphone. the session volume belongs to the session and is set to maximum at every connection (invariant I5); RCP carries no volume. Microphone input (client to session) is foreseen by SPECS.md §10 as not urgent and RCP/1 defines no format for it. Not settled yet: the microphone.

    11.2 · The audio format and its datagram

    The audio format is fixed, not negotiated (RCP §5.3): two implementations choosing two sample rates would produce noise that looks like a network fault. Only the codec is negotiated.

    PCM is 5 ms and not 20 ms because a QUIC datagram cannot be fragmented: 20 ms of PCM would be 3852 bytes. The largest datagram measured on 17 Aug 2026 (wired LAN) was 1024 bytes on Chrome 151, and on Firefox 140 1024 bytes at ready growing to 1214 after 800 ms: PCM fits by 52 bytes. The little-endian byte order of PCM is the only exception to network order in RCP, declared because it is payload, not a protocol field. A datagram shorter than 12 bytes or with another type is discarded and counted, never a reason to close the connection: a datagram is unreliable by definition.

    Negotiation. audio.codec is a capability that both sides declare in HELLO / HERE_I_AM; pcm is mandatory on both sides as the always-available base and positive control of Opus. The page declares opus,pcm only if its WebAssembly decoder loads, or, failing that, if AudioDecoder supports Opus; otherwise only pcm: declaring opus would oblige the server to choose it and nothing would be heard. The server picks inside the intersection following the client's order and logs the choice; the child then opens the encoder for that codec (audio_rule_child()) and never falls back to PCM by itself, which would produce noise instead of an error.

    Audio goes before video. In every write pass of the transport the pending datagrams enter the packet before stream bytes, so on a congestion window of two or three packets audio takes the place of video (SPECS.md §10.1). A late audio block is useless, a late frame is still a frame. The price is bounded by construction: the datagram queue holds WT_DGRAM_MAX = 8.

    11.3 · The session sink and its capture

    A server has no sound card, and a headless session has no sink at all: measured in v1 on 5 Aug 2026, wpctl status showed zero devices, zero sinks, zero sources with PipeWire, pipewire-pulse and WirePlumber all running (a measurement of the first version of the product, on Debian). sound_open() therefore creates one. On Ubuntu 26.04 the sound server is PipeWire 1.6.2 with WirePlumber 0.5.13 and the code of sound.c is the same: the sink is created by REMOTIX in the user's session (REMOTIX's own sink, not a device of the machine), and the audio lines of the checks pass on the four desktops in the rounds of 18 Nov 2026.

    i
    WirePlumber on the virtual machines. on the virtual machines the owner saw an Ubuntu «internal error» notice from wireplumber stopping when the user's session closes, also after an exit from REMOTIX; whether it depends on the machine having no sound card was not cleared. It is an open, non-blocking item of the work on Ubuntu (docs/STORIA-ubuntu-26.04.md), and it is not written up in the register of problems.

    The volume measurement that justified monitor.channel-volumes (8 Aug 2026, a 440 Hz tone at 25.9 % of full scale read on the monitor): with the sink at 100 %, 25 % and 0 %, the capture read 25.39 %, 25.39 %, 25.39 % without the property, and 25.39 %, 0.40 %, 0.00 % with it, which is exactly the cubic volume curve. sound_max_volume() sets channel volumes to 1.0 and mute off at creation, at every connection and at every start of the capture, because whoever restores saved levels does so when the node appears and wins the race at creation.

    11.4 · From samples to datagrams

    Between PipeWire's real-time thread and the child's loop sits a lock-free single-producer, single-consumer ring of one second (AUDIO_RING_FRAMES = 48 000 frames, 192 000 bytes): the producer moves only the head, the consumer only the tail.

    !
    Real-time priority is declared, not assumed. PipeWire collects samples on its real-time thread only if it gets SCHED_FIFO. declare_audio_priority() checks the threads of the audio path and logs whether they are FIFO/RR. Measured on 21 Aug 2026: on a kernel with CONFIG_RT_GROUP_SCHED and cgroup v2, SCHED_FIFO is refused to any process outside the root cgroup, so the LimitRTPRIO of the service is inert, and audio crackles when the desktop works. An independent pw-record on the same monitor hears the same crackles: the fault is born in the session's audio graph, not in the transport. That measurement is from Debian. On Ubuntu the checks' machines record «FIFO NOT OBTAINED: 3 threads out of 3 of the audio path run at NORMAL policy … RLIMIT_RTPRIO = 0» (round 1, GNOME box: the container's limit); on the virtual machines it was not recorded. rtkit-daemon matters in a second way: the real-time module of both PipeWire contexts (sound.c, capture.c) can stay in a D-Bus call to RealtimeKit for up to 25 s where the daemon is installed but does not start; that delays the dismantling of the stage and is the reason the end of a session is announced before it (9.15 “End of session in the page”).

    11.5 · The Opus encoder

    audio.c encodes with libopus directly since 30 Sep 2026: ffmpeg left the product for licence reasons (DECISIONS.md §10.22, §10.25), and libavcodec was only a wrapper around the same libopus.so.0. The parameters are the ones that wrapper used, and the packets were verified identical byte for byte (libopus 1.5.2, a one-off comparison against libavcodec that is not part of this repository; Ubuntu 26.04 has libopus 1.6.1, and the comparison was not repeated with it).

    One block in, one packet out. Measured on 17 Aug 2026: 1000 blocks in, 1000 packets out, no delay. opus_encode() is synchronous, so instant always belongs to the block that leaves. The encoder has a look-ahead of 312 samples (6.5 ms), read with OPUS_GET_LOOKAHEAD and written in the log at open; the decoder removes it, so it cancels end to end, but anyone using these timestamps for audio/video sync must know about it.

    Digital silence is not sent. A block whose samples are all exactly zero produces no datagram: the receiver places blocks at their absolute instant, so a gap is silence, which is what the block contained. Measured on 24 Aug 2026: on a still desktop with Opus, 50 datagrams per second of 3 bytes cost 589 kbit/s of padded packets and shared the congestion window with video. On by default since 24 Aug 2026 (user decision); the only switch is the server option --no-audio-silence, which the parent copies into the child's command line, and which also applies to the test tone of --audio-test, opened in the parent.

    11.6 · Playing audio in the page

    The page has its own Opus decoder: libopus 1.5.2 compiled to WebAssembly, decode only, embedded in page.html as base64 (D-006, decided 25 Sep 2026). AudioDecoder remains only as a declared fallback where WebAssembly is missing; PCM needs no decoder.

    Why. Firefox with a video playing in the session had short repeated sound gaps (0.1–0.4 s) and Chrome did not. Measured on 25 Sep 2026, 60 s on LXQt and KDE: Firefox with video 3–5 re-anchors, Firefox without video 0, Chrome 0, Firefox with video in PCM 0. The only difference was Firefox's AudioDecoder, which under video load returns blocks late and in bunches. A decoder that answers in the same call has no queue. The user rejected a Firefox-only branch: the same path runs on every browser. It runs on the main thread, because a block costs about 0.1 ms and the AudioContext lives there anyway.

    Scheduling. The page never waits for audio: a block that arrives late is dropped. Each block is an AudioBufferSourceNode started at base + instant, where the anchor base maps the server clock onto the AudioContext clock and is set at the first block to give a cushion of AUDIO_BUFFER_MS = 250 ms. Because playback time depends on the block's own timestamp and not on how many blocks arrived, a lost datagram no longer shortens the cushion for ever: before this cure (measured 21 Aug 2026 on a real Windows session) 61 lost blocks in 3½ minutes walked the queue from 419 down to 79 ms and produced three audible gaps.

    A new AudioContext and a fresh decoder are created at each connect(), and the old ones are closed first: Chrome refuses a seventh context per document, and the exception used to stop datagram reading for the rest of the session. aoff_ms() (playback time of a sample minus its server timestamp, plus outputLatency) is the audio half of the audio/video distance metric; it is updated only by blocks that actually played and expires after 600 ms without sound.

    11.7 · Clipboard at a glance

    The clipboard carries plain text only, in both directions (DECISIONS.md §5-ter.1, decided by the user on 9 Aug 2026 and confirmed on the 17th). Text covers almost every use, costs a few bytes and has no format negotiation; images would open the question of formats and of who pays the bandwidth when an 8 MB screenshot is copied on a link that is struggling.

    The protocol announces and pulls instead of pushing: whoever copies a whole document sends it to nobody until somebody pastes. The direction used most is device to session, and it is the harder one, because on the device side the clipboard belongs to the browser.

    11.8 · The clipboard messages and their limits

    Three messages on the clipboard channel (RCP §7.4), each transfer on its own unidirectional stream (high byte 0x02), so several transfers can be alive together.

    The Ctrl+V race. When the user pastes in the remote desktop with Ctrl+V, the keys and the announcement of the freshly copied local text travel on different streams, and the remote application may ask before the announcement arrives. Xpra delays every keystroke by 100 ms; for REMOTIX that is twice the latency budget, paid on every key. Two cheaper cures instead: the server queues a paste request while the client has announced nothing yet (rcp_clipboard_ask(), up to A_STREAM_MAX = 8 requests, one CLIPBOARD_ASK for the whole batch), and the page holds back the V of Ctrl+V until its own announcement has left (11.11 “Clipboard in the browser”).

    Always answer the compositor. A paste request from the session that is left unanswered leaves the pasting application waiting for ever, and the user sees a frozen desktop. The child, which owns the session, keeps up to CLIPBOARD_IN_FLIGHT = 8 requests in flight and answers “nothing” after CLIPBOARD_WAIT_MS = 4000 ms, or at once when no client can serve it. The parent may have no client attached, the client may vanish mid-transfer, and the parent itself may die: the debt towards the compositor stays where the session is.

    11.9 · Clipboard on GNOME

    On GNOME the clipboard belongs to Mutter (MetaSelection); the RemoteDesktop session only owns the door to it (EnableClipboard). clipboard.c (clipboard) uses that door on the session that mutter.c already opened.

    • The text types, in this order and nowhere else: text/plain;charset=utf-8, UTF8_STRING, text/plain (TEXT_TYPES).
    • The text is read in the module, on the clipboard thread, because the announcement needs its length; the limit, a zero in the middle and UTF-8 validity are checked there, in that order, where the text is still whole (the zero first: g_utf8_validate_len() already rejects it, so after it the zero test was unreachable and the log blamed UTF-8; the KDE module does the same); the last text copied in the session is remembered (clipboard_last_text()), so that a client that reconnects finds it (invariant I4).
    • The clipboard is enabled with empty options, so Mutter immediately reports who owns the selection; and at every attach the child reads the current selection with clipboard_read_now() before offering anything, because Mutter does not tell a new session who owns it and the clipboard would be lost.
    • GDBus delivers signals to the context of the subscribing thread, and no REMOTIX thread runs a GLib loop: the module runs a private context on its own thread. Its callbacks may write to the socket towards the parent (a SOCK_SEQPACKET send is atomic) but must never touch libei.
    • Mutter's X11 bridge is unconditional in both directions, so xclip works without a REMOTIX session: the clipboard benches have an external referee.

    11.10 · Clipboard on KDE and labwc

    On KDE Plasma and on labwc (XFCE and LXQt) the same module, clipboard_kde.c, speaks the wlroots data-control protocol on the user's Wayland socket: clipboard_open_kde() and clipboard_open_wlroots() differ only in the compositor name used in log lines. The child chooses with session_on_wlroots() first, then KDE, then GNOME. On KDE the socket found is KWin's: the screenless labwc that hosts the nested KWin has a runtime directory of its own (remotix-kwin-host inside XDG_RUNTIME_DIR), so the scan of wayland-0…wayland-9 (kwin_display_open()) never lands on it.

    i
    Clipboard managers and long offers. a clipboard manager on the user's desktop (Klipper on KDE, a Qt manager on LXQt) can interfere with the selection; the module follows the protocol and cannot tell it from an application. The offer lists are bounded: mimecap.h keeps at most MIME_MAX_TYPES = 64 names per offer, each at most MIME_MAX_LEN = 127 bytes, and the log shows at most MIME_LOG_TYPES = 8 of them and one “not text” line per MIME_LINE_WINDOW_MS ms (audit of the session, S-R10).

    11.11 · Clipboard in the browser

    In the browser the clipboard is not REMOTIX's: the page gets it only under conditions that differ on every engine. The rule of SPECS.md §9 applies to the letter: what cannot be done is declared, never faked.

    1. The hidden V. On every Ctrl+V with the clipboard on, the V is held (paste_hold()) until the page has read the local clipboard and, if it changed, its announcement has left; at most PASTE_HOLD_MS = 400 ms. Any key typed meanwhile, Ctrl's release included, queues behind it, or the desktop would receive a plain v. Only this key waits.
    2. Why the server queue is not enough. After a copy made in the remote desktop the clipboard belongs to the remote application, the remote paste does not ask the server, and the first paste gave the remote text (user test, 2 Oct 2026). And when the client had already announced A, a new copy of B was served as A because B's announcement was still on its way (measured, F-014D 7 of 8).
    3. Echoes. The page remembers the last text read or written (APPUNTI.last_read) and does not announce it again, unless the remote desktop was the last owner: then identical text is announced anyway, or the next paste would give the remote text.
    4. Size. Over 1 000 000 bytes the page does not announce and says so; an incoming announcement over the limit is a protocol error.

    Every step of the clipboard in the page is written to the page's own log because with the desktop full screen the page log cannot be read, and the silence of “no announcement arrived” had six possible causes in the page (measured on Firefox, 17 Aug 2026: the cause was the page's own preventDefault() on Ctrl+V). With the phone in hand the paste field must not open the system keyboard (10.10 “The on-screen keyboard on a phone”). Safari is not tested.

    11.12 · Audio and clipboard decisions

    The decisions of audio and clipboard, with the reason that made each one.

    11.13 · What was verified for audio and clipboard

    What the checks of prove/ exercise for audio and clipboard, and what they do not. They run on the development server, one virtual machine per desktop, with real browsers. What a virtual machine skips is only the private PulseAudio of the checks of avlib.py (ensure_pulse()), which does not exist there; check-audio.py itself runs.

    The automatic round of the 1.2.0 release passed these lines on the four virtual machines (GNOME 125 PASS and one known FAIL unrelated to audio and clipboard, the others 126 PASS). The owner's hand tests of 27 Nov 2026, on the four virtual machines and on a real machine with the four 26.04.1 live images, found clipboard, audio and video regular. On the Lubuntu machine the clipboard passes in both directions with the manager qlipper running. The silence heard once from a phone on Kubuntu was another program on the tablet, not REMOTIX. Not verified: Safari, a real phone through the automatic checks (the owner's phone tests were by hand), Firefox on Windows or macOS, the clipboard with a clipboard manager running on the desktop other than the qlipper case (for instance Klipper on Plasma), images or any non-text format (the protocol carries text only), and the microphone (not part of RCP/1).

    Chapter 12

    The four desktops

    12.1 · The four desktops side by side

    REMOTIX serves four Wayland desktops that belong to three compositor families; on Ubuntu 26.04 they are the four flavours Ubuntu (GNOME), Kubuntu (KDE Plasma), Xubuntu (XFCE) and Lubuntu (LXQt). Capture, input and clipboard talk to the compositor; birth, logout and settings talk to the desktop. XFCE and LXQt share labwc and therefore almost everything except the session. On KDE labwc is also present, but only as an invisible host for KWin, not as the desktop's compositor, and it is REMOTIX's own build of labwc, not the distribution's (12.7 “KDE Plasma: KWin nested in labwc”). Only Wayland sessions are served; X11 applications run through XWayland.

    Versions on Ubuntu 26.04. The versions below are those of the Ubuntu 26.04 packages as read in the studies of this tree (studio/1-gnome50-avvio.md, studio/3-sessione-ubuntu.md, studio/4-mutter50-cattura-input.md, studio/6-kubuntu-kwin-labwc.md, studio/7-xubuntu-lubuntu.md: packages opened in disposable containers) and, for dconf, on the virtual machine of the dconf measurements (docs/REGISTRO-problemi.md C5). They were not read again on a running machine for this manual. GNOME: gnome-shell, mutter and gnome-session 50.1, libei 1.5.0, dconf 0.49. KDE: Plasma and KWin 6.6.7. XFCE: xfce4-session 4.20.4 and libxfce4windowing 4.20.5. LXQt: lxqt-session 2.3.0 and lxqt-panel 2.3.2. The labwc of the distribution, used by XFCE and LXQt, is 0.9.3; REMOTIX's own labwc is labwc 0.9.3 with wlroots 0.19.2 patched. systemd is 259.9; the kernel of the live images on which the owner tried the release is 7.0 (REGISTRO C4). The display managers follow the flavour: GDM for Ubuntu, SDDM for Kubuntu and Lubuntu, LightDM for Xubuntu (dependencies read in studies 3, 6 and 7; the login screens of Ubuntu and of Kubuntu were tried on live images, those of Xubuntu and Lubuntu were not, see 14.5 “Local excludes remote and the session cap”). docs/DECISIONS-11.md §11.8 names GNOME 46, KDE Plasma 6.1, XFCE 4.20 and LXQt 2.0 as minimums, taken from the catalogue of an earlier multi-distribution product that this tree does not have; all four desktops of Ubuntu 26.04 are above those numbers, and nothing in session.c or in the package checks a minimum version.

    One desktop per machine. REMOTIX looks for the desktop that is installed; it does not arbitrate between desktops that coexist (DECISIONS.md §0.6). When two are found the choice is made and declared «ambiguous» (12.2 “How the desktop is recognised”). The package installs no desktop; with none of the four the server says so at startup (debian/control). One case is new in this tree: XFCE or LXQt found on a machine without the package labwc (a Recommends, so --no-install-recommends leaves it out). session_missing_component() says so before any child exists: the parent refuses the login after PAM's yes with 0x0E (delivery_verdict() in main.c), no process is spawned and no logind session is made (14.5 “Local excludes remote and the session cap”); the postinst also warns, at configuration time, on a machine that has XFCE or LXQt and neither GNOME nor Plasma.

    Whose settings these are (DECISIONS.md §8.2-bis, the rule of 13 Nov 2026). From the remote desktop the user may customise the desktop (look, themes, shortcuts, panels) and the changes stay, as they do locally. The user can never suspend, reboot, power off or lock the server. REMOTIX imposes its rules only inside the remote session and writes almost nothing in the user's settings: at the monitor the user finds everything as it was. The ban on suspend, reboot and power-off is the polkit rule of the package (ch. 14 “Security model”, ch. 15 “The package”); what the session imposes on the desktop's own settings is a belt that hides buttons and avoids false notices. Four exceptions remain in the code and are described below: on GNOME the small file ~/.config/dconf/remotix (the layout, three keys) and, while the session lasts, the empty file ~/.local/share/gnome-shell/lock-warning-shown (removed at the end if REMOTIX made it); on XFCE the copy and restore of a few locked keys; and a one-time restore of values written by earlier REMOTIX versions (GNOME and LXQt) (12.10 “What the session imposes, desktop by desktop”).

    12.2 · How the desktop is recognised

    recognize_desktop() in session.c decides once per process, from the programs found in PATH, and keeps the reason in words for the server's start line (session_desktop_explain()). Parent and child both call it and must reach the same answer; they do, because both run on the same machine and read the same files. The parent searches the PATH of the service; the child's PATH is the one PAM composes for a login (12.3 “The composed environment”), so the agreement holds as long as the programs are in /usr/bin, where Ubuntu packages them (comment of recognize_desktop()).

    • Machines with two or more desktops installed. The programs alone do not say which is the machine's. When more than one is present, declared_desktop() reads the configuration of the machine's active display manager: lightdm's user-session (directories read in lightdm's own order, then /etc/lightdm/lightdm.conf) and sddm's Session of the [Autologin] group (/usr/lib/sddm/sddm.conf.d, /etc/sddm.conf.d, /etc/sddm.conf). The active manager is read from /etc/X11/default-display-manager or the target of /etc/systemd/system/display-manager.service (active_display_manager()); if it is another one, such as gdm3 (the Ubuntu flavour), the lightdm and sddm files are leftovers and are ignored. The session name is cleaned (.desktop stripped, only [A-Za-z0-9._+-]) and mapped to a desktop by desktop_of_session_name(): the words xfce or xubuntu give XFCE, lxqt or lubuntu give LXQt, plasma, kde or kubuntu give KDE, gnome or ubuntu give GNOME. They are asked in that order because xubuntu, lubuntu and kubuntu contain «ubuntu»; the comment records the limit that ubuntu as a substring also catches flavours outside the four supported ones (ubuntustudio, ubuntu-budgie). With no usable declaration the order of the table stays. The session a single user picks at login is not read.
    • Xubuntu has both GNOME markers. With the Recommends accepted, a Xubuntu machine has gnome-shell (50.1, pulled in by other packages even without Recommends) and gnome-session-bin (which carries /usr/bin/gnome-session, pulled in with the Recommends): it enters the branch of two or more desktops and is decided by lightdm's declaration user-session=xubuntu (the file 60-xubuntu.conf of /usr/share/lightdm/lightdm.conf.d). With --no-install-recommends gnome-session is not there and there is no ambiguity. Source: package contents simulated in a container (study 7 §3); the owner ran the release on the live Xubuntu image and reported that everything worked, without a log being read.
    • The XFCE marker is xfce4-session, not labwc: labwc is the compositor shared with LXQt and remains a precondition.
    • A machine with none of the four is declared SESSION_DESKTOP_NONE: REMOTIX does not fall back to GNOME. The comment in recognize_desktop() records that such a fallback once made failures blame someone else's drop-in and Mutter while the real cause was a missing desktop.
    • DesktopSession travels as a uint32_t between parent and child, so new values go at the end: GNOME 0, KDE 1, XFCE 2, none 3, LXQt 4 (session.h).
    • Capture, input, clipboard and stage rebuild ask session_on_wlroots() (XFCE or LXQt), not «is it XFCE»: with five comparisons against XFCE, LXQt would have fallen silently into the GNOME/KDE branch. Every desktop branch in session.c is placed in front of the GNOME code with an explicit predicate (e_kde(), e_xfce(), e_lxqt()).

    12.3 · The composed environment

    The environment of the session is composed, not inherited (compose_environment()). Whatever the starter carries ends up in the user's systemd manager and in D-Bus activation, where it outlives the compositor; a stray LC_ALL=C from an SSH shell once stopped every application from opening (the comment in session.h). The table is what the function writes.

    The language. A local graphical login gives the session the language the user chose in the desktop settings and otherwise the system's one; the remote session does the same (child_locale_read() in child.c). LANG is the first item of Languages= (or the value of the older Language=) in /var/lib/AccountsService/users/<name>, read by the child as root before it changes identity, because that folder is root:root 0700; with no such choice it is the LANG that pam_env put in the PAM environment from /etc/default/locale (the second pam_env line of src/remotix.pam). The system's LC_* and LANGUAGE come from the same PAM environment (at most CHILD_LOCALE_MAX = 12 of them). Every value is checked for plain characters before it is written into an execve environment, and local_utf8() in session.c still checks that the locale exists and is UTF-8, falling back to C.UTF-8 with a log line (until 1.0.1 the language was always C.UTF-8). All these names are in OUR_VARIABLES (12.5 “Ending a session and tidying up”).

    The language in the user manager (KDE, XFCE, LXQt). On these three desktops the units of the session (KWin and its labwc, labwc, the panel) are born with the environment of the user's systemd manager, which pam_systemd made with the system's language, not with the one composed for the start command. manager_set_locale() (session.c) therefore puts the LANG, LC_* and LANGUAGE words of the composed environment into the manager with SetEnvironment before the session starts; if the bus does not answer a ⚠ line says the desktop's units may get the system's. At the end of a normal session the values go back as they were (they are in OUR_VARIABLES, so the snapshot of birth restores them); in the close for a local login (session_clear_out_light()) they stay in the manager on purpose: it is the language chosen by that same user, the one the local desktop now coming in uses too, and taking it away could take it from under that desktop. They are put right at the next remote birth, or go away with the manager. GNOME needs none of this: gnome-session exports its whole environment.

    i
    Language on KDE and XFCE. on KDE the language of the desktop follows the user's own ~/.config/plasma-localerc, as at a local login. REMOTIX hands the right language to the session (the processes of the desktop carry it), but Plasma reads that file, which it creates at its first start, and where it holds another language it wins. A user who has already used KDE in one language changes it from KDE's own Settings; REMOTIX does not write that file. On XFCE xfconfd stays in the system's language (register entry H2). The formats (LC_* chosen as «Formats» in the settings) do not reach the remote desktop (register entry H1).

    The PATH is the one PAM gives to a login. The child opens a PAM session with the service remotix (12.4 “How a session is born”) and takes the PATH that pam_env composed from /etc/environment: on Ubuntu that file holds /snap/bin, the sbin folders and the games (comment of child_path_ok()). The value is accepted only if it is a list of absolute folders, without a .. component, of plain characters and at most 400 long; otherwise the fixed fallback /usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin is used (become_and_exec() in child.c). src/remotix.pam warns above its pam_env line not to add user_readenv=1: the user would then choose the session's PATH from ~/.pam_environment.

    The session's own folders. A local login of a session puts the session's folders in front of XDG_CONFIG_DIRS and XDG_DATA_DIRS. The system does it in one of two ways, and the rule of the code is to do what the system itself would do (comment above local_login_adds_folders()): /etc/X11/Xsession.d/60x11-common_xdg_path, where the login runs Xsession.d at all (an X11 session file, or any session under lightdm), and /etc/profile.d/xdg_dirs_desktop_session.sh, the same logic in profile form, which every login that reads /etc/profile runs, notably gnome-session itself, which on Wayland re-executes in a login shell (study 3 §2). Both exist on Ubuntu 26.04 (x11-common 1:7.7+26ubuntu1 and gnome-session-common, read from the packages). REMOTIX sets SHELL empty, so nothing would run the scripts, and local_session() does their work: it finds the session's name (GNOME: the session REMOTIX starts, ubuntu; the other desktops: the session the display manager declares if it names the chosen desktop, else the first session file of that desktop that has a folder of its own), then /etc/xdg/xdg-<name> and /usr/share/<name> (never for gnome) if they exist, and /usr/share/gnome when the profile snippet and the folder are there and the desktop is GNOME or the session's local login is X11. REMOTIX's own folders stay in front, these come next, the system's after. On Ubuntu GNOME the session's data folder /usr/share/ubuntu holds only entries that hide programs (such as the first-run assistant), and /etc/xdg/xdg-ubuntu does not exist (study 3 §2.2, read from the packages). One log line (D-153) states the session name, the config folder, the data folder and the common folder that were found. Declared differences from the real scripts: the config folder is added only if it exists, GDMSESSION is not set, and ~/.gnomerc and ~/.profile are not run.

    The render node. wlroots is given the card chosen by card_pick_desktop() (src/card_pick.c): the BIOS primary card (PCI boot_vga = 1) if it is capable (it has a render node, the node opens and card_can_draw() creates a buffer through GBM), otherwise the capable card with the lowest PCI address, because the node names renderD128 and renderD129 can swap between boots. If nodes open but no card can draw, WLR_RENDERER=pixman is set and declared; otherwise wlroots would fall back to software in silence. GNOME chooses its own card (Mutter's Boot VGA); REMOTIX does not force it. Every choice is one log line in the session area giving node, PCI address, driver and the reason (card_say()). The encoder's fallback card is a separate matter (ch. 7 “Video encoding”).

    12.4 · How a session is born

    The server never starts a desktop itself. The per-user child (ch. 3 “Startup and life cycle”) does, from its loop: when the state of the session is «dead» and no birth was requested in the last BIRTH_REIN_MS (12 s), it calls session_spawn(), which returns at once. The desktop shows up on the bus on a later round and the child's retry loop (STAGE_BIRTH_RETRY_MS = 200 ms while the compositor is unreachable) mounts the capture then. The blocking session_ensure() with its 40 s wait (WAIT_STARTUP_MS) still exists in session.c but the product no longer calls it. Before any step, session_spawn() returns without doing anything, and says why in the session area, if no desktop was recognised or if session_missing_component() names a missing compositor (labwc for XFCE and LXQt): «I am not making anything be born».

    The logind session

    Before any desktop code runs, become_and_exec() in child.c opens a real logind session for the user with PAM: pam_start with the service remotix, XDG_SESSION_TYPE=wayland, XDG_SESSION_CLASS=user, no XDG_SEAT (a session without a seat is headless by construction), the client's address as PAM_RHOST, then pam_open_session. The class must be user: manager is what lingering gives, and it is not enough for Mutter. pam_end() is called without pam_close_session(): logind keeps the session as long as the leader process lives, and the leader is the child after the exec, so the stage outlives the client because the child outlives it.

    On Ubuntu 26.04 nothing has to be carried across the execve. The comment in become_and_exec() records that since systemd 258 logind tracks a session by the pidfd of its leader, not by a fifo: pam_systemd opens the pidfd of the calling process and returns a dummy descriptor, and the exit of the leader stops the session at once; the child keeps its pid across the execve, so the session lasts as long as remotix-child does. This tree is born with systemd 259.9 and no longer looks for the descriptor or passes --session-fd. The comment states the limit: a logind older than 258 still in memory during an upgrade would hand pam_systemd a fifo and the session would close at the execve; the case is excluded on a freshly installed Ubuntu 26.04. Source: the code comment and study 5 §7.1 (systemd sources); the behaviour was not observed with an old logind.

    The steps of session_spawn()

    1. Clear-out and snapshot. session_clear_out_handler() removes what a session that ended badly left in the user manager, then session_snapshot_handler() writes the previous value of each variable REMOTIX is about to set (OUR_VARIABLES) into $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/remotix/manager-before (12.5 “Ending a session and tidying up”). dconf_profile_reinstate() then writes the session's dconf profile (or puts it back, if the end of the session before had neutralised it); in the new model this is where the runtime file is written for the first time, when the child's start found no live desktop (GNOME, 12.6 “GNOME: headless Shell and session dconf”). The snapshot can be old after a close made from the root side: the root side's close does not delete it, so the next clean-up may take it for valid (docs/REGISTRO-problemi.md E3, a known and non-blocking limit).
    2. The drop-in (write_dropin()): zz-remotix-monitor.conf in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/systemd/user.control/<unit>.d/ for GNOME's Shell unit and KWin's unit; nothing for XFCE and LXQt, where the compositor is not a unit. On GNOME the folder is the one of the instance (org.gnome.Shell@ubuntu.service.d, or org.gnome.Shell@user.service.d), never the template's, which would also apply to the Shell of the login screen. It is always re-read after daemon-reload (systemctl --user show -p ExecStart): if another drop-in wins, or --virtual-monitor is still there, the birth is refused with a ⛔ line, because the session would have a monitor of its own and the user would watch an empty screen. If the drop-in is not in force the desktop is not born.
    3. Guards. The user manager must not be «stopping» (systemctl --user is-system-running: a session born in a dying manager dies without writing anything). The previous session must be really over (inactive_unit(), which on GNOME looks at three units, see 12.6 “GNOME: headless Shell and session dconf”; the refusal line now names the unit that is still busy). A pipewire-pulse older than the current pipewire is a leftover and is stopped; its socket brings it back attached to the right pipewire. The first two say no and return, and the child's retry loop tries again; the third does not stop the birth.
    4. Settings before the command, because gnome-session starts the Shell first and a key written afterwards would hold only for the next session: session_dconf_birth() and session_gnome_lock_warning() on GNOME, then session_settings() (12.10 “What the session imposes, desktop by desktop”).
    5. start() composes the environment and the command, then runs setsid --fork sh -c with the user's home as working directory. The shell line begins with exec >>log 2>&1: the session's output goes to session.log (16.5 “Where the log lines go”). Because of setsid --fork the desktop lives outside the server's unit and outside the child, so neither the unit's kill nor the death of the child ends it by itself. Since 17 Nov 2026 (§11.56) the product ends it on purpose: an orderly stop of the service closes every desktop (3.11 “Stopping the service”), and a desktop left without a child is ended by the root side within about 10 s unless its user returns first. A reattach while the child lives finds the same compositor and windows (the claim of the comments in session.c and child.c; the reattach checks of prove/ exercise it, ch. 17 “Testing”).

    The command that starts each desktop (start()):

    The primary client and the size race. labwc's headless output is born 1280×720 and the client's size arrives about 200 ms later (wlr_ask_size() in wlroots.c). If pcmanfm-qt or the XFCE panel is born in between, its wallpaper or its position is made for the wrong size and is never redone: the comments in measured_primary() record about one birth in 13 with a 1280×720 wallpaper on LXQt, and an XFCE panel that redrew itself at every frame on one NVIDIA test. The cure is that the primary client is an sh that runs wlr-randr --output <first output> --custom-mode WxH and then execs xfce4-session or lxqt-session (same pid, so «primary dead, labwc exits» stays true). It is a ;, not &&: if wlr-randr fails, the session is born anyway and the late request remains. That is why wlr-randr is a Recommends of the package.

    12.5 · Ending a session and tidying up

    A session ends in three ways: the user chooses «Log Out» in the desktop, the product asks for it, or the compositor dies. The next login is always a new session (SPECS.md §5.2-bis): the child does not remake a desktop the user closed.

    The user logs out

    The child's loop watches the state of the session. If it was alive and becomes dead, the child records session_closed_by_user, sends the parent MSG_SESSION_FINISHED (the page receives the farewell 0x10 and returns to the login form), runs session_clear_out_scope(), session_dconf_neutralise() and session_clear_out_handler_due(), and then raises SIGTERM on itself (the box at §7.6 in child.c). The last step is the correction of 17 Nov 2026: before it, only GNOME ended the child at logout (by an accident of GIO raising SIGTERM); on the other three the child stayed, held the logind session and the next login resumed it. Now the child dies of the signal on every desktop, the pidfd of the session's leader fires and logind closes the session (the scope has already been emptied). A compositor that dies by itself looks the same from outside and is treated the same way.

    The farewell is said before the stage is dismantled

    session_over_early() in child.c (19 Nov 2026) sends MSG_SESSION_FINISHED before the capture, input and clipboard are taken down, not after.
