The comment records the measurement that made it necessary (Ubuntu 26.04 box, 18 Nov 2026): taking the stage down waits for PipeWire, whose module-rt can be held for up to 25 s by a D-Bus call to RealtimeKit wherever rtkit-daemon is installed but cannot start (containers, hardened machines), and the page stayed on the last image for 17 s without a word. It is said only on a certain death: session_life() has three answers, SESSION_LIFE_ALIVE (0), SESSION_LIFE_DEAD (1: the bus answered and the compositor's name has no owner) and SESSION_LIFE_UNKNOWN (2: no bus, a call failed or timed out), and only DEAD sends the farewell, because the farewell cannot be taken back. KDE is left out (stage_kwin): a KWin restarted by systemd leaves its name without an owner for a moment, so «no owner» is not certain there. The parent also counts the child as «closing» from that message on, so a login in the meantime gets the true 0x0E «still closing» and never a desktop that is going away. session_alive() is now session_life() equal to ALIVE. When the input channel has closed and the answer is UNKNOWN, the child asks again, at most once a second, up to EIS_UNKNOWN_ROUNDS = 3 rounds; if it stays UNKNOWN the old road holds (the stage is dismantled, with no early farewell). The reason, from the comment: at a logout the user's session bus itself goes away for a moment (dbus.service is stopped by gnome-session-restart-dbus.service), so UNKNOWN can come exactly when the session has just ended. 3.9 “Ending a graphical session” has the life-cycle side.

    The product ends it

    session_terminate() calls really_terminate(), which asks politely, waits, and then forces. The wait is wait_until_done(): up to WAIT_EXIT_MS = 10 s, polling every CHECK_INTERVAL_MS = 500 ms, until session_alive() is false and inactive_unit() is true. Success is followed by session_clear_out_scope() and session_clear_out_handler(). If the desktop is already gone when really_terminate() starts, the close counts as done only if inactive_unit() agrees; if the session name is off the bus but units or processes of the desktop are still there, the log says so («not claimed as closed») and the normal road goes on.

    i
    XFCE names, and why XFCE and LXQt are checked by process. on XFCE the bus name is org.xfce.SessionManager and the interface is org.xfce.Session.Manager (one more dot); confusing them gives «unknown method», which looks like «the session does not answer». With force, kill_xfce() sends SIGTERM, not SIGKILL, so labwc closes its clients. On XFCE and LXQt there is no unit to ask, so inactive_unit() looks at processes: systemctl --user is-active on a unit that does not exist answers «inactive», which would make the guard against a second session vanish silently (the comment in inactive_unit()).

    What is left in the user manager

    What the product puts into the user's systemd manager outlives the session if the manager does (the test containers and any user with lingering enabled): the drop-ins under user.control and the variables that gnome-session, startplasma-wayland or labwc export from the composed environment. A user who then logs in at the monitor would inherit them (on XFCE a «Log Out» that does not log out). The cure is four gestures:

    • session_snapshot_handler() at birth, before touching anything: the previous value of each variable in OUR_VARIABLES (DCONF_PROFILE, XDG_CONFIG_DIRS, XDG_DATA_DIRS, XCURSOR_THEME, XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP, GDK_BACKEND, the WLR_* variables and the others in the list) goes into a file that exists as long as the manager does. The list has four entries that only appear with GNOME 50 (GNOME_DESKTOP_SESSION_ID, QT_IM_MODULE, QT_IM_MODULES, XMODIFIERS): the first process that has them is gnome-session-init-worker (comment, read from /proc/<pid>/environ of a live session on 18 Nov 2026), and with lingering they stayed in the manager after the Log Out.
    • session_clear_out_handler() when the session is over (and at the child's start and at birth, for what a crash left): REMOTIX's drop-ins are removed with daemon-reload, its variables are put back as they were or removed, xfconfd is restarted if it had the session's folder, and on XFCE xfce_restore_keys() puts the user's values back. A DCONF_PROFILE that is REMOTIX's own, left in a manager that outlived an upgrade, is removed too (dconf_env_is_ours()). Only with the session dead: with a live session it would pull the ground from under a working desktop. Without a snapshot (a manager born before) only variables carrying REMOTIX's mark are removed, and it is said. If the session still answers when the child leaves, the child retries for at most CLEAR_OUT_EXIT_WAIT_MS = 2 s and otherwise leaves the work to the next child, with a ⛔ line.
    • session_dconf_neutralise() (GNOME): a belt for when that clear-out is late. It is called by every road that ends a session (the user's logout, SIGTERM, the light close, the child's exit, and the root side's fork after a local login), and does three things: it removes the file lock-warning-shown if REMOTIX made it, it neutralises the fallback's profile file, and it deals with the runtime profile as described in 12.6 “GNOME: headless Shell and session dconf”. Never under a live desktop.
    • session_clear_out_scope(): after the session has exited, what is left in the session's logind scope and belongs to the user (programs that detached from the session manager by D-Bus activation or a double fork) gets SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 2 s. The comment records the case: after a XFCE logout, localsearch-3 and geoclue's agent stayed in the scope.
    !
    Known limit. two places treat «I could not ask the desktop whether it is alive» as «it is closed»: the clean-up of the user manager (near session_alive() in session.c) and the child's exit (child.c). The preparation of the session's dconf was corrected on 19 Nov 2026 to use the three answers; these two were not. It was not corrected because the cases are forced (an old snapshot, lingering and a failed birth together; a live desktop that does not answer at that very moment) and cannot be provoked on the bench (docs/REGISTRO-problemi.md E3).

    The close for a local login. When a local login of the same user is held in PAM and the remote desktop must go first (14.5 “Local excludes remote and the session cap”), the orderly step on KDE waits KDE_PRELOCAL_ORDERLY_MS = 5 s instead of 10 before the forced one. Plasma waits without limit for a program that does not close by itself (a «save changes?» dialog, a terminal running a program) and nobody is there to answer, so the ten seconds were only a delay of the local login. Every other close and every other desktop keeps WAIT_EXIT_MS. The forced step is StopUnit of graphical-session.target, which takes the whole desktop down. If the parent that asked for the close is gone by then (the root side released its hold and the local desktop may be starting), the forced step is not taken and a line says so (force_refused()). The owner saw on the four live images that the local login starts a few seconds later for this reason, and accepted it.

    KDE: a Log Out that stops halfway

    «Log Out» calls plasma-shutdown, which stops plasma-workspace.target and then asks the user manager to stop graphical-session.target, which is what really stops KWin, plasmashell and the rest. If any unit has a start job queued at that moment (the comment names xdg-desktop-portal in its first seconds), systemd refuses the stop («Transaction … is destructive»), plasma-shutdown ignores the refusal and exits, and the desktop stays up (docs/REGISTRO-problemi.md D, Kubuntu 26.04, Plasma 6.6, 18 Nov 2026). The first remedy of 17 Nov watched plasma-workspace.target seen active in this child's life and then not active while org.kde.KWin is still on the bus. On Plasma 6.6 that signal never fires: plasma-shutdown never stops the workspace target, so the logout was lost. It stays in the code as a second road.

    The first road is now the name org.kde.Shutdown. plasma-shutdown owns it for the whole of its run and releases it when it exits. shutdown_name_listen() subscribes to NameOwnerChanged on a private GLib context that the watch turns at each round (a poll would miss a short run). A release alone is not a logout: plasma-shutdown is also started to save the session and holds the name while an application asks «save changes?», and if the user cancels it exits without stopping anything. So after the release shutdown_released_judge() asks ksmserver (isShuttingDown): true arms the watch; false (cancelled, or not a logout) or no answer forces nothing and writes one line, a choice recorded in the comment so as not to lose a user's unsaved work. After a grace of KDE_LOGOUT_GRACE_MS = 4 s, in which the normal road wins if it works, the stop of graphical-session.target is asked again every KDE_LOGOUT_RETRY_MS = 3 s: KDE_LOGOUT_TRIES = 10 attempts with mode fail (as plasma-shutdown does), then up to 10 more with mode replace, which passes even with a start job queued; one log line per attempt. After 20 refusals (about a minute) session_kde_logout_watch() returns true (it returns a boolean for this purpose) and the child closes the session by the product's own road (terminate_and_clear()), with the line «giving up on it». The function runs at every round of the child's loop and limits itself to one look per second.

    Limits declared in the comment: logoutAndShutdown and logoutAndReboot of Plasma 6.6.7 do not release the name, so a power-off or reboot requested in the first seconds and refused would stay lost (reachable only without the menu entries, which REMOTIX removes); and a restart of KWin by its wrapper during the wait resets the request (rare). A lesson recorded in REGISTRO D: a first remedy, stopped in review and never released, closed the session as soon as plasma-shutdown started, so also with an unsaved document or after «Cancel». What the comment records as measured about ksmserver's answer: true in the lost case, where it stays true until resetLogout; one NoReply was seen once, and that case forces nothing.

    !
    Scope of the KDE watch. whether a refused stop can also happen on other desktops was not investigated in the code; only KDE has this watch. On XFCE the register records the opposite case: XFCE refuses a Log Out requested while the session is still starting («must be at rest»), seen on 17 and 18 Nov; the cure is the force after the ten seconds (kill_xfce()), and the same behaviour was confirmed in the sources of xfce4-session 4.20.4 (study 7 §14). The code does not retry the polite request (12.11 “Behaviours of the four desktops worth knowing”).

    12.6 · GNOME: headless Shell and session dconf

    GNOME is started through the machine's own GNOME session (on Ubuntu 26.04 the session ubuntu), with a systemd drop-in that makes gnome-shell headless and without monitors: the only monitor is the virtual one that the capture creates with RecordVirtual, and that is where GNOME puts its top bar and dock.

    The session on Ubuntu 26.04

    1. Which session. gnome_session() chooses it as described in 12.4 “How a session is born”: on stock Ubuntu the only candidate is ubuntu (/usr/share/wayland-sessions/ubuntu.desktop: Exec=/usr/bin/gnome-session --session=ubuntu, DesktopNames=ubuntu;GNOME), so XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP is ubuntu:GNOME. The value matters: Ubuntu's defaults are gschema overrides keyed to ubuntu in XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP, and with plain GNOME the Shell would have Adwaita's look (comment in compose_environment(), study 3 §4.1). The session file is read from the package and is not under REMOTIX's control.
    2. Which Shell unit. On GNOME 50 the Shell is a template, org.gnome.Shell@.service (SESSION_UNIT_SHELL_MODEL), whose instance is the mode: gnome-session@ubuntu.target requires org.gnome.Shell@ubuntu.service, gnome-session@gnome.target requires org.gnome.Shell@user.service (study 1 §3.3, read from the packages). unit_shell() therefore asks the user manager for the Requires of gnome-session@<session>.target (systemctl --user show -p Requires --value) and takes the instance that is not the template; if there is none it refuses, with a ⛔ line («I do not recognise the Shell unit»), and does not guess a name. The old name org.gnome.Shell@wayland.service does not exist on Ubuntu 26.04.
    3. The drop-in. zz-remotix-monitor.conf in the instance directory under $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/systemd/user.control/org.gnome.Shell@ubuntu.service.d/ replaces ExecStart with gnome-shell --headless --no-x11 --mode=%i. The --mode=%i is essential: the instance name is how the Shell learns its mode (the GNOME_SHELL_SESSION_MODE variable is overridden by the option), and the mode ubuntu is where the dock, the colours and the extensions live (the next paragraph). No root, gone at reboot, named zz- so that it applies after any system drop-in. The checks of write_dropin() are those of the previous section.
    4. The previous session must be over: inactive_unit() asks three units of the user manager, gnome-session-manager@<session>.service, gnome-session-restart-dbus.service and, new with GNOME 50, graphical-session.target, and says which one is busy. A session started while GNOME restarts the session bus dies without writing anything (the comment, measured 16 Aug 2026); with graphical-session.target still active gnome-session-init-worker aborts with «A graphical session is already running!» (comment, read in gnome-session's sources) while start() would answer true all the same.
    5. Capture and input use Mutter's own D-Bus interfaces, not xdg-desktop-portal (the portal asks permission from a user in front of the screen, which a session without a monitor cannot give). The order in mutter.c is fixed and punished by different errors if permuted: RemoteDesktop.CreateSession, ScreenCast.CreateSession declaring remote-desktop-session-id, RemoteDesktop.Session.Start, RecordVirtual, Stream.Start. Keyboard and pointer go through libei (ConnectToEIS); the clipboard through the same RemoteDesktop session. The size of the virtual monitor is part of the PipeWire negotiation, so a new size is a renegotiation (docs/LESSONS.md §3 table, question 13; ch. 6 “Screen capture”). Study 4 reads in Mutter 50's sources that each monitor change republishes the stream's parameters (one more renegotiation after every resize) and that with libeis 1.5.0 the answer to a client's ping leaves only when Mutter releases the event; this is not verified in the code of this manual.
    6. The pointer. Mutter delivers the cursor as metadata (cursor-mode=2); cursor.c turns it into the wire's CURSOR_SHAPE and discards sizes the protocol forbids.
    7. The first movement is sent twice. The comment in input_pointer() (input.c) records that the first absolute motion after the pointer device is (re)started reaches the windows with one of the two coordinates at 0, so a click made at once (a tap from a phone) lands on the edge of the screen; the following motions, and the same position sent a second time right after the first, are exact. The first one is therefore sent twice (pointer_primed); a compositor that needs no such thing ignores the repeat. The comment marks it as to be removed when Mutter is fixed (measured on Mutter 51; Ubuntu 26.04 has Mutter 50.1, where it was not measured).

    The Ubuntu mode and its extensions. The mode ubuntu is the file /usr/share/gnome-shell/modes/ubuntu.json of the package gnome-shell-common: parentMode user, the Yaru style sheet and the enabled extensions ubuntu-dock@ubuntu.com, ubuntu-appindicators@ubuntu.com, ding@rastersoft.com (the icons of the desktop), tiling-assistant@ubuntu.com, snapd-prompting@canonical.com, snapd-search-provider@canonical.com and web-search-provider@ubuntu.com (study 3 §1.3, from the package; the extensions come from gnome-shell-ubuntu-extensions). REMOTIX loads none of them and writes nothing about them: they arrive with the mode. The earlier tree recorded, on 30 Sep 2026, a remote Ubuntu 26.04 session with the dock on the left, the 26.04 wallpaper and the orange Home folder of the icons extension (study 3 §3.1); that was not repeated for this manual.

    Leaving and coming back. The way out is Logout(1) then Logout(2) and the deciding fact is the three units above (12.5 “Ending a session and tidying up”). On the Ubuntu 26.04 container box rxu-gnome (18 Nov 2026, study 12 §A) the Log Out asked 1, 2, 4 and 8 s after the desktop was ready ended with no session, no process and no runtime folder left in 48 attempts out of 48, from the page and from the desktop. The rejoin right after a Log Out was either admitted with a working desktop 1.5 to 2.9 s later or refused with the generic «could not open your session» text (0x0E: the child is still closing); no blank screen was seen, and the guard of the three units never fired in the roughly 100 tests of that study, because the parent's rule on a closing child stops the rejoin first. Those runs predate the early farewell of 19 Nov 2026 (12.5 “Ending a session and tidying up”).

    The session is born in the Overview, and without the lock notice. The first thing a person sees and the first tap go to the Activities Overview (12.11 “Behaviours of the four desktops worth knowing”). On the first desktop of any user, GNOME 50's Shell would also show «Screen Lock disabled», because a session without GDM has no screen lock: the Shell touches lock-warning-shown in its data folder and, only if it has just created it, shows the notice. session_gnome_lock_warning() makes that empty file first, at birth, before the Shell starts. This is one of the four writes in the user's home (12.1 “The four desktops side by side”) and the product's rule is that the session leaves nothing of its own there: a sign in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/remotix/lock-warning-made records the inode and ctime of the file, whether REMOTIX also made the folder, and the folder's path, because the end of the session may be done by another process (the child that exits, the root side's fork). session_dconf_neutralise() removes the file only if it is still that same empty regular file, without following links, and removes the folder only if REMOTIX made it and it is empty; otherwise it says that the file was left alone.

    The session's dconf (D-015)

    What the session imposes on GNOME is a table of keys, DCONF_KEYS in session.c: 24 keys, 21 with a value and a lock and three with the lock only (the keyboard layout, whose value changes during the session). The Shell and the gsd-* daemons read them through dconf; the user's own file ~/.config/dconf/user must never be written. Since 19 Nov 2026 the rules reach the session in the following way, which is different from the model of the Debian 1.0.0 release; that model survives, as a declared fallback, further down.

    Why the model changed. docs/REGISTRO-problemi.md C5: on the first real Ubuntu 26.04.1 live image (19 Nov 2026) the live installer showed «Something went wrong» (Unknown DConf source) and the Firmware Updater and the Security Center said No DConf source to write to; the desktop opened all the same. The 1.0.0 model put a profile of three layers (file-db and service-db lines) under $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/remotix/dconf/ and pointed DCONF_PROFILE at it. The Flutter programs of Ubuntu have a dconf reader of their own that knows only user-db and system-db and, at any other line, drops the whole profile (the measurement lists the strings of the program's libapp.so, among them «Unknown DConf source» and «No DConf source to write to»: /media/REMOTIX-UBUNTU/log/dconf-misure/q2-strings.txt on the dev server), and a confined snap has another XDG_RUNTIME_DIR and cannot even open a profile under REMOTIX's folder. The containers had no snaps and AppArmor did not act in them, and Debian does not have those programs, which is why it had not been seen before. After the change the journal of the same live had zero such errors and the installer started in the remote session without an error (state «WAITING»; docs/STORIA-ubuntu-26.04.md, 19 Nov 2026).

    A lock in a database hides the layers above it and cannot be written by the session. The top layer user-db:user stays the writable one, so a wallpaper, a theme or a shortcut changed from the remote desktop stays and is there at the monitor (comment of the code). REGISTRO C5 records the user file as identical after the test sessions, and the sha256 of ~/.config/dconf/user read after the logout was the same in five test cycles on the measurement machine (ciclo5.out to ciclo7.out, ripiego.out and t2.out in /media/REMOTIX-UBUNTU/log/dconf-correzione/ on the dev server). The twenty-one keys with a value get it from system-db:remotix; the three lock-only keys of the layout take their value from user-db:remotix, below the lock. On the stock Ubuntu there is no /etc/dconf/profile/user: the base profile is the default alone, and the log says «base profile: user-db:user» (study 3 §4.1; the measurement logs).

    No DCONF_PROFILE. In the normal case the variable is not set in the child's environment (session_dconf_prepare() removes it), not in the environment composed for the session and not in the user manager. The reason, from the comment: a confined snap has another runtime folder, does not see the file and uses the plain user-db:user. Exceptions: an administrator's own DCONF_PROFILE, if it is in the child's environment or only in the user manager's (for example environment.d), stays the base profile (dconf_base_profile() reads it as dconf would: an absolute path, or a name looked for in /etc/dconf/profile and in <XDG_DATA_DIRS>/dconf/profile/<name>), and in the session the variable is set to REMOTIX's runtime file, otherwise dconf would ignore it. The first line of the runtime file then also carries [referenced by DCONF_PROFILE: rewrite, never remove]: a variable that points at a missing profile would mean no settings at all, so the end of the session rewrites the file and never removes it. The case of a variable only in the user manager was seen once, in a test on the Ubuntu virtual machine (docs/REGISTRO-problemi.md E3); the case of a variable in the child's own environment is verified by reading the code only.

    What the child does at its start. The runtime file is a window onto every program of the user, a local login included, so a child that dies between its start and the birth must not leave it. session_dconf_prepare() therefore asks session_life() and acts on the three answers (REGISTRO C5, «life of the desktop at the child's start»):

    The DEAD branch was seen in the tests (a service restart with a live desktop: the file was removed when the child exited and written again at the next birth, t2.out of the same folder). The ALIVE branch is the case of a child that finds a live desktop again (the comment's words); it was not provoked as such in the tests that were read. The UNKNOWN branch is verified by reading the code only: it was not provoked on the bench (REGISTRO C5).

    The end of the session. session_dconf_neutralise() works on the runtime file with no memory of the child: it touches the file only if its first line is the mark, so it can run in the root side's fork and in a close-only child. It reads the base profile from the file itself, without REMOTIX's lines. If the base is the default alone (and the file is not marked as referenced) the file is removed: an absent file is exactly what a local login had before REMOTIX came, and nothing stays that could change a later local session. Otherwise it is rewritten, through a temporary file and a rename, with the base alone under a head that still carries the mark. The log says «REMOVED» or «NEUTRALISED», and ⛔ if it could not. It is never done under a live desktop. On the measurement machine the file was gone after the logout and in the same second as the close for a local login on the live Ubuntu image (docs/STORIA-ubuntu-26.04.md). The runtime file is written at birth and not earlier, so a child that dies before the birth leaves nothing; a child that dies after the birth leaves the file until the root side closes the orphan desktop, by the road of the light close, which runs the belt as the user.

    A foreign file between the child's start and the birth. If a runtime profile that is not REMOTIX's (no mark) appears after the child has started and before the birth, dconf_profile_reinstate() does not touch it: the session is born without REMOTIX's locks and without its database, and the log says «exists and is NOT ours (no mark): left alone, so the session is born WITHOUT our locks and our database» with ⛔.

    The declared fallback

    The model of the Debian 1.0.0 release is kept for the cases in which the new one cannot hold, and every use of it is said in the log as «DECLARED FALLBACK, D-015 (19 Nov 2026)». It has two levels. First level, when /etc/dconf/db/remotix is missing or not readable, or when a runtime profile that is not REMOTIX's (no mark on its first line) is already there (that file is never overwritten, removed or rewritten, and it is taken as the base): the child writes $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/remotix/dconf/profile, a profile of three layers, compiles the locks at its start with dconf compile and sets DCONF_PROFILE to the profile in the child and in the session:

    Second level, when the dconf program is missing from PATH (dconf-cli is a Recommends), or when dconf compile fails: without the program dconf_compile_locks() cannot run, dconf_locked stays false and the session takes the last branch of session_dconf_prepare(): the profile is the in-memory layer on top and the user's databases below, with no lock at all. The keys that have a value are written into the in-memory layer at the birth, but nothing prevents the user from changing them (for example scaling-factor is not locked), nothing goes in the user's file, and what the user changes from the remote desktop is lost at the next birth. In this level the user's keyboard layout is not copied into the session (that branch of session_dconf_birth() does not do it) and it does not need to be: without locks the user's values are read from the layer below, and the negotiated layout is written into the in-memory layer. Without the program the one-time cleanup warns and waits. (Read in the code; not provoked on a machine.) A mandatory profile in /run/dconf/user/<uid> wins over any profile and over DCONF_PROFILE: the locks cannot hold, and it is declared; the session is then born without them and the layout is not written. The fallback profile is neutralised at the end like the runtime one (only the file, locks.db stays). On the measurement machine the fallback was provoked by taking the database away: the same twenty-one keys were in force and the profile was neutralised after the logout (ripiego.out in the same folder). The comments of the code that describe dconf's behaviour (only the first source is written, a lock hides the sources above it, a recompiled file-db is not seen by programs already open) carry the mark of dconf 0.40, the version of Debian 13, and were not re-measured on 0.49; Ubuntu 26.04 has 0.49, and the model above was measured on it.

    One-time cleanup. session_dconf_restore_once() (called by session_dconf_birth(), in the new model and in the fallback) removes from the user's own dconf, once, the four keys that older REMOTIX versions wrote there (the two power-sleep types, idle-delay and lock-enabled), if they still hold exactly those values. The mark is ~/.local/state/remotix/gnome-ripristinato; without the dconf program nothing is done and no mark is written. No earlier REMOTIX was distributed on Ubuntu, so in this tree it matters only for a machine where an older build was tried. The postrm removes the mark at purge.

    Verification. After the birth nothing is written: session_dconf_verify() re-reads every key through the session profile, as the Shell and the gsd-* daemons do, and says whether it is in force («session keys re-read: 21 in force, 0 NOT» on the measurement machine, in the new model and in the fallback). Every schema and key is looked up before use, because g_settings_new() on a missing schema aborts the process (the comment records a child dead of SIGTRAP from a key renamed between GNOME versions).

    The scale. The input's coordinate space is the logical monitor's layout, and with a scale other than 1 the layout and the stream's pixels diverge: with scaling-factor 2 the layout of a 2133-pixel canvas becomes 1067 × 2 = 2134 and the pointer goes elsewhere without any line saying so (measured 14 Aug 2026, comment of mutter.h). The first cure is the key above, locked to 1: the user's file is not touched and at a local login they find their own value again. The safety net is in the child (guard 2 of DECISIONS.md §5.0-sexies): if the scale read from Mutter for REMOTIX's monitor is not 1, the child makes one attempt, mutter_scale_to_one(), with ApplyMonitorsConfig method 1 (temporary, never monitors.xml) and only in the plain case of one logical monitor, which is ours, with one monitor; three synchronous D-Bus calls of up to WAIT_CALL_MS = 15 s each, so about 45 s at worst, only in a broken Mutter. If the scale re-read is not exactly 1.0 the stage is refused: MSG_STAGE carries fatal = 1, the parent sends 0x0E to every login of that user (stage_refused_by_child() and wt_dismiss_user_session_over(), 14.5 “Local excludes remote and the session cap”), and the child closes the graphical session, retrying every 10 s if that fails, instead of remounting the stage for ever in front of a black page. The likely causes the log names when the net is needed are a scale saved in ~/.config/monitors.xml, a mandatory dconf profile of the administrator, or the fallback without dconf compile. A scale that could not be read is not taken for 1.0: the child goes on and says so.

    Known limits of the session's dconf

    • A child that dies after the birth leaves the runtime file until the root side closes the orphan desktop (the light close runs the belt as the user). A local login of a user with no known REMOTIX session does not run the belt, because that would need a new fork as that user; the probability is low, since the file now exists only after a birth (REGISTRO C5, limit 1).
    • A hot upgrade with a desktop born by the old model: its programs go on reading the in-memory layer while a new child writes the database remotix, so a keyboard layout change does not reach that desktop until the next birth. The old model was never distributed on Ubuntu (limit 2). The clean-up of the user manager also removes a DCONF_PROFILE that an earlier version of the package left in a manager that outlived the upgrade.
    • The purge removes ~/.config/dconf/remotix as the user, only that regular file (a link is not followed, user and the folder are never touched); a user the system does not list at that moment, for example a network home that is down, keeps it, and it is inert without REMOTIX (limit 3; 15.7 “Removal: prerm, postrm and purge”).
    • The profile is in the runtime folder, so any program born in the meantime with that folder reads it, not only those that inherited a variable as before; the mandatory profile still wins and is declared.
    • A foreign runtime profile that appears between the child's start and the birth leaves the session without the locks and the database (above).
    • Not proven in the field: the UNKNOWN branch at the child's start (in the new model and in the fallback), the branch of the database that is different or older at the service's start (only «missing» was tried), the case with no dconf program at all, and an administrator's variable in the child's own environment. They are verified by reading the code only (REGISTRO C5).
    • The manager's snapshot can be old after a close made from the root side, and the question «is the desktop alive» treats an unanswered question as «closed» in two places (REGISTRO E3, 12.5 “Ending a session and tidying up”).

    Inhibition. session_inhibit() calls org.gnome.SessionManager.Inhibit with flags SUSPEND | IDLE (4 | 8 = 12) and never the logout bit: with it, the user's own logout would be blocked by REMOTIX. The cookie is never released; it lives as long as the session.

    12.7 · KDE Plasma: KWin nested in labwc

    Plasma is started with startplasma-wayland, which starts KWin as the user unit plasma-kwin_wayland.service. REMOTIX overrides that unit's ExecStart the same way as GNOME's shell, but the line does not start KWin directly: it starts the REMOTIX binary in --kwin-nested mode, which starts REMOTIX's own labwc without a screen and then becomes KWin, running as a window inside that labwc (DECISIONS.md §10.40). The desktop is KWin's single output; KWin's output follows the size of its window; the window follows labwc's output. To change the desktop's size at a reattach, REMOTIX changes the size of labwc's output. On Ubuntu 26.04 this is Kubuntu: Plasma and KWin 6.6.7 (12.1 “The four desktops side by side”).

    The KWin drop-in written by write_dropin(), for a 1920×1080 canvas (the binary path is <code>/proc/self/exe</code>)
    [Service]
ExecStart=
ExecStart=/usr/libexec/remotix/remotix --kwin-nested 1920 1080 /dev/dri/renderD128 -- /usr/bin/kwin_wayland_wrapper --xwayland --width 1920 --height 1080 --no-lockscreen

    Our own labwc (KDE)

    The labwc that hosts KWin is not the distribution's. build/labwc-ospite/README gives the reason: KWin 6.5 and later draws a single black pixel as the root of its window and puts the content in subsurfaces; wlroots never reports that root as «presented», KWin gives its clients a frame clock stuck at 0, and Firefox takes its window for covered and stops painting. The fix is a few lines in wlroots (types/scene/surface.c, the frame_done handler: the root of a surface shown on an output counts as presented at every output frame; wlroots-0.19.2-remotix-presented-root.patch). Study 6 checked that the wlroots source of Ubuntu 26.04 is byte for byte the upstream 0.19.2 file, that upstream's master and 0.20.0 do not have the fix, and that the earlier tree had seen the symptom with the distribution's labwc on this very release: the windows of a KDE session stayed on their first frame and the picture came one to three seconds late. So the package carries labwc 0.9.3 with wlroots 0.19.2 patched, linked statically, as /usr/libexec/remotix/labwc: the sources are pinned with their sha256 in build/labwc-ospite/VERSIONS, build/labwc-ospite/build.sh fails if the binary links any libwlroots, and the build packages are in debian/control (15.6 “Our own labwc (KDE)” has the build and licence side). The path is fixed at build time: LABWC in src/Makefile becomes -DREMOTIX_LABWC, and debian/rules passes LABWC_PATH. XFCE and LXQt use the distribution's labwc, and the labwc Recommends of the package serves only them.

    The start line (kwin_nested_alive() in kwin.c). write_dropin() writes it with the path of the running binary, the canvas size and a render node chosen like XFCE's labwc (pixman if no card can draw, - if no node opens, with a ⛔ line). The helper then runs as the user, inside the unit:

    1. It checks the line W H NODE -- <wrapper> …, W and H between 200 and 8192; otherwise exit 2.
    2. It checks that REMOTIX_LABWC (the path fixed at build time) is executable, and starts that labwc, never the distribution's. If it is not there, the session is still born: the helper runs the KWin wrapper with --virtual added and writes ⛔ our labwc is not installed: KWin --virtual, and the desktop will NOT take the window's size at reattach (DECLARED FALLBACK) to the unit's output (the user's journal). The desktop then keeps the size it was born with.
    3. It writes labwc's configuration $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/remotix-kwin-host/labwc/rc.xml (folder 0700, rewritten at every birth) and starts labwc -C <that folder> with XDG_RUNTIME_DIR set to $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/remotix-kwin-host, WAYLAND_DISPLAY, WAYLAND_SOCKET and DISPLAY removed, WLR_BACKENDS=headless, WLR_LIBINPUT_NO_DEVICES=1, the node or WLR_RENDERER=pixman, and LABWC_UPDATE_ACTIVATION_ENV=0. labwc's socket is then inside that folder, and KWin's wayland-N stays the only socket in the user's runtime folder, so capture, input and clipboard cannot land on the host by mistake. With activation updates off, labwc never publishes its own display to the bus or to systemd, where the session's programs would open on a screen nobody sees.
    4. It waits for labwc's socket for at most HOST_BIRTH_MS = 10 s and stops if labwc exits first.
    5. labwc's headless output is born 1280×720; the helper sets it to W×H at HOST_MHZ = 240 Hz and reads the size back before KWin opens its window, so the desktop is born at the right size.
    6. It starts the ticker and the ScreenSaver sidecar (below), sets KWIN_FORCE_SW_CURSOR=1, and becomes the KWin wrapper with --wayland-display <labwc's socket> added.

    The labwc configuration is deliberately minimal. -C makes labwc read only that folder, so a user's ~/.config/labwc never gets in. The single window rule matches on the window title with ToggleFullscreen and no server decoration, because the window must be exactly the output's size; the comments record that on one distribution a rule on the identifier never fired. The configuration also carries one key binding and one root mouse binding, each with the single action None: a configuration with no bindings makes labwc load its default ones, which start programs, and any program of the same user could press them through the virtual-keyboard protocol on its socket. The measurements behind this are in the comments of kwin.c and DECISIONS.md §10.43; they were made on labwc versions the comments name and are not repeated here.

    The ScreenSaver sidecar. From Plasma 6.4 on, Ctrl+Alt+Del did nothing: the shortcut calls requestLogoutPrompt(), which first asks org.freedesktop.ScreenSaver.GetActive («never show the logout prompt on top of the lock screen»). That name belongs to KWin's lock-screen daemon, KWin starts with --no-lockscreen (locking is REMOTIX's), nobody owns the name, the call fails with ServiceUnknown and the failure is read as «the screen is locked» (comment in kwin.c, measured 18 Nov 2026 on Plasma 6.6.7: with a stand-in that answered false the prompt came up in one second). The cure is screensaver_alive(), a second process beside the ticker, in the unit's cgroup, that owns the name (DO_NOT_QUEUE: if a real owner is there first, the sidecar ends and says so) on the two paths /ScreenSaver and /org/freedesktop/ScreenSaver and answers every method of the standard interface: «not locked» and zero times for GetActive, SetActive, GetActiveTime, GetSessionIdleTime and SimulateUserActivity; the standard error NotSupported for Lock, Throttle and UnThrottle. Inhibit is forwarded to powerdevil's org.freedesktop.PowerManagement.Inhibit with the same arguments and the same cookie back, and given back when the caller leaves the bus or calls UnInhibit: measured with VLC, which asks the ScreenSaver name first and, on an error, does not go on, so a fake cookie would have left the video without a real inhibition. The sidecar dies with the unit and leaves nothing on the user's bus or in the user's files.

    The lost frame. KWin can leave a window on an old picture when nothing damages it. kwin_poke() (kwin.h, 19 Nov 2026) re-commits the transparent pixel with damage, on the capture's own connection, to make KWin draw a frame, and capture_watch_sequence() and capture_frame_lost() count the holes in KWin's buffer numbers; the behaviour, its constants and its limits are in 6.5 “The lost frame (KWin)”.

    1. At a reattach of another size (child.c, §7.1), if KWin's output is not the canvas asked for and the host exists, the child first dismantles the capture: KWin's stream would otherwise renegotiate to a size the fixed offer refuses, and die.
    2. kwin_host_resize() asks labwc's output for the new size (read back, not believed), then reads KWin's output on a connection of its own until it has the same size, for at most 3 s.
    3. The capture is mounted again at the new canvas.

    A reattach at the same size asks for nothing. A Plasma session with no host (our labwc missing, or born with --virtual) keeps the size it was born with, and the child declares ⚠ §7.1 KDE: this Plasma session has no host for KWin … DECLARED FALLBACK. The capture takes KWin's only output (WL-0 when nested, Virtual-0 with --virtual).

    Capture, input, cursor and clipboard

    Capture uses KWin's zkde_screencast_unstable_v1 on a PipeWire stream, with the pointer requested as metadata (POINTER_METADATA = 4; the choice cannot be changed on a live stream), so a pointer movement produces a buffer with no new pixels marked corrupted, which capture.c discards. KWin only allows the screen-cast global to a program it recognises: kwin_check_permission() verifies at startup that /usr/share/applications/org.kde.remotix.desktop (shipped by the package, debian/org.kde.remotix.desktop) exists (RX-KDE-001), that its Exec resolves to the running binary (RX-KDE-002) and that X-KDE-Wayland-Interfaces lists the interface (RX-KDE-003). Input goes through libei from KWin (kwin_eis_fd()), and the keyboard layout is written to a kxkbrc in the session folder, which KWin is told to reload with the D-Bus signal org.kde.keyboard reloadConfig (kwin_layout()). The clipboard uses the wlroots data-control protocol (clipboard_kde.c) on KWin's socket. The shape of the pointer comes from the metadata, where the session's cursor theme remotix-invisible has one-pixel opaque images of unique colours that the dictionary shape_from_pixel() maps back to a real cursor image (shape.c; ch. 6 “Screen capture”).

    i
    Remedy text. kwin_check_permission() ends its failure messages with «Remedy: reinstall the package from its file (sudo apt install --reinstall ./remotix_<version>_amd64.deb)» (RX-KDE-001, RX-KDE-002 and RX-KDE-003, kwin.c): the remedy is the package's, since there is no installer.

    12.8 · XFCE: labwc and a locked xfconf

    XFCE on Wayland has no compositor of its own: it runs on labwc, the distribution's (labwc 0.9.3 on Ubuntu 26.04). There is no unit to override, so write_dropin() does nothing and says so, and REMOTIX starts the compositor itself with exec labwc -m --session '<primary>', where the primary client is xfce4-session preceded by the size step (measured_primary()). The picture, pointer and input paths are the wlroots ones of ch. 6 “Screen capture” and ch. 10 “Input”. The Xubuntu panel has the whisker menu and no actions button (study 7), so on Xubuntu the lock on the whisker menu is the only protection of the shutdown entries.

    The panel. xfce_panel_xml() locks only the items array of each actions plugin (lock-screen, switch-user, suspend, hibernate, hybrid sleep, restart and shut down are turned from + to -; logout stays) and, for every whiskermenu plugin, the six keys show-command-lockscreen, …switchuser, …suspend, …hibernate, …restart, …shutdown set to false. The plugin ids come from the user's panel channel before birth, or from the standard default.xml for a user with no panel yet. Declared limit (comment): an action button the user adds by hand during the session has a new id and is not locked in that session; it is locked from the next birth. There is no inhibition on XFCE: xfce4-session does not consult the inhibitor when it logs out, so one would give a false sign in the log and no protection (session_inhibit()).

    Only the leaf keys are locked (D-X3). In the lock files the nodes that are only the parent of a lock (plugins, plugin-N) are written as type="empty", never as a value the user must own (the comment above xfce_panel_xml()). The reason was seen: with plugin-N = whiskermenu in the lock, xfconfd does not write into the user's file a value equal to the system's, so the user's file kept type="empty" and, once the lock was gone, the plugin had no type and the panel dropped it. xfce_panel_integrity() runs at every birth (in xfce_session_xfconf()) and repairs once the /plugins/plugin-<id> entries of a panel's plugin-ids that have no type: from a copy still pending, or from the standard layout, but only for the two types REMOTIX locks (PLUGIN_ACTIONS, PLUGIN_WHISKER) because the number may belong to another plugin by now, and never while xfconfd still holds the lock in memory (xfconfd_holds_lock() reads /proc/<pid>/environ looking for /remotix/xdg-xfce; if it cannot tell, it does not write).

    The autostart cover. The entry in the session's autostart folder has the same file name as the system's and Hidden=true, so XFCE does not start it. The list is SESSION_NOT_IN_REMOTE_AUTOSTART (blueman.desktop and xiccd.desktop). xiccd (colour profiles, a dependency of xfce4-settings) at every login asks colord to create a device, an action polkit gives to the seated user only: measured on Xubuntu 26.04 (bench machine, 26 Nov 2026), started by hand inside a remote desktop it opens an administrator's password window in the middle of the screen, holding the keyboard and the pointer. It is deliberately not a polkit rule: colord's devices and profiles are one set for the whole machine, and granting the action to remote sessions would let any remote user touch the seated user's screen; a remote desktop has no monitor to profile anyway. An entry is written only if the system's one exists, otherwise only an entry of ours (marked X-REMOTIX) of an earlier birth is removed. It was measured on Xubuntu 26.04 that a Hidden=true entry hides the file name wherever it is, so the user's own visible ~/.config/autostart/blueman.desktop is not started either (a differently named entry is). The code does not remove the cover at the end of the session: it disappears with /run/user/<uid>; with another session of the same user alive (ssh, lingering) it stays, harmless because no non-remote session reads that folder.

    The copy and the restore. A lock on a single property has a price: at the first save of the channel, xfconfd writes each locked key into the user's file as type="empty" and the user's value is lost. REMOTIX therefore keeps a copy of the user's value of each key it locks, before locking, and puts the values back at the end of the session (xfce_restore_keys()). The copy goes to the user's state folder; if that cannot be written it goes to RAM under the runtime folder (declared, with the warning that a reboot takes it); if neither works the locks are applied all the same and the line says that the user's values will not come back and lists them. Keys that cannot be put back stay pending and keep their originals in the next copy. This and the one-time restores of earlier versions' values are the exceptions to «nothing permanent» (12.1 “The four desktops side by side”). xfconf-query exits with zero even when the daemon refused and put the previous value back, so every write is re-read.

    i
    Lock syntax. the locked-key mechanism depends on locked="<user>": the comment in session.c records that locked="*" locks nothing (measured 13 Nov 2026 with xfce4-session 4.20.2, in the earlier tree), and that before that date the code thought four keys were locked that were not. Ubuntu 26.04 has xfce4-session 4.20.4 and the measurement was not repeated (not verified there). The copy file ~/.local/state/remotix/xfce-chiavi is not deleted after the restore, only marked as restored (comment in session.c); the package's postrm removes it on purge.
    i
    Black wallpaper. on Xubuntu the session has a black wallpaper (docs/REGISTRO-problemi.md E1, seen by the owner on the live image on 18 Nov 2026). The cause found is libxfce4windowing 4.20.2, which loses the compositor's message that names the monitor of the workspace if it arrives before the monitor is known, so xfdesktop paints black; the authors fixed it from 4.20.4. Ubuntu 26.04 has 4.20.5, so the wallpaper should appear, but that was not checked with a picture of a session on Ubuntu 26.04 (not verified).

    12.9 · LXQt: labwc folder and session commands

    Ubuntu 26.04 has a launcher for LXQt on Wayland, lxqt-wayland-session 0.3.1, but Lubuntu does not install it (study 7 §3.1, from the package dependencies), and the code does not look for one: REMOTIX starts labwc itself with labwc -C <folder> -S '<primary>', where the primary client is lxqt-session (2.3.0 on Ubuntu) preceded by the same size step as XFCE. The wallpaper is made by pcmanfm-qt from the output's size, which is why the output must have its size before the session starts (12.4 “How a session is born”).

    The pieces are written only if the program and the system's entry exist; otherwise only what is REMOTIX's (marked X-REMOTIX) is removed. The log line of lxqt_session_commands() counts the X11 composition managers and the programs that count every user's processes that it covered. The crash windows that these pieces cover were seen in the Ubuntu 26.04 test rounds (a «Lubuntu Update crashed too many times» window on one user was not reproduced); the comments of the code date the cures to 18 and 19 Nov 2026.

    The one-time restore. restore_user_settings_lxqt() runs once per user (mark ~/.local/state/remotix/lxqt-restored) before the birth and removes only what is surely REMOTIX's, from earlier versions that wrote into the user's files: a lock_command_wayland=true line, an enableIdlenessWatcher=false line in a file that holds nothing else of the user's, the mainmenu panel type, and menu stubs marked X-REMOTIX that hold nothing but REMOTIX's lines (deleted only in that case, with one log line per file, by the owner's decision recorded in the comment). Anything else is left and said.

    Exit. exit_lxqt() calls org.lxqt.session.logout() without waiting, because the method is Q_NOREPLY; the verdict comes from wait_until_done(). The comment still marks as unmeasured whether the polite request alone brings lxqt-session (and so labwc) to exit within the ten seconds; if not, the force runs and the log says so. Before mounting the capture on labwc the child waits for the session manager to be on the bus: the comment records, from a measurement of the earlier tree, that without it, on LXQt, «Log out» made the session be born again 16 times out of 20; that was not repeated on Lubuntu.

    12.10 · What the session imposes, desktop by desktop

    One table to answer «where does REMOTIX write, for this desktop?». session_settings() dispatches to the per-desktop code; the common rule is that everything lives under $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR (gone with the user's runtime folder) and the user's own files are not touched, with the exceptions in 12.1 “The four desktops side by side”: on GNOME ~/.config/dconf/remotix and, during the session, lock-warning-shown; on XFCE the copy of the locked keys; and the one-time restores.

    KDE's powerdevil inhibition. powerdevil_guard() runs as a thread in the child: powerdevil's default is to switch the screen off after 10 minutes, which in a remote session means the desktop goes black. The thread waits for org.kde.Solid.PowerManagement on the bus (it is not bus-activated and may appear late; the child has no GLib loop, so ownership is polled every POWERDEVIL_STEP_US = 2 s for as long as the child lives; after POWERDEVIL_PATIENCE_S = 120 s without powerdevil one warning line is written and the watch goes on) and calls PolicyAgent.AddInhibition with type 4 each time the owner changes, so that a powerdevil restart is covered. The machine's own suspend is not handled here: it is refused by the package's polkit rule for all desktops. The comment also names the AllowSuspend=no drop-in, but the package ships that one switched off in /usr/share/remotix/belts/ (debian/rules); it holds only if the administrator puts it in force (ch. 14 “Security model”).

    The checks are the log. For every desktop the lines of the session area name each file written and each value re-read, with ⛔ when something is not in force (ch. 16 “Logging and diagnostics”). A desktop whose protection did not apply still starts, and says so: the rule in the comments is that a missing belt is declared, not silent.

    12.11 · Behaviours of the four desktops worth knowing

    What follows is what the maintainer will meet on the four desktops. The sources are docs/REGISTRO-problemi.md (sections D and E), the studies of the tree, the code and its comments; what was not seen on Ubuntu 26.04 is said.

    The AppArmor profile and what was observed on a real Ubuntu 26.04 are in 14.4 “The AppArmor profile and its mode”. The canvas limits that the product guarantees (3K, eight users) are in ch. 14 “Security model” and ch. 19 “Performance and capacity”; the maximum canvas that the decoder of the test browser reached on Debian is not a result of this tree and is not repeated.

    Places that differ per desktop (the list to walk when a fifth is added): recognize_desktop(), desktop_name(), compose_environment(), write_dropin(), start(), inactive_unit(), really_terminate(), session_settings(), session_inhibit(), session_alive(), session_life(), session_missing_component(), local_session(), unit_shell() in session.c; session_over_early() in child.c; the capture, input and clipboard branches in child.c (session_on_wlroots() first, then KDE, then the Mutter default); and the cursor shape road. ch. 20 “Extending REMOTIX and porting to another distribution” has the general procedure.

    Chapter 13

    Login and its defences

    13.1 · The path of one login attempt

    A login is the one place where an unknown person on the network makes REMOTIX do work as root. The defences are therefore spread over every hop of the path, and each hop assumes that the previous one may be wrong or hostile. This chapter follows one CREDENTIALS message from the browser to PAM and back; the process shapes themselves are in ch. 2 “Overall architecture”, the wire format in ch. 5 “The RCP/1 protocol”, and the isolation of the network side in ch. 14 “Security model”.

    The design rule behind it is invariant I3 (helper.h): the guard starts from denied. The value true for «admitted» is born at exactly one place, the byte 1 that the grandchild writes after PAM_SUCCESS on both PAM steps; a lost message, a timeout, a dead process, a short or mangled answer and any byte other than 1 are all a «no».

    A login that PAM admits can still be refused. On a machine with a screen the same person may already be at the keyboard of a local graphical session, and then the answer is 0x05 and not a desktop: the rule «local excludes remote» and the behaviour of the real login screens of GDM, SDDM and LightDM are in 14.5 “Local excludes remote and the session cap” and 14.6 “The local-login hold”, with what was measured on Ubuntu 26.04 live images.

    i
    Scope. Everything below describes the packaged service, started with --split by remotix.service. In that shape the counters of hop 1 live in the network side and the pause tables of hop 2 live in the root side; the single-process build of the same program (--no-split) exists in the code but is not what the package starts.

    13.2 · The PAM service file remotix.pam

    REMOTIX authenticates against its own PAM service, named remotix, whose file is src/remotix.pam, installed by the package as /etc/pam.d/remotix (a dpkg conffile, see 15.5 “Files the package installs”). The service name is the constant SERVICE_PAM in authentication.c; the child that later opens the logind session uses the same name (pam_start() in child.c).

    The file mirrors the system's own /etc/pam.d/sshd line by line, with one extra line on top (Debian's and Ubuntu's files are the same). The rule behind it (DECISIONS.md §10.18) is that REMOTIX must not drift from the machine's default network authentication: whatever the administrator puts in common-auth (lockout with pam_faillock, a second factor module, an LDAP or sssd line) holds for REMOTIX as it does for ssh. The header of the file says that the comparison with sshd's file was made on 30 Sep 2026, on a Debian 13 image and an Ubuntu 26.04 image (identical to each other), and found 15 lines equal out of 15. Study 5 (§3.1) repeated it for Ubuntu 26.04 on the openssh-server package 1:10.2p1-2ubuntu3.8 extracted in a container: remotix.pam, without the pam_listfile line, equals the sshd file line by line, 15 of 15. The comparison on the installed images of the four flavours was postponed (study 11, item S5.P6) and was not made; for the sessions of the four flavours see the ordering of the pam_exec line below. The header of src/remotix.pam still carries Debian-only wording («DEBIAN 13 ONLY», the other distribution families): these are leftovers of the earlier tree and not statements about this tree.

    The other PAM line the package adds. /etc/pam.d/common-session is not a REMOTIX file (it belongs to libpam-runtime, which the package depends on, and it is not a conffile of REMOTIX), but the package edits it through pam-auth-update: the profile /usr/share/pam-configs/remotix (debian/remotix.pam-config: Default: yes, Priority: -1, Session-Interactive-Only: yes, Session-Type: Additional) adds session optional pam_exec.so quiet /usr/libexec/remotix/remotix-local-login. Every service that includes common-session (sshd, su, the display managers, and /etc/pam.d/remotix itself) runs it at each opening and closing of a session (the non-interactive stack, used for example by cron, does not carry the line: Session-Interactive-Only); the program acts only for a graphical session on a seat and returns 0 at once everywhere else, and the line is optional, so it can never make a login fail. What it does, and why, is in 14.6 “The local-login hold”; the package side (postinst, prerm, the dependency) is in 15.5 “Files the package installs”.

    The line is checked at every start of the service. Since 1.2.0 remotix.service runs ExecStartPre=-/usr/libexec/remotix/remotix-pam-hook check (the script is src/remotix-pam-hook). It looks in /etc/pam.d/common-session for a real session line with pam_exec.so and remotix-local-login (a commented line does not count). If it is there nothing is touched; if it is not (an update of libpam-runtime, a hand edit), it runs pam-auth-update --package, the same call as the postinst, and checks again. One summary line is written either way in the journal of the service: «the local-login hook is in place», «was missing … and has been put back», or a warning that it is not there and could not be put back. The script never uses --force or --enable: a common-session edited by hand, or a profile the administrator switched off in pam-auth-update, stay as they are because pam-auth-update refuses by itself, and the warning says so. The - in front of the command and the exit status 0 of the script mean that it can never prevent the service from starting. On removal the line goes out in the prerm after the service has been stopped, because the check would otherwise put it back at a restart in between (15.5 “Files the package installs”).

    The reason the service is not login: on Debian and Ubuntu /etc/pam.d/login is the local console stack (pam_securetty and others), policies meant for whoever sits at the machine, and the network login would inherit them in a way that depends on how that machine is configured. sshd's stack is the network-access one.

    !
    Warning. If /etc/pam.d/remotix is missing, Linux-PAM falls back to the service other, which on Debian and on Ubuntu 26.04 includes the common stacks (study 5 §3.1) and does not exclude root. Two protections live in the program for that: look_pam_service() in main.c says at start-up whether the file is there, and why_no() in authentication.c tells in the log «PAM refused» from «PAM could not judge» and names this file and the denied-users file in the second case.

    Two PAM items are set before authenticating, as sshd does: PAM_RHOST is the client's bare address (no brackets, no port, an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address turned back into IPv4; rcp_rhost_from_provenance()), so pam_faillock, pam_unix and logind see where the attempt comes from; PAM_TTY is the service name.

    i
    PAM file message. The message an administrator reads when the file is missing is a run-time log line: look_pam_service() in main.c writes at start-up “the PAM service «remotix» DOES NOT EXIST”, says that PAM falls back to other, which on Debian and Ubuntu includes the common stacks and is not the REMOTIX stack, and ends “The package installs that file: reinstall the package from its file (sudo apt install --reinstall ./remotix__amd64.deb).”

    13.3 · One PAM transaction in authentication.c

    Only one function in the product touches libpam: rcp_authenticate_judged() in authentication.c. It is called only by the grandchild of the PAM helper, never by the serving process. It returns one of three values, which are the byte the grandchild writes back.

    Details that a maintainer needs:

    • Both PAM calls pass PAM_DISALLOW_NULL_AUTHTOK. sshd refuses empty passwords itself, before PAM; REMOTIX copied sshd's stack but not that check, and without the flag pam_unix nullok in common-auth admitted an account with no password whatever was typed (measured 16 Nov 2026 according to the comment in the code). The stock Ubuntu 26.04 common-auth with libpam-sss has pam_unix.so nullok followed by pam_sss.so use_first_pass (study 5 §3.1), so the flag is needed there too.
    • The conversation function (conversation()) answers one kind of question only, the echo-off prompt, with the password; echo-on prompts and informational messages get no reply. A conversation of more than 16 messages is refused.
    • The password copy handed to PAM is freed by libpam, not by REMOTIX. The code does not overwrite it; the comment documents that Linux-PAM does it in its reply-dropping routine and that anyone porting the file to another PAM library must re-read that line.
    • The «locked» judgement is PAM's own, never a guess: the line «The account is locked due to » (constant FAILLOCK_LOCKED) must have been sent through the conversation before the password prompt, and pam_authenticate() must have returned PAM_AUTH_ERR. The text is matched in English because the program never calls setlocale(); a translated or silenced module simply produces value 0, the old behaviour.
    • Both outcomes of a refusal are one wire answer for the client (REJECTED with reason 0x07), on purpose: telling the outside «your account is locked» would be an oracle. The distinction exists only in the server log.
    • The log lines of this file go to stderr, not through log.h, because the same file is compiled into a test host that has no log module. The name in them never appears as typed (13.9 “What the login logs and what it never logs”).

    13.4 · The PAM helper: dispatcher and grandchild

    PAM blocks, and it is not reentrant. A PAM check was measured at 1.0 to 2.2 s (the helper.h header cites 2123, 2198 and 1086 ms medians under the old login service, measured on Debian; the difference between a refused and an admitted attempt is the signature of pam_faildelay; these times were not measured on Ubuntu 26.04, where pam_sss and pam_motd may add their own). In a single-threaded poll loop that would freeze every connected screen at each login. So PAM runs in separate processes, by a decision of the owner: a process, not a thread, and one transaction per process.

    Why SOCK_SEQPACKET: the kernel delimits the messages, so a request cannot arrive halfway and an answer cannot merge with another grandchild's. With a stream a framing of our own would be needed, and a parsing defect there would produce «somebody else's answer», invariant I3 broken by a bug.

    The dispatcher is not only forked but re-executed: spawn() forks and at once runs /proc/self/exe --pam-helper with its socket on descriptor 3, and main() sends that argument to helper_main() before reading any option, certificate or key. A plain fork would copy the server's heap, with TLS keys, other users' password buffers and clipboard text, into every grandchild, and a crashing PAM module would dump all of it into a root core file. helper_main() refuses to run unless descriptor 3 is a SOCK_SEQPACKET socket.

    The password lives, on its way, in the requester's buffer and in the receiver's buffer; both are zeroed with explicit_bzero() as soon as they have served. A request of the wrong length is discarded, not repaired, and expires as a «no». In the split server the same questions travel as AUTH and VERDICT messages over the root channel and the dispatcher is the root side's child; the network side never sees it (ch. 2 “Overall architecture”).

    13.5 · The fixed answer time and the floor of a refusal

    Without a delay, «no such user» would answer in a millisecond and «wrong password» in fifty, and the distinction the protocol forbids writing in the reason could be read with a stopwatch. The server therefore never answers a login sooner than a fixed time, and the time is chosen by the kind of answer, not by how long PAM took.

    The floor of 2500 ms for refusals exists because PAM's own failure delay (about 2.0 to 2.2 s for a real user with a wrong password and for an unknown name, according to the comment citing the pam-tempi measurement) runs inside the helper, while a name rejected by the denied-users list is refused before the password stage and came back after only the fixed second: the time told whether a name was on the list. Making every PAM refusal leave not before 2500 ms hides that. It is a floor like FIXED_DELAY: a slower verdict still sets the pace, so a PAM delay above 2.5 s (the comment says it can reach 2.5 s with the default 2 s base) leaves a residual tail. The comment itself calls the number a margin to be re-measured, not a proof.

    The other bytes are not held to the floor because their own byte already says which road they took, and a connection in S_WAIT_VERDICT cannot be evicted by the transport: holding 0x08 and 0x0E answers for 2.5 s would let about 51 CREDENTIALS per second fill the 128 pre-login places instead of 128 per second. A name that the system could not look up (an NSS error) is answered as a plain 0x07 at the floor, not as 0x0E, for the same reason. This matters on Ubuntu: on Ubuntu Desktop /etc/nsswitch.conf has passwd: files systemd sss (the line libnss-sss adds, study 5 §3.2), and a lookup of a non-existent name there may end in an error and not in «not found»; root_user_lookup() and user_refused_as() in rootside.c turn that error into a refusal and handle_auth() answers it like any other (RXR_NO). Study 11 (item S5 N.7) records the check row for this case as verified, with the risk rated low; the times of the Ubuntu rounds themselves are not in this tree and were not read (not verified).

    The check check-ban.py (wrong-password and same-answer) lists the measured times, requires the floor, and compares a wrong password with a non-existent user (medians within 500 ms). Its individual times on Ubuntu 26.04 were not read for this manual: the logs of the rounds are on the dev server and not in this tree (not verified). On the virtual machines of the Ubuntu bench every client appears to the server as 10.0.2.2 (QEMU's user network; ADDR in check-ban.py), which has no effect on the product.

    13.6 · The three counters and the progressive ban

    The limiter is in rcp.c, in the network side. It is the rule of SPECS.md §4.2 and DECISIONS-11.md §11.53: three levels of sliding-window counters and, for each level, a ban whose length grows with repetition.

    • The key is built by rcp_key_address(): an IPv4 address whole, an IPv6 address reduced to its /64 (a link-local address too, with its zone cut), an IPv4-mapped or NAT64 address turned back into the IPv4 inside it, ::1 whole. The user level uses the HMAC of the name, never the name.
    • The ladder (LADDER_MS[]): the first ban of a level lasts 15 min, the second 1 h, the third and every later one 12 h. The memory of past bans is forgotten after 24 h without a ban (FORGET_MS). The three levels have separate ladders.
    • The window slides. The time of the last N failures is kept, not their number, so failures at 0:00, 4:59 and 5:01 still count as three. A window anchored to the first failure would never stop someone trying at a pace just slower than the window.
    • The attempt in flight counts. login_reserve() checks and books in one step before PAM is asked: counters are «failed in the window plus in flight», so sixteen attempts sent together cannot all pass before the first verdict. At most MAX_PER_USER_IN_FLIGHT (2) verifications run for the same (key, user). The key level counts only failures, not attempts in flight, so eight people behind one NAT logging in together are not refused by their own number.
    • What counts as a failure: a PAM «no» (value 0), and an attempt that got no verdict (helper timeout, the 12 s ceiling), because a PAM that does not answer is exactly what an attacker would try to produce. A late verdict for a connection that has gone is still counted, by name and address (rcp_orphan_verdict()).
    • What does not count: a refusal in which the question never left (helper off, socket full, 16 already in flight; login_release() gives the booking back), a refusal by the limiter itself, a protocol error, the second connection of the same user (0x0F). Also a «no» given while pam_faillock had the account locked, but only for a key that logged in within 30 days (GOOD_AGE, GOOD_KEYS = 64 keys): the owner locked out by a stranger must not ban his own address. For any other key a locked-account «no» is an ordinary failure.
    • A success clears only the failures of its (key, user). Neither the ladder nor the other two levels are touched: an attacker with one valid account must not be able to wash the key's count.

    The table has a bottom. attempts[] holds MAX_ATTEMPTS = 256 entries. BAN_QUOTA = 160 of them may be bans; a compile-time assertion keeps room for the counters and the bookings. A new ban never evicts another ban. When the quota is full, keys that never logged in share one common counter (UNKNOWN_LIMIT = 5 in UNKNOWN_WINDOW_MS = 5 min) and are refused with 0x08 before PAM when it is full: the declared price is that a legitimate new user from an address that never logged in is refused too, while the quota and that counter are both full. The comment in the code marks «256 slots are enough» and «5 in 5 min» as not measured.

    What the banned person sees. The page still loads and says that the attempts are used up, with the time left (rcp_banned() answers for the key and /48 levels only: the page does not know the user). An attempt at the login gets 0x08. A ban is never silence.

    The ban survives a restart (invariant I7). save_ban() writes --ban-file, which the unit sets to /var/lib/remotix/net/ban (mode 0600, owner remotix), to a temporary file created with O_EXCL and O_NOFOLLOW, synced and renamed over the final name, at every change. rcp_ban_load() reads it at start-up, after the log secret is loaded. The format has two kinds of line:

    The ban file (comments added)
    B2 <U|K|N> <level> <epoch> <key>[ <user HMAC>]    # a ban or a remembered level: user, key, /48
G2 <epoch of the login> <key or HMAC of the key>   # a key that logged in lately

    The epoch is an absolute time because the in-memory clock is monotonic and restarts with each process. The file never holds a typed name: the user is a full HMAC-SHA256, and the known keys are HMACs when the log secret persists. check-ban.py verifies the file holds no typed name and that the key is still banned after systemctl restart remotix.

    13.7 · The root side's own bounds on logins

    The root side applies a second, independent set of bounds, because a network side that has been taken over must not be able to make PAM an unlimited password oracle (DECISIONS-11.md §11.50, review R2). They are in rootside.h and rootside.c, all in the root side's memory only (they do not survive a restart of the root side).

    A paused AUTH is answered RXR_PAUSED: for the browser a plain refusal, 0x07 at the 2.5 s floor, counted by the network side like any refusal (except for a key that logged in within 30 days, by the same rule as the locked account; refusal_uncounted() in rcp.c). It is deliberately not RXR_NOT_CHECKED (0x0E at 1 s): a different byte and a different time would tell anyone who can provoke the pause that the name exists. The tables never fail open: when the per-user table has no room the AUTH is refused.

    Before any of this, the root side refuses, with the plain «no» and without PAM, an empty name, a name in /etc/remotix/denied-users (comments and blanks allowed, one name per line), uid 0, a name NSS does not know, a lookup error, and a name whose canonical spelling NSS returns is in the list. A denied-users file that exists but cannot be read refuses everybody (user_refused_as()). The same check is repeated at the SPAWN, and the list is the one the PAM stack reads with pam_listfile: the package ships it containing one line, root.

    13.8 · No administrator unblock, by design

    There is no administrator command to lift a ban, and that is a decision, not an omission. On 17 Nov 2026 the owner decided that an unblock command is not a planned function (docs/DECISIONS-11.md §11.54); the ban of the address stays at 20 failed attempts in 5 minutes. A ban ends only when its time passes: 15 min, 1 h or 12 h.

    What the code actually contains, so that nobody is surprised:

    • command.c implements an UNBLOCK <address> line on a Unix socket (PING answers PONG; the answers are REMOVED, NOT-BANNED and NOT-UNDERSTOOD), calling rcp_unblock(), which removes every level of the address and writes a log line. It is opened only when the server is started with --command-socket (command_open()).
    • The packaged unit does not pass that option; its comment lists --command-socket among the bench options that must not be there. The package ships no CLI either. check-ban.py has a check, unblock-shipped, that asserts this and passes with the message «by design the package ships NO administrator unblock».
    • The option is nevertheless reachable: REMOTIX_OPTIONS in /etc/remotix/remotix.conf.d/*.conf is appended to the command line of the unit, and check-ban.py uses exactly that, with a drop-in that it removes at the end, to unblock its test address. It is a test hook, not a supported administrator function; it would be reachable by whoever can write that folder, that is by root.
    • Restarting the service does not lift a ban: the ban file is loaded again (rcp_ban_load()).
    !
    Warning. The text the banned person reads is page.c (the notice with the countdown) and the reason text for 0x08 in page.html. Both now say that the block ends by itself when the time is up and that there is no other way back in, which matches the package. SPECS.md and DECISIONS-11.md still describe an unblock command. See ch. 24 “Appendix C — Known issues and open points”.

    13.9 · What the login logs and what it never logs

    The log is a file that is kept, so the rule is that what is typed by an unauthenticated person never reaches it. The rules, all in code:

    !
    Warning. Two limits of the claim. First, check-ban.py (typed-names-not-logged) fails only on two things: a name that does not exist appearing anywhere in the journal of the boot, whoever wrote it, and the real user's name in REMOTIX's own lines before the verdict. The lines that PAM modules and other system programs write with the name of an existing user (pam_unix logs the user and the address of a failed authentication through syslog; on Ubuntu with libpam-sss pam_sss is a second such module, and whether it writes the name was not checked) are only reported as notes: REMOTIX does not control them. Second, the log lines of authentication.c go to stderr and do not pass the cleaning of log.c, which is why the name there is never printed as typed. The log itself is described in ch. 16 “Logging and diagnostics”.

    13.10 · Login defences against SPECS

    Every number in this chapter was read in the code. Against SPECS.md §4.2 and DECISIONS-11.md §11.53 the result is:

    The 1.0 form of the rule (three failed attempts from one address, twelve hours) is kept in SPECS.md §4.2 as history; it is not in the code.

    One comment in the code still contradicts the code next to it, and the code wins: rootside.h says a paused request gets «not checked» and is not counted (it gets RXR_PAUSED, a plain refusal that is counted unless the key logged in within 30 days, as rootside_proto.h and rootside.c say). The other two that this manual used to list, the key limit written as 12 in rootside.h and in check-ban.py, were corrected on 17 Nov 2026 (both say 20 now).

    Chapter 14

    Security model

    14.1 · Trust boundaries and the processes of the service

    REMOTIX has two security levels and no third (SPECS.md §4.1): the transport, so that nobody reads or rewrites what passes, and the access, that is address, port, user name and password checked by the machine's own PAM. The rest of this chapter is about what happens if something in the first process that touches the network is wrong. The packaged service is split in two for that reason (the shape is in ch. 2 “Overall architecture”); the login itself is in ch. 13 “Login and its defences”.

    The principle is that root does only what needs root: verifying anyone's password, and descending to anyone's uid. Everything that faces the internet runs without it. The desktops are not behind the walls: their children are forked by the root side, never from the network side, so that for example sudo apt install in a remote desktop keeps working (walls.h).

    14.2 · The closed list between the network side and the root side

    The root side and the network side talk over one SOCK_SEQPACKET socket pair with SO_PASSCRED, created by the root side before it forks the network side (descriptor 3 there). The messages are a closed list in rootside_proto.h; nothing else crosses.

    • Exact sizes. Every message is one packet of exactly the size of its kind (size_of_request()). A different length, an unknown kind, a wrong magic (RXR_MAGIC) or version (RXR_VERSION = 3) is not skipped: rootside_check_packet() refuses it, the root side logs it, closes the channel, kills the network side and starts it again.
    • Kernel credentials on every packet. The root side checks SCM_CREDENTIALS: uid = remotix and pid = the network side it forked. The network side checks uid 0 and its own parent.
    • Options come from the root side. Every option of a child (canvas, card, encoding route, session cap) comes from the root side's own command line, never from a request of the network side.
    • A birth needs a grant. A right password mints a single-use grant bound to (user, address), valid RXR_GRANT_LIFE_MS = 30 s (rootside_grant_mint(), rootside_grant_take()). The SPAWN presents it, and the name is checked again against the denied list, uid 0 and NSS (birth()).
    • CLOSE_ORPHAN is a birth without a password, so it has its own limits: ROOTSIDE_ORPHAN_PER_S = 2 per second with a burst of ROOTSIDE_ORPHAN_BURST = 5, one per uid per ROOTSIDE_ORPHAN_UID_MS = 30 s, only if logind shows a live session of that uid whose PAM service is remotix, and only if the root side's own abandonment clock says the desktop was really abandoned.
    • Signals go only to the root side's own children, and a child is reaped by the root side, which then tells the network side.

    The logic of the list is that a hijacked network side is the attacker the root side is built against. The list gives it no message that reads a file, runs a command, names a uid or chooses an option.
