What it can still do is ask for a login with a password it guesses (bounded, see ch. 13 “Login and its defences”) and ask for the birth of a desktop for a user whose password it knows.

    14.3 · The walls of the network side

    The walls are put up by the root side in the fork that is about to execve() the network side, still as root, by walls_apply() in walls.c. The order is part of the design (each step needs the power the next one takes away), and any step that fails makes the root side refuse to start the network side: a network side without its walls is the unprotected server with extra steps, and that must never happen silently.

    The root side writes one log line with what is actually in force (walls_in_force(): the AppArmor state, the folder, the limits). The package check check-package.py (first-start) confirms the process layout of a running service, one root side as root and one network side as remotix, records CapEff, NoNewPrivs and Seccomp from /proc/<pid>/status of the network side, and checks the owner and mode of every file under /var/lib/remotix/net (directories 700, secrets and the ban file 600). It records those three status values as evidence; it does not compare them against fixed expected numbers.

    What Ubuntu's AppArmor sysctls do not touch. Ubuntu 26.04 sets kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns and kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_unconfined to 1 (/usr/lib/sysctl.d/10-apparmor.conf, study 5 §1.1, read from the package). They concern the creation of unprivileged user namespaces. REMOTIX creates namespaces of other kinds, as root, in the fork of the root side (walls.c), and its seccomp filter denies CLONE_NEWUSER, so they do not apply; that is read in the code, and the behaviour of the kernel of Ubuntu on this point was not measured. The tests of the studies ran in containers on the dev server's Debian kernel, so no kernel fact of Ubuntu comes from them. The AppArmor profile is the second wall (14.4 “The AppArmor profile and its mode”).

    i
    Who owns what. The state folder /var/lib/remotix/net and the run folder /run/remotix/net are created by tmpfiles (remotix.tmpfiles) owned by remotix with mode 0700. The root side's own state, /var/lib/remotix, is root's and mode 0755: a remotix-writable folder holding root's files would let a hijacked network side swap them.

    14.4 · The AppArmor profile and its mode

    The profile is debian/remotix_network.apparmor, installed as /etc/apparmor.d/remotix_network (a conffile) and loaded by the dh_apparmor lines that debhelper adds to the postinst (debian/rules runs dh_apparmor --profile-name=remotix_network). It ships in complain mode: its flags are complain,attach_disconnected, so it logs what it would refuse and refuses nothing, with one exception that matters on Ubuntu: a deny rule holds in complain mode too (below). The profile has not been moved to enforce.

    How a process enters it. The profile has no attachment path. Executing /usr/libexec/remotix/remotix never puts anything in it, so the root side, which runs the same program, and every desktop stay unconfined. Only the root side's fork, by writing exec remotix_network to the process's AppArmor exec attribute right before its execve() (what aa_change_onexec() does, without the library), puts the network side in it (apparmor_exec_net()).

    The two deny unix lines (REGISTRO C4). The profile of the Debian release said deny unix addr=@*, to forbid only the «abstract» sockets (those whose name starts with an «@»). That rule also carries the permission to create a socket, which has no address to compare; on the kernel of Ubuntu, which mediates unix sockets, it forbade every local socket, so no D-Bus and no question to logind, and REMOTIX, unable to verify that no local session exists, refused every login (the log said logind unreachable (Unable to create socket: Permission denied)). A deny holds in complain mode too and leaves no warning line. The cure is two lines that name the operations: bind and listen on an abstract address, and connect, send and receive towards a peer with one. The pattern is @** and not @*, because one star stops at the / and the names to close contain it (@/tmp/.X11-unix/X0). Declared limit: the autobind (a socket that lets the system give it a random abstract name) stays allowed; it only serves to be reached by an accomplice process, not to reach the machine's sockets, and the second wall remains: the network side has a network namespace of its own, where the machine's abstract sockets do not exist, and Landlock scopes abstract sockets where the kernel allows (14.3 “The walls of the network side”). To be looked at again when the profile goes from complain to enforce.

    What was observed on Ubuntu 26.04, and what was not. The test containers have no AppArmor in force (no /sys/kernel/security/apparmor), so check-package.py answers BLOCKED on its apparmor check there, telling only whether the profile text compiles; a defect of the profile could not appear in them. The first test on a real machine was the owner's, on a live Ubuntu 26.04.1 image (kernel 7.0), on 19 Nov 2026: that is where C4 was found (a correct password followed by «the server could not open your session, and it is not your mistake» for every user). After the correction it was measured on the same machine: the system bus and the journal reachable, the abstract sockets still refused, and the check of local sessions answering «CONNECTED» (the start-up log line of §5.1). The owner then tried the release by hand on the four virtual machines (QEMU, with a Radeon handed to them) and on the four live images, Ubuntu, Kubuntu, Xubuntu and Lubuntu (docs/STORIA-ubuntu-26.04.md, 19 Nov 2026). Since 1.2.0 the sessions of the bench's virtual machines (a video card passed through) are checked by check-apparmor.py: it reads the kernel journal of the machine (and the audit log if there is one) and fails on any apparmor="ALLOWED" or apparmor="DENIED" line of the profile since a given moment (complain mode shows what the profile does not cover as ALLOWED); the bench's full round runs it last, and in the 1.2.0 round it gave no failure. Not verified: the profile was not moved to enforce, and moving it is a decision not taken; the rule «not to enforce without a session observed with no unexpected audit line» stays (REGISTRO C4: to be looked at when it passes to enforce; study 5 §1.4 notes that Ubuntu's kernel supports AppArmor mediation of D-Bus and the profile has no dbus rule, which enforce might need). The rules for /proc are still marked «not tried» in the profile. The parser of Ubuntu (apparmor 5.0.2) compiles the profile without warnings, with and without an abi line (study 5 §1.3, apparmor_parser -QTK -S in a container); the profile has no abi line. The header of the profile still describes the state of 17 Nov 2026 on a Debian 13 virtual machine: it is a leftover of the earlier tree and does not describe this tree.

    i
    Lesson of C4. the lesson recorded in REGISTRO C4 for a new distribution: the containers do not test the security profile, so before closing a distribution there must be one successful login on a real or virtual machine with AppArmor in force, and the start-up line «§5.1 … CONNECTED» must be read in the log; after a change of kernel, Debian too is to be tried again.

    On removal, debian/remotix.postrm writes the profile name to the kernel's .remove file of AppArmor, so the profile leaves the kernel even if its file is already gone.

    14.5 · Local excludes remote and the session cap

    The rule is that a user with an active local graphical session gets a refusal from REMOTIX and nothing alive. REMOTIX never mounts anything on a local desktop. The reason is practical and was measured: on GNOME the user's session bus is one and shared, and a child spawned for the same user finds the local Mutter and mounts a virtual monitor, input and the clipboard on it (DECISIONS.md and the box above local_guard() in child.c). What counts as a local session is a session with a seat (sentinel_local()), not logind's Remote flag, which would make REMOTIX's own seatless sessions look local.

    Each of the first three defences is enough alone. The 0x05 is sent only after PAM's yes, so whoever has no password learns nothing about the account, and only to the login that asked, because the other connections carrying the same name may be strangers. The decision to fail closed, so that a lookup that fails is a refusal and never a yes, is the owner's of 15 Nov 2026 according to the comments in main.c and child.c. A light close ends the REMOTIX desktop of that user without touching the local session; the details are in ch. 3 “Startup and life cycle”. A desktop found again, with no child, whose user now has a local session is not revived. The network side does not close it (it is user remotix: found_again_close_for_local() in main.c logs “the root side ends its scope by itself”), and in the packaged (split) service the root side ends its scope within about ten seconds (localx_sweep()); in the single-process mode (--no-split, not packaged) the process itself is root and closes that session with logind's TerminateSession; only if that fails is the stage left alone.

    Who is told, and when, when the session ends. In defence 3 the child's guard now tells the parent first, local_found_by_child(): the logged-in clients receive 0x04 at once, and only then does the child do the light close, because the closing can wait for PipeWire for up to 25 s where RealtimeKit cannot start (comment in child.c). When a child ends because the graphical session ended, session_ended_by_child() and the dismissal of a gone child call wt_dismiss_user_session_over() and not wt_dismiss_user(). Of the connections that carry the name, a logged-in one gets the farewell at once; one that was admitted but is still inside the fixed second (rcp_admitted_waiting()) gets 0x10 at the end of that second, in the place of ADMITTED; one still waiting for PAM, or whose «no» is being kept, is skipped, because it was never attached to that session and a stranger trying passwords under that name must learn nothing about the account. Before, a login refused with 0x0E «still closing» could receive a false 0x10 (seen on 18 Nov 2026 in a rejoin 8 to 10.5 s after the logout of a young session; comment in webtransport.c).

    What else answers 0x0E. The text the page shows for 0x0E is generic on purpose, because the byte covers several different causes (a comment in page.html lists them as six routes). Two are new in this tree: the desktop's compositor is not installed (XFCE or LXQt without labwc: the parent says it before spawning the child, in delivery_verdict() through session_missing_component(); no process, no logind session; the log names the package the administrator must install; 12.1 “The four desktops side by side”), and the child's refusal of the stage because of the scale (MSG_STAGE with fatal, stage_refused_by_child() answers with RCP_SESSION_UNSERVABLE to every connection of that user, admitted or logged in; 12.6 “GNOME: headless Shell and session dconf”).

    The session cap answers 0x0E. The default cap is RCP_SESSION_CAP = 10 users served at once (rcp.h; changed by --session-cap at start-up, rcp_cap_set()). Whoever does not fit gets 0x0E SESSION_UNSERVABLE with the detail in the body. The cap is checked at two points: in delivery_verdict() in main.c, on the count of desktops, before a child is spawned, so a user who does not fit costs no process, no logind session and no compositor; and in slot_take() in rcp.c, on the registry of attached sessions, at the attach. It is deliberately not 0x06 (no composition capacity left, which is the budget, see ch. 8 “Quality, degradation and budget”) and not 0x0F (this user already has a session): the person must be told that the table is full and not, falsely, that they are connected elsewhere. The cap is administrative, not a physical limit, and 10 is a technical default: the declared limit of the product (owner's decision, DECISIONS-11 §11.51, confirmed 18 Nov 2026) is 8 users at the same time. Related: a second device of a user whose first client is alive gets 0x0F ALREADY_ACTIVE_REMOTELY; a client silent for long enough is detached and does not hold the slot.

    14.6 · The local-login hold

    The problem. A user who has a REMOTIX desktop and then logs in at the machine starts a second graphical session of the same user. GNOME's login screen holds that login while the user has another graphical session that is active or online; SDDM and LightDM hold nothing, and the local desktop starts on the user manager and the bus that the remote one is still using (read in the sources on 18 Nov 2026: Plasma adopts the remote units and dies with them, the local xfce4-session finds its bus name taken and leaves, so KDE and XFCE return to the login screen). The owner's order (DECISIONS-11 §11.57, 18 Nov 2026) is one rule for every desktop and display manager: a local graphical login closes the user's remote desktop first, completely, and goes on only after that.

    What happens, in order.

    1. The hook decides if the login is its business. Only for PAM_TYPE=open_session with XDG_SEAT set, session class user (or none), type wayland, x11 or mir (or none), a user that is not root, and a PAM service that is not remotix. Everywhere else (ssh, a text console, REMOTIX's own sessions, and the closing of any session) it returns 0 at once. Cron never runs it: with Session-Interactive-Only: yes the line is not in common-session-noninteractive.
    2. It looks for the root side. The folder must belong to root and not be writable by others; the hook opens .lock and, if a shared lock can be taken (nobody holds the exclusive one: the service is not running), it returns at once. No login waits for a service that is not there.
    3. It leaves a request and waits. It creates the empty file named by the uid and checks every 50 ms (the first look after 5 ms) whether the root side has removed it; every half second it also checks that the service is still there.
    4. The root side sees the request (inotify, and the folder is read every second). If a child of ours serves that uid, it sends RXR_LOCAL_COMING: the network side sends the logged clients 0x04 and asks the child for the full close, the logout's road, because the local desktop has not started and must find a user manager with nothing of REMOTIX in it. The log line starts “local login of … HELD in PAM”.
    5. If there is no child (a desktop that nobody holds), or the order could not leave, or the child has not finished after PL_GRACE_MS (13 s), the root side ends the scope itself with the machinery of the rule “no orphan desktops” (SIGTERM, SIGKILL after 3 s, the clean-up of what REMOTIX put in the user manager).
    6. The login goes on. When no child of that uid, no seatless REMOTIX session of that uid with processes and no ending in progress are left, the root side removes the file and the hook returns. At most PL_CEIL_MS (20 s): then the file is removed anyway and the log warns that the desktop is still there.
    7. New births are refused for a while. While the login is held and for PL_HOLD_MS (10 s) after the answer, a birth for that uid gets no child; the root side answers it as it does for a child that is still closing (RXR_REF_CLOSING) and logs “SPAWN for … refused: a local login of uid N is being held”. Once the local session is in logind, the usual refusal (0x05) takes over.
    • It never makes a login fail. The hook always exits 0, the PAM line is optional, and the hook's own ceiling is LOCAL_CEIL_MS = 25 s, above the root side's 20 s. Up to PL_MAX (8) logins can be held at the same time.
    • The request is only a uid. The folder is writable only by root; the root side reads logind's own files to decide what to end, and does so again just before the signal. Nothing in a request is believed beyond “look at this uid now”.
    • While the service stops no request is served: every desktop is being closed anyway, and the hook returns when the root side exits.
    • The older defences stay as a second belt: the sweep of the root side every 5 s (localx_sweep()) and the network side's 2 s sweep (LOCAL_SWEEP_MS).

    The real login screens on Ubuntu 26.04. The bench's check prelocal runs the PAM line and the hook in boxes (containers and virtual machines) that have no real login screen: the line landed after pam_systemd in common-session on the four flavours, with six PASS rows of that group on each (study 11 S8.11), and study 5 §3.1 reads that the PAM files of GDM, SDDM and LightDM all include common-session. The first tests through real screens were the owner's, by hand, on live images on 19 Nov 2026, with the remote desktop open and a local login of the same user:

    GDM 50.1 has a new behaviour that was read in its sources and not tried (study 2, item S2.3 postponed): its «Force Stop» button now asks logind to terminate every graphical session of the user that is active or online, including the REMOTIX one, where GDM 48 did nothing for a session that was not its own. The dialog («Session Already Running») appears after pam_open_session, that is after the hook, so the order «close the remote desktop first, then the screen looks» holds on GDM 50 (study 2 §0); GDM's worker waits without a limit, so the hook's 25 s are not cut by it.

    The second rule, “no orphan desktops” (DECISIONS-11 §11.56), uses the same machinery. A seatless REMOTIX session whose scope still has processes and whose user has no child of ours must not stay: while the service runs, the root side ends it when it is seen so in two scans in a row (LX_EVERY_MS = 5 s), and at an orderly stop it ends whatever is left (3.11 “Stopping the service”). A user who comes back before the second scan gets a child, and a desktop with a child is not an orphan.

    i
    Elsewhere in this manual. Where the rest is: the log lines in ch. 16 “Logging and diagnostics”, the files and maintainer scripts in 15.5 “Files the package installs”, the checks in ch. 17 “Testing”, and what was and was not proven in ch. 24 “Appendix C — Known issues and open points”.

    14.7 · The denied-users list

    The denied-users list. /etc/remotix/denied-users (installed from debian/denied-users, with one line, root) is consulted twice by two different programs, so that neither is a single point of failure: by the root side before PAM and at the birth of a desktop (user_refused_as()), and by pam_listfile as the first auth line (onerr=fail). Uid 0 is refused by the root side whatever the list says. The root side's check also compares the spelling NSS returns, so that «BRUNO» resolving to «bruno» is refused when «bruno» is listed. An unreadable list refuses everybody. The file is a dpkg conffile: the administrator may add names, and an upgrade keeps them.

    The list is the only way the product offers to keep a given account off REMOTIX. It is not a group or a role mechanism and it does not restrict which users may log in in the other direction (there is no allow list).

    14.8 · Polkit rules, password windows and the power belts

    A REMOTIX session has no seat, so polkit gives it the answer meant for a remote subject (allow_any, usually a password) even for actions that a distribution grants to the user sitting at the machine without one. Two polkit rules and one helper script handle the two consequences. Both rules are installed active in polkit's vendor folder, not in /etc, so the package owns them and removing the package removes them; an administrator overrides them with a rule of a lower number in /etc/polkit-1/rules.d/, since polkit stops at the first rule that decides.

    • Administrative actions still ask a password, exactly as with sudo, seated or remote. That is not touched.
    • Root needs no exception for power. logind checks the caller's capabilities before polkit, and root has CAP_SYS_BOOT, so sudo systemctl poweroff keeps working. On Ubuntu 26.04 sudo is sudo-rs 0.2.13 (study 5 §4.3); the logic is the same, because it runs as root, and it was not verified that it keeps CAP_SYS_BOOT in a way different from GNU sudo. The consequence for testing is that the rule cannot be checked from the root side: it must be checked as the user, from inside the session. check-desktop.py does that: logind's CanPowerOff and its siblings answer no, pkcheck refuses the 15 actions it is asked about, and a real systemctl poweroff as the user fails (check power-entries-absent). The check was adapted to the messages of sudo-rs («I'm afraid I can't do that», «interactive authentication is required»). The child repeats the question about CanPowerOff, CanReboot, CanSuspend and CanHibernate every time it mounts the stage (sentinel_shutdown_forbidden()): an answer no or na («not available here», a virtual machine or a server) counts as safe, any other answer or an error is an alarm in the log, and the error line names the call and the reason.
    • Why nineteen and not fifteen (REGISTRO C6, 20 Nov 2026). On the owner's own Debian tablet, in front of the machine, the local user could reboot: logind's CanReboot said yes and pkcheck authorised reboot, although the rule says NO to it and the round said «no power off, no reboot». The cause: in logind's policy four actions that the rule did not forbid (set-reboot-parameter, set-reboot-to-firmware-setup, set-reboot-to-boot-loader-menu, set-reboot-to-boot-loader-entry) carry the annotation org.freedesktop.policykit.imply = reboot and the default «yes» for the active user seated at the machine; whoever is authorised for one of them is authorised for reboot by implication, despite the explicit NO on reboot (an explicit NO is not enough against an implication from an authorised action). The four are now forbidden, With other users logged in, logind asks reboot-multiple-sessions, which was and is denied, so the hole let only a local user reboot, only when he was alone on the machine, and it never allowed a power-off. The round had not seen it because it looked only at the remote session, which is not «seated at the machine» so the «yes» for the active user does not apply to it, and only at the fifteen actions known by name. The same four annotations were found on Ubuntu 26.04 (systemd 259.9, 51 policy files read) by the check below, on 20 Nov 2026.
    • The checks that look from the right places. Two checks of prove/check-desktop.py were added on 20 Nov 2026, next to power-entries-absent (which now says in its header what it does not see). power-implied needs no session: it reads the installed rule /usr/share/polkit-1/rules.d/50-remotix-no-poweroff.rules and all the .policy files of the machine, builds the graph of the imply annotations (chains included) and fails if an action that is not forbidden implies a forbidden one. power-local-seat runs from root, with no REMOTIX session, and asks pkcheck about every forbidden action as a process of the active session on seat0 (the greeter's user, the one at the machine): all must be refused, calibrated against login1.chvt, which must be granted. In the latest version of the script the process is one of the session's own non-root user, because the leader of GDM's greeter session can be a root process and polkit authorises root unconditionally, which would make everything look granted; with no greeter (containers) the check answers BLOCKED. The greeter case, in which someone in front of a machine with nobody logged in might reboot from the login screen's menu, was deduced when REGISTRO C6 was written and is now measured on Ubuntu. Both checks were run on an Ubuntu 26.04 virtual machine on 20 Nov 2026 (/media/REMOTIX-UBUNTU/albero/prove/log/vm-gnome-poweroff-prima2/ and vm-gnome-poweroff-dopo/ on the dev server). With the rule at 15 actions (package unione10): power-implied FAILED (the four set-reboot-* imply reboot on Ubuntu too) and power-local-seat FAILED («polkit GRANTS: reboot» from the greeter's session). With 19 actions (package unione11): both PASS, 19 of 19 refused, the calibration chvt granted; that run was a partial round of the desktop check only, 8 PASS plus the known failure users-shell-and-environment. The same test from the local user's seat with the corrected package on Debian was not yet made.
    • Snaps and the first rule. The snap policies io.snapcraft.snapd.login, manage, manage-interfaces, manage-configuration and manage-fde are auth_admin (any) and auth_admin_keep (active), so even a seated user is asked for a password: they ask no unrequested password window and the rule 40 needs no extension for them (study 5 §2.2, read from the packages). polkitd is 127-2ubuntu1.1 (the rules were written for 126; study 5 §6); the administrator groups of Ubuntu are sudo and admin (49-ubuntu-admin.rules), both already in rule 40's test, and polkit.service is the same as Debian's, with a strict sandbox: the helper reads only /run/systemd/sessions/* and the .policy files, so it works inside it (read, study 5 §6; the runtime outcome was not read).
    • How the second rule recognises a REMOTIX session. Not from the subject's fields (local and seat are the same for ssh, and the programs that ask run under the user manager's service, where polkit hands the rule no session) but by remotix-polkit-seated, a shell script that reads logind's state files in /run/systemd/sessions for a session of that user with SERVICE=remotix, and prints what the machine gives the seated user for the action (the allow_active of the policy file). It does not use D-Bus, loginctl, pkaction or pkcheck: logind's checks call polkitd synchronously, and polkitd would be waiting for the helper, a deadlock measured at 10 s. The user name is passed as an argument, never inside a script text, and the script exits 0 always (with systemd 259 the state files keep SERVICE=, USER= and SEAT=; the .ref file that the script skips no longer exists, which is harmless, study 5 §7.1); anything unexpected becomes none, which the rule turns into NOT_HANDLED, or ?, which the rule reads as «the seated user does not get yes» (NOT_HANDLED, except the silent NO of an ordinary user for the two machine actions).
    • Declared: a REMOTIX user who is also logged in over ssh gets the same answers there; a REMOTIX session that is still closing counts too. check-desktop.py also has a check no-password-windows

    The other two belts of the owner's rule «nobody switches off the server» (DECISIONS.md §4.7) are not active. remotix-power-keys.conf (logind ignores the power, reboot, suspend and hibernate keys and the lid switch, including long presses) and remotix-no-suspend.conf (systemd's Allow*=no for sleep) are installed under /usr/share/remotix/belts/, where nothing reads them. REMOTIX does not modify the system beyond what it needs (the list of what it changes is in 14.10 “What the security model does not defend”); an administrator who wants them copies them into /etc/systemd/logind.conf.d/ and /etc/systemd/sleep.conf.d/. Consequence: without them, a person at the machine can still switch it off with the power button, and the polkit rule does not see that road, because logind acts on its own account there.

    14.9 · The service unit and why it is not sandboxed

    remotix.service has no sandboxing directive on purpose. There is no User=, no ProtectSystem=, no NoNewPrivileges=, no PrivateTmp=. The unit's comment gives the reason: the process systemd starts is the root side, and whatever the unit restricts, every desktop born from it inherits (walls.h names sudo apt install in a remote desktop as the thing that must keep working). The network side's confinement is done in the program (walls.c), where only that process receives it.

    !
    Warning. The unit does not make REMOTIX safe against a compromised root side. That process runs as root, unconfined, and runs PAM in grandchildren as root: PAM modules are other people's code loaded into root processes. What bounds the damage is that the root side never reads from the network, that its only input from the network side is the closed list above, and that the PAM transaction runs in a fresh image with a 20 s alarm.

    14.10 · What the security model does not defend

    The honest list, from the code and the decisions:

    The transport limits that bound a flood of connections before login (a cap on connections, on pending connections and per address) are in ch. 4 “Transport”; the encodings of the identity in the log are in ch. 16 “Logging and diagnostics”.

    Chapter 15

    The package

    15.1 · What the package is and how it is built

    REMOTIX for Ubuntu 26.04 is one binary package, remotix, built from the debian/ folder (source format 3.0 (native), debhelper-compat (= 13), Rules-Requires-Root: no). It is installed with apt install ./remotix_*.deb; there is no installer program. The build itself, in the build virtual machine costruzione with the static ngtcp2 and nghttp3 and with the sources of the package's own labwc (no containers), is in ch. 18 “Build and release”. The package is Architecture: any: the binary is compiled for the machine, and the walls of the network side exist only for x86_64 and aarch64 (ch. 14 “Security model”). The version of the file is 1.2.0-1+ubuntu26.04 and the changelog names the suite resolute (18.7 “Version and release”).

    The package changes the machine as little as possible, and says so in the maintainer scripts. It creates one system user and a few folders, defines a firewall profile without opening it, installs two polkit rules and an AppArmor profile and one PAM line, and leaves the service disabled and stopped. The PAM line is the one change to a system file: through pam-auth-update the package adds session optional pam_exec.so quiet /usr/libexec/remotix/remotix-local-login to /etc/pam.d/common-session (a file of libpam-runtime, not a conffile of REMOTIX) and takes it away when the package is removed (14.6 “The local-login hold”). Two optional system-wide protections (the power keys and suspend) are shipped switched off. Three things are specific to this package and not to a plain server program: a second program, the guest labwc that hosts KWin (15.6 “Our own labwc (KDE)”), a system dconf database that the postinst compiles (15.4 “The postinst: user, folders and encoding test”), and a drop-in that tells needrestart never to restart the service by itself (15.8 “Service policy: installed disabled”). The sections below follow the life of the package: what it needs, what it refuses, what it installs, what it does after unpacking, what it does on removal, and what the service policy is.

    i
    Stale wording. Comments in debian/control, debian/rules, the maintainer scripts and debian/remotix.service still speak of «the engine» and «the installer» (a program of the old multi-distribution product that no longer exists in this tree) and of phases/ documents. Where they say that something is done by the engine, in this package it is done by the administrator or not done. Four comments also say that the desktops survive the stop (SPECS §5.2): the one before dh_installsystemd in debian/rules, the one at the head of debian/remotix.postinst (upgrade restart, “the desktops stay alive”), the one in debian/remotix.prerm (why the sessions are closed first) and the one in debian/remotix.service about KillMode. Since 17 Nov 2026 (DECISIONS-11 §11.56) an orderly stop closes the desktops; those comments are product text, to be corrected at the next build. A fifth statement of the same age is gone in this tree: the child no longer passes --session-fd to keep the logind session alive (DECISIONS-11 §11.55, with a note of 18 Nov 2026: since systemd 258 logind holds the session by a pidfd of its leader; this tree has systemd 259). The leftovers are listed in ch. 24 “Appendix C — Known issues and open points”.

    15.2 · Package metadata: Depends and Recommends

    The dependencies are those that dpkg-shlibdeps cannot see: it computes the libraries linked into the binary (${shlibs:Depends}), and the rest is what the program uses at run time through PAM, D-Bus and commands.

    What apt really installed is on record for the three flavours that are not GNOME. The virtual machines of the bench (17.8 “The VM bench”) had the desktop installed from its ISO; installing the package with the Recommends pulled in labwc (with libwlroots-0.19, libseat1, libsfdo0, libliftoff0 and a few libxcb-* libraries), dconf-cli and wlr-randr, and xwayland (with libei1 and liboeffis1) on Xubuntu and Lubuntu; va-driver-all, mesa-vulkan-drivers and fonts-dejavu-core were not in the transaction on any of them, because the desktop already carried them (logs vm-radeon-installa-<name>.log on the dev server, taken with the package of an earlier construction that has the same Depends and Recommends). The GNOME machine had received earlier builds of the package, so labwc and dconf-cli were already there as automatic packages: the installation of the release package on it was a --reinstall and brought nothing in.

    • No desktop is a dependency. The package never installs a desktop by itself; with none of the four present the server says so at start-up. Nor does it recommend gnome-session (the «vanilla» GNOME session of universe; the session criterion lives in session.c).
    • Whoever installs with --no-install-recommends loses the drivers and the compositor packages, and a desktop that needs them will not start. The server refuses the login of an XFCE or LXQt machine without labwc with the code 0x0E and a line that names the package (16.9 “The startup declarations”); the postinst also warns, but only on a machine with neither gnome-shell nor Plasma. Xubuntu carries gnome-shell even without its Recommends (studio/7-xubuntu-lubuntu.md), so there the warning does not fire and the refusal of the server is the only signal. check-package.py has an informative check, recommends, that only reports which Recommends the installation pulled in (it always passes).
    • Static-Built-Using: ngtcp2 (= 1.25.0), nghttp3 (= 1.18.0), labwc (= 0.9.3) and wlroots (= 0.19.2). The build refuses (test lines in debian/rules) if pkg-config reports another version of ngtcp2 or nghttp3, so that the field never lies; the versions of the two are also written to /usr/share/remotix/linked.json for a software bill of materials. The versions of labwc and wlroots are pinned by hash in build/labwc-ospite/VERSIONS, not by a test in debian/rules.
    • Build-Depends carry the development headers the product links (libssl-dev (>= 3.5), libpam0g-dev, libglib2.0-dev (>= 2.80), libpipewire-0.3-dev, libdrm-dev, libva-dev, libopus-dev, libei-dev (>= 1.3.901), libxkbcommon-dev, libgbm-dev, libwayland-dev, libvulkan-dev (>= 1.3.274), zlib1g-dev), dh-apparmor, and what the package's own labwc needs (meson, patch, hwdata, wayland-protocols, libegl-dev, libgles-dev, libinput-dev, libpixman-1-dev, libseat-dev, libudev-dev, libdisplay-info-dev, libxml2-dev, libcairo2-dev, libpango1.0-dev, libpng-dev). There is no ffmpeg: encoding is on the card through libva and Vulkan Video, and audio through libopus.
    • The universe component. libva-dev, dh-apparmor, meson, libseat-dev and, among the run-time packages, labwc, wlr-randr and va-driver-all are in universe on Ubuntu 26.04 (checked with apt-cache in studio/8-pacchetto-e-prove.md; the flavours other than GNOME are entirely in universe). On a machine with main only, the build image cannot be made and the Recommends do not arrive.

    15.3 · The preinst refusals

    The preinst runs before the files are unpacked and has two refusals, each of which stops the installation with a message on stderr and exit status 1. They replace two checks of the old installer.

    Besides refusing, the preinst remembers: on a first installation ($1 = install, no previous version, and /usr/lib/sysusers.d/remotix.conf not yet there) where an account remotix already exists but is not a person's, it writes /var/lib/remotix/net-user-preexisting. The postrm reads that file so that a purge never deletes an account REMOTIX did not create.

    What the preinst does not check: that the card can encode. A card that exists but cannot encode H.264 is said by the postinst and by the server at start-up. A virtual machine that has only the emulated virtio-vga card passes the check (the card gives a render node, /dev/dri/renderD128) and cannot encode: the install logs of the Kubuntu, Xubuntu and Lubuntu machines, taken without the Radeon (server/vm-radeon-installa.sh), show the two lines of the postinst (the video card of this machine did not encode a test frame (H.264)…), and the server then says THIS SERVER CANNOT ENCODE VIDEO (16.9 “The startup declarations”).

    Verification on Ubuntu 26.04: check-package.py has a preinst check, which tries the refusal of a person's account only (it creates one with uid 1500 and a shell); it was not run for this manual and it is not part of the VM bench (17.5 “The package check”). The refusal without a card is in no check; it was not verified on Ubuntu 26.04. The installation without a card was not tried in this tree either: the install logs of the four VMs list a render node.

    15.4 · The postinst: user, folders and encoding test

    The postinst does, on configure, in this order, and never lets a failure make apt fail (each failure is a warning on stderr):

    • systemd-sysusers remotix.conf: creates the system user remotix (and its group) from /usr/lib/sysusers.d/remotix.conf. It is run explicitly because dh_installsysusers belongs to the debhelper sequence only from compat 14 (studio/8-pacchetto-e-prove.md read it in the sources of debhelper 13.31ubuntu1, the version of the build image, which has the same rule as the 13.24.2 of Debian 13; the explicit step is therefore still needed).
    • systemd-tmpfiles --create remotix.conf: creates the folders and sets the modes (below).
    • The system dconf database. If the dconf command exists (package dconf-cli) and the folder /usr/share/remotix/dconf/remotix.d is there, it runs dconf compile into a temporary file /etc/dconf/db/remotix.new.$$, sets mode 0644 and renames it over /etc/dconf/db/remotix: programs of a living session may have the old file open, so it is replaced, never rewritten in place. The keyfiles are the package's own, made at build time (debian/rules, remotix --dconf-keyfiles, next section); they hold the value and the lock of 24 keys of the GNOME session (the twelve VT switches, Log Out kept, no user switching, no lock, no automatic suspend, the integer scale 1, and three keyboard-layout keys that are only locked). Two warnings on stderr: remotix: ⚠ dconf (package dconf-cli) not found: /etc/dconf/db/remotix not made; the GNOME remote session will use its fallback and remotix: ⚠ /etc/dconf/db/remotix could not be compiled…. The service does the same work at every start (session_dconf_system_db_ensure(), called by the root side): it compiles to a temporary file, and replaces the database only if the bytes differ or the file is missing, saying so with a line of area rootside (16.9 “The startup declarations”). This is why a failed or skipped step here is not fatal: dconf-cli is only a Recommends, and may arrive after REMOTIX.
    • The PAM line of the local-login hook. If pam-auth-update exists, pam-auth-update --package reads the profile /usr/share/pam-configs/remotix (Default: yes, Priority: -1, Session-Interactive-Only: yes, Session-Type: Additional, the single line session optional pam_exec.so quiet /usr/libexec/remotix/remotix-local-login) and rewrites /etc/pam.d/common-session; then the script checks that remotix-local-login is in that file. Two cases print a warning on stderr and do not stop apt: remotix: ⚠ pam-auth-update not found, and remotix: ⚠ common-session was edited by hand (the line is not in the file after the step: a local login is then not held and only the periodic check remains). A failure of pam-auth-update itself is said too. The step runs at every configure, upgrades included; whether an administrator's deselection of the profile survives an upgrade was not verified. The line is also checked at every start of the service (below). The check of the step uses a pattern that matches the line itself (session … pam_exec.so … remotix-local-login), not a comment that merely names the file.
    • The encoding test, on the first configuration only (the second argument of the script is empty) and only if the binary is there: MESA_SHADER_CACHE_DISABLE=true timeout 30 /usr/libexec/remotix/remotix --encoding-test h264 (Mesa then does not open a shader cache in /root/.cache for a probe that runs once). Its exit status is 0 if the card encodes a test frame, 3 if no card can encode, 1 if it opens and produces nothing. Any non-zero status prints a two-line warning that REMOTIX will show no desktop until the card encodes, naming the driver to check (Intel and AMD: va-driver-all; NVIDIA: its proprietary driver) and the command to repeat. It does not stop the installation: the VA driver may arrive with a Recommends configured after REMOTIX itself.
    • The missing guest compositor. If labwc is not on the PATH, and xfce4-session or lxqt-session is, and neither gnome-shell nor startplasma-wayland is, the script says remotix: ⚠ the package labwc is not installed (it is only a Recommends): the XFCE/LXQt desktop of this machine cannot start in REMOTIX and, on a second line, install it: sudo apt install labwc. The test is deliberately narrow: where another desktop is present nobody can know which one REMOTIX will start, so nothing is said.
    • The debhelper part (#DEBHELPER#): the AppArmor lines of dh_apparmor (load or reload the profile remotix_network) and the systemd lines described in the service policy section. The service and the user groups are not touched.

    The encoding test is the product's own mode: main() answers --encoding-test before reading any other option. On an upgrade the test is not repeated.

    Checking and switching off the local-login line. To see whether it is in force: grep remotix-local-login /etc/pam.d/common-session. To follow what it does: journalctl -t remotix | grep 'local login' (ch. 16 “Logging and diagnostics”). To switch it off, the way of Debian and Ubuntu is pam-auth-update (untick the REMOTIX entry) or pam-auth-update --package --remove remotix; this was not tried for this package, and the effect of switching it off is that a local login of a user who has a remote desktop is no longer held (the periodic checks of ch. 14 “Security model” remain).

    !
    Warning. The postinst does not enable the firewall profile, does not put the user in any group and does not enable the service. The only change it makes to a system file is the PAM line above; the dconf database is a file the package owns outside its file list, and the postrm removes it. The comment at the head of the script says that the groups, the firewall and the belts are set up by «the engine», which is the old installer; in this package the groups are set up by the product at each user's first connection (ch. 14 “Security model”) and the rest is the administrator's. The same comment says that on an upgrade “the desktops stay alive”, which is no longer true: the restart closes them (3.11 “Stopping the service”).

    15.5 · Files the package installs

    Everything is installed by override_dh_auto_install and execute_after_dh_auto_install in debian/rules, plus what debhelper adds by itself and the one line of debian/remotix.install (the needrestart drop-in). The tree below is the package's file list.

    • Conffiles. debhelper marks everything under /etc as a conffile, so dpkg keeps the administrator's edits on upgrade and on removal, and deletes the files on purge. The release package declares five: the AppArmor profile, the needrestart drop-in, the PAM file, the denied list and the ufw profile (the list is printed by build-deb-vm.sh in controlli.txt). remotix.conf in /usr/share/remotix is not one: choices go in /etc/remotix/remotix.conf.d/*.conf, with the same lines, and win.
    • The page certificate is not in the package. The server makes its own certificates at start-up in /var/lib/remotix/net/certificates (certificates_prepare()); an administrator's own, put there without the .ours mark, is used instead.
    • The KDE file org.kde.remotix.desktop has Exec=/usr/libexec/remotix/remotix, NoDisplay=true and X-KDE-Wayland-Interfaces=zkde_screencast_unstable_v1. The package ships it and the program only checks it at start-up (kwin_check_permission()); it never writes it.
    • The two polkit files and the helper are active as soon as they are installed (the 40- rule has a fourth refresh action, org.freedesktop.fwupd.refresh-remote, which gnome-software asks at login; fwupd 2.1.1 of Ubuntu 26.04 has no such action, so the line is inert there); the two files under belts/ are not (ch. 14 “Security model”).
    • The unit comes from debhelper. dh_installsystemd picks debian/remotix.service and installs it under /usr/lib/systemd/system/; rules has no line for it.
    • The licences. debian/copyright carries the licence text of REMOTIX (appended by build-deb-vm.sh) and a section for usr/libexec/remotix/labwc («GPL-2 and Expat»: labwc is GPL-2, two of its files LGPL-2.0-or-later, wlroots is Expat). THIRD-PARTY-LICENSES is installed (compressed) under /usr/share/doc/remotix/: it holds the full texts of the third-party components (ngtcp2, nghttp3, libopus, the Emscripten and musl parts of the page's decoder, the Wayland protocol files, and labwc and wlroots). LICENSE.md (section 8) says the same of labwc and wlroots and promises the corresponding source with every release; there is no installer and no Go module in the package any more, and the licence files do not mention them.
    • No benchmark file and no bench option are in the package. The build refuses to package if BENCH_ON in rcp.c is not 0, and its checks on the finished package assert that the unit passes no bench option and that no bench file is in the file list (ch. 18 “Build and release”). That does not remove --command-socket from the binary; see ch. 13 “Login and its defences”.

    Folders created at run time. remotix.tmpfiles (installed as /usr/lib/tmpfiles.d/remotix.conf) makes /var/lib/remotix (0755, root), /var/lib/remotix/net (0700, remotix) and its content owned by remotix at every boot, fixes the modes of the certificates folder (0700), the keys, quic-secret, log-secret and the ban file (0600), and makes /run/remotix (0755, root) and /run/remotix/net (0700, remotix). The file is installed and run by the postinst, and check-package.py (first-start) checks the owners and modes it produces. One more folder is not made by tmpfiles: /run/remotix/prelocal/ (root, 0700) is made by the root side when it starts, for the requests of the local-login hook (14.6 “The local-login hold”); it goes with /run/remotix at a purge.

    The system user. remotix.sysusers is the single line u remotix - "REMOTIX network side" / /usr/sbin/nologin: a system user, automatic id, home /, shell nologin, no groups, because it never opens a card. The user is the one the unit's network side drops to (--network-user defaults to it). On the release run of the virtual machine it got uid 972.

    The firewall profile. remotix.ufw defines the application REMOTIX with ports=7447/tcp|7447/udp (TCP for the page, UDP for QUIC). The package does not run ufw allow: defining is not opening. An administrator who uses ufw runs ufw allow REMOTIX.

    The AppArmor profile

    The conffile /etc/apparmor.d/remotix_network holds the profile remotix_network with the flags complain and attach_disconnected. It has no attachment path: running /usr/libexec/remotix/remotix puts nothing in it, so the root side (PAM, the births of the desktops) stays unconfined. The root side writes exec remotix_network into /proc/thread-self/attr/apparmor/exec just before it execs the network side (apparmor_exec_net in walls.c), and only that process is confined. The text ends with include if exists <local/remotix_network>, so the empty file /etc/apparmor.d/local/remotix_network that dh_apparmor makes is really read: the administrator's additions go there. Three rules matter on Ubuntu 26.04:

    • The unix-socket denials name their operations. The two lines are deny unix (bind, listen) addr=@**, and deny unix (connect, send, receive) peer=(addr=@**),. A bare deny unix addr=@*, also carries create, which has no address to compare: on the kernel of Ubuntu 26.04 (7.0, which mediates unix sockets) it forbade every unix socket, and a deny holds in complain mode too. Result on the first real machine (19 Nov 2026): no D-Bus, no logind, every sign-in refused, with logind unreachable (Unable to create socket: Permission denied) in the log. The register of problems has it as C4; the containers cannot show it because they run no AppArmor. Two asterisks and not one, because one stops at a / and the names to close contain it (@/tmp/.X11-unix/X0). Not closed: the «autobind» (a socket that lets the system give it a random abstract name).
    • The keyboard files are listed under the real folder. On Ubuntu 26.04 (xkb-data 2.46) the data are in /usr/share/xkeyboard-config-2 and /usr/share/X11/xkb is a symlink to it. AppArmor judges the resolved path, so both are listed, with /usr/share/xkeyboard-config-2.d, /etc/xkb and /etc/X11/xkb.
    • It is still in complain mode. The profile logs what it would refuse and refuses nothing except the two deny lines and what the rest of the walls do. Nobody has run the whole functional suite with the profile in enforce: on Ubuntu 26.04 that is not verified. What was seen on a real kernel: aa-status lists remotix_network and the line /usr/libexec/remotix/remotix (<pid>) remotix_network//&unconfined (the root side is not in it, the network side is), and the server's own line says AppArmor: born in remotix_network (16.9 “The startup declarations”).

    The two polkit rules

    Both are in polkit's vendor folder, so polkit reads them in file-name order together with /etc/polkit-1/rules.d/; an administrator writes a rule with a lower number there to decide otherwise. 40-remotix-remote-sessions.rules is about five actions that a distribution grants without a password only to a user at a seat: refreshing the software catalogue (Flatpak.metadata-update, Flatpak.appstream-update, packagekit.system-sources-refresh, fwupd.refresh-remote (inert on Ubuntu 26.04: fwupd 2.1.1 has no such action), yes for a REMOTIX user where the seated user gets yes) and, for network control and system repositories, yes for an administrator and a silent no for anybody else. A REMOTIX session is recognised by the helper remotix-polkit-seated, which looks in logind's state files for a session of the user with the PAM service remotix. 50-remotix-no-poweroff.rules returns NO for 19 login1 actions: power-off, reboot, halt, suspend and hibernate, each in the plain form, -multiple-sessions and -ignore-inhibit (15 actions), and the four set-reboot-parameter, set-reboot-to-firmware-setup, set-reboot-to-boot-loader-menu and set-reboot-to-boot-loader-entry. The last four were added on 20 Nov 2026 (register C6): in logind's policy each of them implies reboot and defaults to yes for the user at the machine, and polkit grants an implied action even when a rule says no to it. The first package that had the rule carried 15 actions; the rule of the release has 19. Root is not affected, because logind does not ask polkit of a caller that holds CAP_SYS_BOOT. The checks are in 17.3 “The checks of all.sh and what each proves” (power-entries-absent, power-implied, power-local-seat).

    i
    Port and profile. The unit starts the server with --address 0.0.0.0: once enabled it listens on every address, TCP for the page and UDP for QUIC. The port is the variable REMOTIX_PORT (7447) in /usr/share/remotix/remotix.conf; changing it in a drop-in does not change the ufw profile, which names 7447.

    15.6 · Our own labwc (KDE)

    The package carries a second program, /usr/libexec/remotix/labwc: labwc 0.9.3 with wlroots 0.19.2 and one patch of the project, statically linked. Its only job is to be the screenless host of the KWin of a KDE session. It is not the labwc that XFCE and LXQt use: those take the one of the distribution, a Recommends.

    The build of it runs inside override_dh_auto_build with the dpkg flags already in the environment (hardening, -ffile-prefix-map), from the two tarballs that the build image fetched and checked. meson is called with -Dwerror=false: wlroots 0.19.2 is built with -Werror, and the libinput of Ubuntu 26.04 raises a warning that it was not written for (a switch value not handled). build.sh checks the sha256 again before it extracts anything. Details of the build are in 18.5 “debian/rules: the overrides and the guards”.

    !
    One path, two places. The path of the program is the same in the build and in kwin.c: a build that changes LABWC must run make clean first, because the path is in the object code. That a KDE session really uses this binary was shown on the Kubuntu virtual machine and on the live Kubuntu (17.11 “What only a real machine or a real phone can prove”); the effect of removing it was not tried for this manual.

    15.7 · Removal: prerm, postrm and purge

    Removal has two scripts and two outcomes. apt remove keeps the configuration and the state; apt purge also removes what the program created by itself, so that the uninstallation leaves the system clean (the owner's rule of 19 Nov 2026). A purge of an installed package runs the prerm with the argument remove first, so the closing work lives in one place.

    prerm (only on remove; on an upgrade it closes no session itself, but the restart of the service that the postinst does if it was running closes them, see the last section). The order matters and each step was added deliberately (the closing of the sessions before the stop, after a measurement on 17 Nov 2026):

    • Take the PAM line out, now that the service is down. pam-auth-update --package --remove remotix (if pam-auth-update exists) removes the local-login line from /etc/pam.d/common-session while the profile file is still in place. It is done only after the stop because the ExecStartPre of the unit would put the line back if the service restarted in between. A failure is said (remotix: ⚠ pam-auth-update --remove remotix failed: check /etc/pam.d/common-session) and does not stop dpkg. A purge passes here too, because it runs the prerm with remove first.
    • Close the sessions, with the service still running. remotix_close_sessions() finds the logind sessions whose Service is remotix and which have no seat (remotix_sessions(); a seated session is never ours whatever its service says) and runs loginctl terminate-session on those whose scope is alive (remotix_scope_alive()). Only those: never the whole user. The order is the point: if the service were stopped first, the child that leads the logind session would exit, logind would close the session and abandon its scope with the desktop inside, and terminate-session would have no scope left to stop (that is the historical reason for the order: it was written when the desktops outlived the service by design, before the decision of 17 Nov 2026 that a stop closes them, and it was kept); with the user's manager lingering the desktop then stayed up for minutes after apt remove.
    • It waits up to 15 s for the desktops to end by themselves, then sends SIGKILL to the scope of each session that did not (systemctl kill --kill-whom=all --signal=SIGKILL session-N.scope, saying so on stderr), then waits up to 5 s more. Never a process outside a REMOTIX session's scope.
    • Stop the service with deb-systemd-invoke stop, because --no-start makes debhelper not do it on removal and a started service would otherwise stay alive on a deleted binary.
    • Sweep again for what the stop left in an abandoned scope, then, for each person who had a REMOTIX session and has no other graphical session (a non-REMOTIX session of type x11, wayland or mir), stop graphical-session.target in that user's manager.
    • Undo the group enrolments recorded in /var/lib/remotix/group-enrollments.jsonl with gpasswd -d, only if the record is a regular file, not a link, owned by root, and after checking that the names contain nothing but A-Za-z0-9._-.
    • Take back the card ACLs by running remotix --drop-render-grants, with the service stopped and before the record and the binary go. If it fails, a warning is printed and /run/remotix/render-grants-kept is left as a marker so the postrm keeps the record.

    postrm. On upgrade and the abort cases it does nothing. On remove, purge and disappear it does two things: it deletes /etc/dconf/db/remotix and any /etc/dconf/db/remotix.new.* left by an interrupted compile, and it writes the profile name to /sys/kernel/security/apparmor/.remove if that file is writable, so the profile leaves the kernel even if its file is already gone. On purge it also:

    • removes /var/lib/remotix/net, /var/lib/remotix/certificates, /var/lib/remotix/ban, ban.new and /run/remotix; removes render-grants unless the marker says the ACLs could not all be taken back (then it keeps it and says so);
    • walks every account the system lists (getent passwd) and, for each one that has a folder ~/.local/state/remotix or a file ~/.config/dconf/remotix, acts as that user through runuser, so that a link planted in a home cannot make root delete something else. In the state folder it removes the product's files by name (session.log, xfce-chiavi, xfce-vecchi-ripristinati, lxqt-restored, gnome-ripristinato) and the folder if it is left empty. Of the dconf folder it removes only the regular file remotix (the small database of the three keyboard keys that change during a session), never through a link, never user, never the folder dconf. Never rm -rf of a folder in a home. If the product writes another file there its name must be added to the list. Homes that are absent are skipped in silence, and the walk never makes the purge fail;
    • deletes the user remotix and its group, unless net-user-preexisting exists and only if its uid is between 1 and 999;
    • removes net-user-preexisting and group-enrollments.jsonl, and the folder /var/lib/remotix if it is empty.
    !
    Limit of the clean purge. The purge acts on the users that the system lists when it runs. A user that is not listed at that moment (a network directory that is down, an account in a database that is unreachable) keeps the file ~/.config/dconf/remotix and the state folder. The file is inert without REMOTIX, but the claim «the uninstallation leaves the system clean» holds for the listed users only. Declared limit, not measured on a machine with such a directory.

    The lintian override in debian/remotix.lintian-overrides explains why the prerm calls systemctl itself: a desktop that ignores SIGTERM is killed through its own session scope, a transient unit that deb-systemd-invoke cannot address. The other override is about page.html, which is the program and not documentation.

    Verification on Ubuntu 26.04. The four VMs and the live systems ran installation, restart and (for the three flavours installed from a clean state) the first start of the package, and the service came up active and enabled with remotix_network loaded; the removal and the purge were not run by a check on this tree. check-package.py names its checks install, first-start, apparmor, remove, purge, reinstall, preinst, recommends and fresh-end, and compares snapshots of /etc, /usr, /var/lib and /run, of users, groups and unit files, before and after; it needs a box that can be reset, which a VM cannot (17.5 “The package check”), and no run of it on Ubuntu 26.04 is on record. The clean purge, with the two new removals of 19 Nov 2026, is therefore a reading of the script, not a measurement. The AppArmor check is BLOCKED in containers, which have no AppArmor interface.

    15.8 · Service policy: installed disabled

    The package installs the service disabled and does not start it. The administrator enables it with systemctl enable --now remotix, as the package description says. This is decided in debian/rules:

    debian/rules
    override_dh_installsystemd:
	dh_installsystemd --no-enable --no-start --restart-after-upgrade

    Two lines of the unit. ExecStartPre=-/usr/libexec/remotix/remotix-pam-hook check: at every start the script looks for the hook's line in /etc/pam.d/common-session and, if it is missing (an update, a hand edit), puts it back with pam-auth-update --package and writes one line in the service's log saying what it found; the - means a failure never prevents the start, and the script never uses --force or --enable, so a file edited by hand or a profile switched off in pam-auth-update stay as they are (the line then says the hook is not in place). And Environment=MESA_SHADER_CACHE_DISABLE=true: the codec probe of the root side would otherwise make Mesa open a shader cache in /root/.cache; the users' desktops get their environment from PAM and keep their cache. That the root side no longer creates that folder was not measured on Ubuntu, and a 1.0.1 folder stays after a removal (register H5).

    Installing as the administrator does

    The administrator's way is two commands, and it is the one the bench follows (server/vm-radeon-installa.sh):

    Install and start
    sudo apt install ./remotix_1.2.0-1+ubuntu26.04_amd64.deb
sudo systemctl enable --now remotix

    The same version installed over an earlier build of itself is not a change for apt, which then does nothing; apt install --reinstall ./remotix_*.deb replaces the files (it is what prove/banco-vm/box.sh install, server/live-installa.sh and server/vm-radeon-installa.sh run, so that a package rebuilt with the same version number is really installed). A reinstall runs the maintainer scripts as an upgrade would: the service is restarted if it was running, and the encoding test of the postinst is not repeated. The messages that tell the administrator to reinstall (the KDE permission file, a missing PAM file) give the command for a .deb: sudo apt install --reinstall ./remotix_<version>_amd64.deb.

    needrestart

    On Ubuntu, needrestart (run by apt after an upgrade, by unattended-upgrades or by hand) restarts a service that uses a library that has just been upgraded (libc6, libssl3, libpam…) without asking, and a restart of REMOTIX closes every remote desktop. The package therefore installs /etc/needrestart/conf.d/remotix.conf with the single line $nrconf{override_rc}{qr(^remotix\.service$)} = 0;: the service is then listed under «Services to be restarted manually» and left running, with the old library loaded, until the administrator restarts it when no remote desktop is open. The display managers and xrdp are exempted in the same way by the distribution's own file. That the line has this effect on a machine that gets an upgrade of a library was not observed (study 11, item P9, is marked postponed); the bench runs apt with NEEDRESTART_MODE=a on purpose, so it does not show it either. The file is a conffile, so an administrator's edit survives.

    The rule of the installed-disabled service comes from point 1 of decision §10.12 of DECISIONS.md (the package switches nothing on; the rest of that decision is about the old installer) and is stated in the repository's CLAUDE.md: the service is installed disabled and not started, and the administrator enables it. The unit uses the machine's name (%H) for the certificate; an administrator who connects by IP address puts REMOTIX_OPTIONS=--name 192.0.2.10 in a drop-in under /etc/remotix/remotix.conf.d/ (the last --name wins). The runtime life cycle of the service is in ch. 3 “Startup and life cycle”.

    Chapter 16

    Logging and diagnostics

    16.1 · The log module

    Every line the server writes goes through one module, src/log.c. The four writing functions are macros over four _in functions that add the source file and line, and all of them end in one static function, line(). There is no scattered printf in the server.

    The reason is written at the top of log.h: a log spread over many fprintf(stderr, …) has neither a timestamp nor an area, and those two are what make a line readable to whoever hunts a defect hours later. The second reason is a security check: the review item B13.2 asks that the password appear in no log, and a single funnel makes «it is not there» verifiable (16.8 “What never enters the log”). docs/LESSONS.md §2.7 calls the log the main diagnostic instrument of the project.

    i
    Outside the funnel. a few places write straight to stderr and are outside the funnel: authentication.c (the PAM check, lines prefixed RCP:), the child between fork and exec (become_and_exec(), lines prefixed child:), the usage text and the refusals of the command line in main(), and the KDE start-line helper kwin_nested_alive() (lines prefixed remotix --kwin-nested:), which runs as the user inside KWin's unit. These lines have no timestamp, no area and never reach the journal through --journal.

    16.2 · Anatomy of a log line

    A line is HH:MM:SS.mmm area [identity] body: local wall-clock time with milliseconds, the area left-aligned in seven columns (%-7s), the identity in brackets only when there is one, then the body.

    The body follows one convention across the code: a body that starts with ⛔ is a fault, with ⚠ a declared fallback or a warning, ⭐ marks a notable fact (a decision in force, a cure that fired). Only the mark at the head counts, because many normal lines quote a ⛔ in the middle; the journal priority reads only the head (16.7 “Journal priorities and the rule of the head mark”).

    Shape of three lines (text abbreviated; the real bodies are longer)
    08:41:07.312 startup ⭐ ready: https://server.lan:7447 …
08:41:19.884 rcp     [anna] … PAM answered …
08:41:21.040 child   [anna] ⭐ …

    The time is CLOCK_REALTIME in local time, for the human reader. Every interval the code measures uses log_now_ms() (CLOCK_MONOTONIC); the two are never mixed.

    16.3 · Log areas

    The area is the second column of every line and the REMOTIX_AREA field in the journal. It exists to read the log by column when transport, protocol and session speak at the same time. The names below are the string values; the constants are defined in log.h unless said otherwise.

    i
    Note. the area is padded to seven characters; session, keyboard, rootside and clipboard are longer and push the body to the right. A tool that parses the log must split on white space, not on column positions.

    16.4 · Whose line it is

    With several users on one machine, a line that does not say whose it is sends the reader to look at somebody else's desktop. The identity in brackets is the user name, and it reaches the line by two roads because the processes are of two kinds.

    The comment in log.h records the measurement behind this (finding R10-A4): with four real GNOME sessions (57,121 lines in 90 s) only 4.2 % of the diagnostic lines said whom they were about, and a reader who guessed the name was wrong 96 times in 100. The identity is composed in one place only, line(); the callers pass the bare name. It is stored as a copy in a static buffer of the process, not as a pointer, and it does not cross exec, which is why the child sets it again from its own command line.

    !
    A claimed name is not an authenticated name. the bracket of a line written by the parent for a login attempt is the name the client claimed, also before PAM has answered. The server therefore does not write that name as such: log_user() in rcp.c writes user [a1b2c3] (or unknown user [a1b2c3] when the name is not a user of the machine), where the six hex digits are the first three bytes of an HMAC-SHA256 of the name under a secret kept in the file log-secret (mode 0600). The same tag reaches the PAM helper through REMOTIX_PAM_LOG_TAG (16.11 “Environment variables read by the product”). Read the outcome line, not the bracket, to know who got in.

    16.5 · Where the log lines go

    The log has no file of its own: the server writes to its standard error, and the unit that starts it decides where that goes. The child inherits descriptors 0, 1 and 2 across exec, so parent and child lines land in the same stream and can be read in order.

    A stderr that never blocks the loop

    stderr under systemd is journald's stream socket, which is blocking. The child's single loop delivers every frame, so a stalled journald must not stop it. err_write() in log.c therefore never waits: it looks at descriptor 2 at every line (err_look()) and writes without waiting when it can block. On a socket it uses send(MSG_DONTWAIT) and refuses to start a line the send buffer cannot take whole (SIOCOUTQ against SO_SNDBUF). On a pipe it opens /proc/self/fd/2 a second time with O_NONBLOCK (not fcntl on descriptor 2, which would change the open file for the shell that shares it). A file or a terminal is written as usual. A line that does not fit is dropped and counted, and as soon as the stream accepts again the count is written: log ⚠ N log lines DROPPED: stderr was not accepting (dropped_notice()). A hole in the log is therefore declared instead of the loop stopping. A line cut in the middle by a stream socket is closed with the mark …[line cut: stderr full].

    The session log

    Whatever the desktop session itself prints goes to a file chosen by log_session_path() in session.c: session.log in the folder remotix under the user's state directory (g_get_user_state_dir(), normally ~/.local/state). The shell command that starts the session begins with exec >>FILE 2>&1 (in start()). The folder is created with mode 0700 and must be a real directory (not a link), owned by the user and not writable by others (is_our_dir()); the file is opened with O_NOFOLLOW, mode 0600, and must be a regular file of the user (our_file()). If that cannot be done the fallback is $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/remotix-session.log, which disappears with the session, and the server says so with a ⚠ line; if even that fails the session starts with exec >/dev/null 2>&1 and a ⛔ line says that the session has no log. The reason for the location is in the comment of log_session_path(): a predictable name in a shared directory could be created first by another user, and a log in XDG_RUNTIME_DIR would be gone exactly when a session that died at once needs it. The package removes the file when the package is purged, as that user, together with the small dconf file ~/.config/dconf/remotix (debian/remotix.postrm, 15.7 “Removal: prerm, postrm and purge”). The folder of a user who is not listed by the system at the moment of the purge keeps it.

    16.6 · The systemd journal output

    With --journal every event line also goes to the systemd journal, with fields that can be filtered. The line on stderr keeps its text; the journal is added, not substituted (except where stderr is itself the journal, as under the packaged unit: «No second copy» below). The packaged service always passes --journal.

    The child, after pam_open_session, lives in the scope of the user's logind session, not in the server unit, so journalctl -u remotix does not find its lines; query by identifier.

    Reading the journal
    journalctl -t remotix -f                         # everything, parent and children
journalctl -t remotix -p warning --since today   # faults and fallbacks only
journalctl -t remotix REMOTIX_TENANT=anna        # one user
journalctl -t remotix REMOTIX_AREA=budget        # why somebody was refused
journalctl -t remotix -o verbose -n 1            # every field of the last line

    At startup the parent declares the outcome: log also in the systemd journal (--journal): … or ⚠ --journal requested but the socket does not open (…): the log stays ONLY here. The journal is switched on before the first line, so the first line goes there too.

    i
    Priority 7. the box in log.h says priority 7 is used for the chatter. The code in line() never sends detail lines to the journal, so 7 does not occur; the help text of main.c says the same as the code. The code is right.
    i
    A profile can silence the journal. the journal socket is a unix socket, and the network side writes to it from inside its AppArmor profile: the profile lists /run/systemd/journal/socket and /run/systemd/journal/stdout and allows network unix dgram. On the first real Ubuntu 26.04 machine (19 Nov 2026) an earlier form of the profile, deny unix addr=@*,, forbade every unix socket, journal included, and the refusal was not announced by any line of the profile (a deny says nothing in complain mode). The symptom was in the server's own log: logind unreachable (Unable to create socket: Permission denied) and every login refused (register of problems, C4). The profile now names the operations (15.5 “Files the package installs”).

    16.7 · Journal priorities and the rule of the head mark

    The priority of a line is decided in line() by the first non-blank characters of the body: ⛔ gives 3 (error), ⚠ gives 4 (warning), anything else 6 (info). The file docs/REGISTRO-priorita.md records the pass of 17 Nov 2026 (31 lines of code changed) that moved lines between the levels by changing only the mark at the head of the body; text, logic and the log_detail levels were left alone. The aim was that journalctl -b -p err should contain only what needs a person. The counts below come from that document (a full run on the four test containers of the Debian 13 work, 17 Nov 2026) and were not re-measured on Ubuntu 26.04; the lines this tree added (D-015, the scale refusal, the KDE logout, the guest labwc) were not part of that pass, and each of them follows the same rule of the head mark.

    The document counts 33 patterns seen in the run: 5 moved to info, 24 to warning, 4 kept as error. It lists what is not ours and was left alone (for example the pam_env message about a missing /etc/default/locale in the test image, rtkit and colord messages in containers).

    !
    Open points of the priority pass. two things the document itself leaves open. (1) On the test containers POWERED OFF OR SUSPENDED appeared as an error because logind answers no question there and the check counted that as a failure; it was kept as an error because it is the safety belt. Since 1.2.0 the guardian (sentinel_shutdown_forbidden()) accepts no and na (not available on this machine: nobody can do it, as safe as no) and counts only yes, challenge and an error as unsafe; an error is still an alarm, but the detail now names the call and the reason, as in CanSuspend=(ERROR: …), where it used to say «(no answer)». (2) About 700 call sites start with ⛔ and did not occur in the run, so their level is unverified; the document names the quality-down line of encoder.c (a bandwidth adaptation) as a candidate for ⚠. The warning level was not measured in depth.

    16.8 · What never enters the log

    Three things never enter any log at any level: passwords, what the user types, and the content of the screen. The first is a protocol rule (RCP.md, see ch. 5 “The RCP/1 protocol”), the second a decision of phase 16 recorded in log.h (keystrokes are logged as «key», never as a character), the third follows: the only images the server can write are those of the bench option --survey, which is off by default.

    A sequence of evdev codes such as 30, 48, 46 is a word: a key code is a character up to the keyboard layout. That is why the list of speakable keys is the only question a caller must ask before writing a code. rcp.c carries its own copy because it is also compiled into a test host that has no server log.

    i
    Two different PAM lines. the PAM check in authentication.c writes to stderr and so it never goes through line(): its lines (RCP: PAM REFUSED …, RCP: ⛔ PAM COULD NOT JUDGE …) are the ones to read when a login is refused. The first means PAM said no; the second means PAM could not judge (for example a missing PAM service file). The client receives the same refusal in both cases.

    16.9 · The startup declarations

    At startup the parent writes the value in force of every mechanism that changes what users see or that can close a session, whether switched on or off. A threshold that is off and a threshold that never fired produce the same log, and a long clock is never verified by waiting for it, so the line is the verification. The order is that of main(); the table lists what is declared and which function writes it.

    A real start on Ubuntu 26.04

    The service was enabled on the Ubuntu virtual machine with the Radeon passed through (the control of 19 Nov 2026, server/vm-radeon-controllo.sh). The excerpt is verbatim, shortened with «…» where the line goes on, and it shows two things that a reader of an Ubuntu log meets at once. First, the root side writes before the network side exists, and the lines of the network side carry the pid of the confined process (1357, not 1282). Second, the encoder finds no card at the first measurement and the server says THIS SERVER CANNOT ENCODE VIDEO with two marks of fault, then, two seconds later, the card arrived 2 s after startup. The node /dev/dri/renderD128 did not exist yet when the service started; the code treats a missing node as a matter of time and measures again after 2 s, doubling up to 60 s (codec_step()); a node that opens but encodes nothing gets five more tries and then the server stops measuring. All four virtual machines of the control show the same two lines, 2 s apart. It is not a defect of the package; it is what a start before the video driver has made the node looks like, and the line that matters for the diagnosis is the second one.

    Start of the service on the Ubuntu 26.04 virtual machine (journal of 19 Nov 2026, shortened)
    startup ⭐ phase 18 — encoding test at startup, in a separate process: …
child   ⛔ no video for codec 3: «h264_card» on /dev/dri/renderD128 did not open («/dev/dri/renderD128» does not open: No such file or directory) ⇒ this codec is NOT available on this machine: … ⚠ Retrying in 500 ms …
startup ⭐ the card's node does not open yet: measuring again (2 s, then doubling up to 60 s) until it does
rootside ⭐ ROOT SIDE on (pid 1282, DECISIONS.md §11.50): single-threaded, PAM helper and children below it, up to 10 children; the network side runs as uid 972
rootside ⭐ the network side's walls in force: AppArmor: born in remotix_network; folder /; landlock ABI 8: abstract unix sockets scoped; PID 1 of its own PID namespace, /proc of its own; own network namespace (loopback only; the inherited sockets work); …
startup ⛔⛔ THIS SERVER CANNOT ENCODE VIDEO: no capable card, no codec in the HERE_I_AM, every HELLO ends in NOTHING_IN_COMMON until the card arrives (measured again) — card /dev/dri/renderD128 (route requested «card») — HEVC: NO («/dev/dri/renderD128» does not open: No such file or directory) · H.264: NO (…).  ⛔ REMOTIX encodes ONLY on the card …
startup the desktop of this machine: GNOME (gnome-session and gnome-shell are there)
startup ⭐ the card arrived 2 s after startup — video.codec offered in the HERE_I_AM from now on: «hevc,h264» — card /dev/dri/renderD128 (route requested «card») — HEVC: yes via vulkan · H.264: yes via vulkan

    The line about the walls is the one to read for the AppArmor profile: AppArmor: born in remotix_network says the network side entered the profile; landlock ABI 8: abstract unix sockets scoped is the second wall (Landlock, ABI 8 on the kernel 7.0 of Ubuntu 26.04): the process cannot reach an abstract unix socket made outside its own domain.
