    Chapter 18

    Build and release

    18.1 · The build of the .deb on the build VM

    REMOTIX is not built on the machine where it is edited, and the 1.2.0 build uses no container. build/build-deb-vm.sh [label] copies the tree to the virtual machine costruzione, builds the package there with dpkg-buildpackage (which builds the package's own labwc too), examines the finished package and brings the .deb, the source archive of the labwc and the logs back to /media/REMOTIX-UBUNTU/pacchetti/<label>/ on the dev server. The machine that runs the script needs ssh access to the dev server (its address is the variable RX_SERVER) and a network connection: it does not compile; it fetches the two upstream tarballs of labwc and wlroots (labwc from GitHub and wlroots from gitlab.freedesktop.org, checked by hash) and makes the source archive of the labwc. It needs no git, Go, bench folder or old repository. If the build machine is off, the script turns it on (virtual only, never the Radeon) and turns it off again at the end; KEEP_VM=1 leaves it on (17.8 “The VM bench”). Inside the machine the static QUIC libraries are cloned from GitHub and apt reads the Ubuntu archives.

    The virtual machine, and not the editing machine, is the point: the package is built against the libraries of Ubuntu 26.04 (measured in the buildinfo of the package of 19 Nov 2026, numbered 1.0.0: gcc 15.2.0, debhelper 13.31ubuntu1, dpkg-dev 1.23.7ubuntu1, libssl-dev 3.5.5, libva-dev 2.23.0, meson 1.10.1). The build folders on the server are one per label, under /media/REMOTIX-UBUNTU/pacchetti/.

    i
    Note. What the package contains and how its maintainer scripts behave is in ch. 15 “The package”. This chapter is about how the bytes are made and what is checked on them.

    18.2 · The build machine and the static QUIC libraries

    Ubuntu 26.04 packages ngtcp2 1.16.0 and nghttp3 1.12.0, both in universe (the report studio/8-pacchetto-e-prove.md, read from apt-cache; not re-measured for this manual). The comment in src/Makefile still gives the figures of Debian (1.11 and 1.8), which is wrong for this tree and is a comment of the source, not of the manual. Either set is too old: the product needs ngtcp2 at least 1.25 with the ngtcp2_crypto_ossl bridge (the NGTCP2_STREAM_CLOSE2_FLAG_* flags used by transport.c) and OpenSSL at least 3.5 for the native QUIC API (Ubuntu 26.04 has 3.5.5: make deps printed openssl 3.5.5 (>= 3.5.0) in the build of the package of 19 Nov 2026, numbered 1.0.0). So the build machine builds the two libraries from source, pinned at one version, and installs only the static archives.

    • Static only. quic-static.sh configures with -DENABLE_SHARED_LIB=OFF and -DENABLE_STATIC_LIB=ON, library directory fixed to lib (not lib64 or a multiarch directory) so that the LIBRARY_PATH=/usr/local/lib that the build sets works and the Makefile needs no path. At the end the script fails if any libngtcp2*.so* or libnghttp3*.so* exists in /usr/local/lib: a shared object there would be picked up by the linker. The -dev packages of Ubuntu for the two libraries are not installed on the build machine, so the static ones win; if a Build-Depends ever brought them in, the test of debian/rules (below) would stop the build.
    • The result. The package has no run-time dependency on ngtcp2 or nghttp3; its control file says so with Static-Built-Using: ngtcp2 (= 1.25.0), nghttp3 (= 1.18.0), labwc (= 0.9.3), wlroots (= 0.19.2).
    • The versions are written in four places for ngtcp2 and nghttp3, and a change must touch all of them: the defaults of quic-static.sh, the two test lines of debian/rules (R24, below), Static-Built-Using in debian/control, and MINIMI in src/Makefile (and the test of what is already installed in build-deb-vm.sh, which compares the two versions with 1.25.0 and 1.18.0). Those of labwc and wlroots are in build/labwc-ospite/VERSIONS, in Static-Built-Using and in the name of the patch file; the build of the labwc checks the tarballs against VERSIONS and the patch by its name, and debian/rules has no test line for them.
    • ngtcp2 and nghttp3 are not pinned by hash. The script clones the two tags with git clone --depth 1 -b <tag>. The tag is the pin; no commit id or archive checksum is checked, so a moved tag could in principle be fetched. labwc and wlroots are pinned by hash: VERSIONS holds the SHA-256 of both tarballs (labwc 0.9.3 and wlroots 0.19.2), fetch.sh checks them even when the files are already there, and build.sh checks them again before it extracts.
    !
    Warning. The build needs network access to GitHub (the first time the libraries are built, and every time for labwc) and to gitlab.freedesktop.org (wlroots), from the machine that runs the script, and to the archives of Ubuntu (only if a build dependency is missing: the script tries the installation first and runs apt-get update only if it fails). The libraries are built once: the script skips the step if pkg-config already reports ngtcp2 1.25.0 and nghttp3 1.18.0 and libngtcp2_crypto_ossl.a is in /usr/local/lib. The compiling itself does not need the network (meson runs with --wrap-mode=nodownload, and the two labwc tarballs travel with the copy).

    18.3 · What build-deb-vm.sh does, step by step

    The script is a sequence of steps. The label names the output folder /media/REMOTIX-UBUNTU/pacchetti/<label> (default: the date and time); it may contain only letters, digits, dot, underscore and dash, and not be . or ... If the folder exists already, the script stops (exit 2): a previous package is never overwritten.

    In order:

    • The labwc sources. labwc-ospite/fetch.sh fetches the two upstream tarballs on the machine that runs the script and verifies them against VERSIONS; a missing tarball or a different hash stops the script (exit 2).
    • Copy. A clean copy of src/, debian/, build/labwc-ospite/ (as labwc-ospite/) and THIRD-PARTY-LICENSES is made in a temporary folder. The text of LICENSE.md is appended to debian/copyright as continuation lines of License: LicenseRef-REMOTIX (an empty line becomes " ."), the leftovers of a local build (the binary, *.o, the generated protocol sources) are deleted and debian/changelog is written with one entry for the distribution resolute, with the line "Ubuntu 26.04 build", dated from SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH. The working tree is never touched.
    • The machine. If it does not answer, the script starts it virtuale and waits; it checks that it is the build virtual machine (host name rx-ub-costruzione) and copies the work folder in (~/debwork/<label> in the guest). A work folder left there by a failed run is kept for inspection and never removed: the script stops and asks for another label.
    • Dependencies. In the guest, apt-get install --no-install-recommends of build-essential, pkg-config, git, cmake, ninja-build, the -dev packages of OpenSSL, PAM, GLib, PipeWire, libdrm, libva, Opus, zlib, libei, xkbcommon, gbm, Wayland and the Vulkan loader, the build tools of labwc and wlroots (curl meson patch hwdata wayland-protocols libegl-dev libgles-dev libinput-dev libpixman-1-dev libseat-dev libudev-dev libdisplay-info-dev libxml2-dev libcairo2-dev libpango1.0-dev libpng-dev) and the packaging tools debhelper, dh-apparmor, dpkg-dev, fakeroot, lintian and binutils. Log apt.log.
    • Static libraries. quic-static.sh, unless the right versions are already there (18.2 “The build machine and the static QUIC libraries”). Log quic.log.
    • Build. dpkg-buildpackage -b -us -uc (binary only, unsigned) in a copy of the tree; it builds our labwc too, from the tarballs that travelled with the copy. Log costruzione.log. The .deb and the .buildinfo come out, with a .sha256 of the .deb and the file list (elenco.txt, from dpkg-deb -c).
    • Lintian. lintian -I --pedantic --no-tag-display-limit on the .deb, into lintian.txt. Warnings are only shown; a lintian error fails the script (the line lintian: E=0 must be in controlli.txt).
    • Checks R13, R14, R4 on the finished package, one line each ending SI or NO, into controlli.txt, followed by the control fields Depends, Recommends, Static-Built-Using and the list of conffiles. R4 has two lines, one for the server and one for the guest labwc. The host script requires the lines (R13 banco-nel-binario, R13 opzioni-di-banco-nell-unita, R14 file-del-banco, R4 ldd, R4 ldd-labwc, labwc-source) to be there and to say SI: a line missing, or any line with NO, fails.
    • The source of the guest labwc. The corresponding source of the labwc that the package carries is made on the machine that runs the script and saved as $OUTPUT/remotix-<version>-labwc-source.tar.gz with its .sha256: the two tarballs, the patch and the recipe (VERSIONS, fetch.sh, build.sh, README). The archive is made deterministic (tar --sort=name --owner=0 --group=0 --numeric-owner --mode=go-w --mtime=@SDE | gzip -n) and must hold the 7 expected files. The result is the line labwc-source SI|NO of controlli.txt; on a failure the archive is removed. It is the file that a release has to publish: labwc is GPL-2 (18.7 “Version and release”).
    • Second build (R23) only with TWICE=1: a second clean copy is built and the two .deb are compared with cmp; the source archive of labwc is also made twice and compared (R23 labwc-source-riproducibile).
    • Exit. 0 when everything passes. 1 if a check fails, if dpkg-buildpackage fails or no .deb comes out: then no package is brought back, the logs go to <OUTPUT>-fallita-<time> on the server and the guest's work folder stays. 2 if the label or the output folder is refused, the labwc tarballs are wrong or the machine does not answer.

    Output files in $OUTPUT: the .deb, the .buildinfo, the .sha256 of the .deb, costruzione.log, costruzione-vm.log, apt.log, quic.log, lintian.txt, controlli.txt, elenco.txt (the file list of the package; from dpkg-deb -c), and the labwc source archive with its checksum. The server folder holds one sub-folder per package built.

    18.4 · src/Makefile: sources, libraries, minimum versions

    One Makefile, no configure step. It builds 40 C files (the variable SORGENTI) into the server binary remotix, plus 10 Wayland protocol files generated at build time. The target all also builds a second, separate program, remotix-local-login, from local_login.c alone: libc only, the same flags, no library (the rule $(LOCAL_LOGIN)). It is the PAM hook of the local-login hold (14.6 “The local-login hold”).

    The declared minimum versions

    make deps checks every module against its minimum, then tries to compile and link an empty program that includes each header the product needs (ngtcp2/ngtcp2.h, ngtcp2/ngtcp2_crypto_ossl.h, nghttp3/nghttp3.h, OpenSSL, PAM, GIO, PipeWire, drm_fourcc.h, libva, gbm, opus, vulkan, zlib). It prints OK, NO or ?? per item and exits non-zero on any failure; debian/rules runs it first, so a missing or old library stops the build with a line that names it.

    The twin comparison and TWIN=none

    rcp.c, rcp.h, authentication.c and msgrate.h (variable GEMELLATI) were designed to exist in two copies, the product's and a bench's, and the target fingerprints, part of all, compares them with cmp before compiling. The default TWIN ?= ../benches/rcp points to a folder that this repository does not have. With a missing twin folder the target stops the build (exit 2) unless the caller declares TWIN=none, in which case it prints that nothing was compared. debian/rules passes TWIN=none everywhere, so the package build never compares anything.

    !
    Warning. A plain make in src/ fails at fingerprints unless TWIN=none is given. This is the result of reading the Makefile; it was not run for this manual.

    18.5 · debian/rules: the overrides and the guards

    debian/rules is a debhelper (compat 13) recipe with a few deliberate overrides. Each one has a reason written in the file.

    The destination paths and the role of each shipped file are described in ch. 15 “The package”.

    18.6 · The package checks R4, R13, R14, R23 and R24

    The labels R4, R13, R14, R23 and R24 are requirement names carried over from the project's earlier packaging work. In this repository they are defined only by the scripts that implement them, build/build-deb-vm.sh (and the older build/build-deb.sh) and debian/rules. (R followed by a number is also used for unrelated audit findings elsewhere, for example in the comments of hsrate.h and tls.c.)

    What was recorded

    The values below are those of controlli.txt and lintian.txt of the package of 19 Nov 2026, numbered 1.0.0 (the build called unione10 in the work); the build after it, unione11, has the same lines and the same counts, with a different checksum (the polkit rule changed). They were read from the server for the earlier manual and were not taken again for 1.2.0: the 1.2.0 package was built on the build VM with build-deb-vm.sh and lintian was clean (register G2); its controlli.txt was not read for this manual.

    • R13 SI: package: 0, positive control rcp.o with BENCH_ON 1: 1, and no bench option in the unit. R14 SI (none). R4 SI: 33 libraries, none missing; R4 ldd-labwc SI: no libwlroots, none missing, labwc 0.9.3 (-xwayland -nls -rsvg -libsfdo).
    • The control fields printed: Recommends: va-driver-all, mesa-vulkan-drivers, labwc, dconf-cli, wlr-randr, xwayland, fonts-dejavu-core; Static: labwc (= 0.9.3), nghttp3 (= 1.18.0), ngtcp2 (= 1.25.0), wlroots (= 0.19.2); the five conffiles: the AppArmor profile, the needrestart drop-in, /etc/pam.d/remotix, /etc/remotix/denied-users and the ufw profile. The Depends line has the libraries that dpkg-shlibdeps found (among them libseat1, libinput10 (>= 1.28.0), libxml2-16, libpixman-1-0 and libwayland-server0, which are those of the guest labwc) followed by the fixed ones of 15.2 “Package metadata: Depends and Recommends”.
    • labwc-source SI: the archive remotix-1.0.0-labwc-source.tar.gz, 7 files. R23 SI: identical in two clean copies, and R23 labwc-source-riproducibile SI. Both were made with TWICE=1.
    • Lintian (version of the build of 19 Nov 2026, with --pedantic): 0 errors and 0 warnings; one information line, systemd-service-file-missing-documentation-key for remotix.service. The two overrides of debian/remotix.lintian-overrides (the page is the program, the prerm calls systemctl) still apply; that lintian of Ubuntu 26.04 reports no new tag for them is shown by this result and not by anything else.
    • The file list has 59 entries (folders included); the guest labwc in it is 1,456,680 bytes and the server 3,707,960 bytes.
    !
    Limit of the reproducibility check. R23 compares two builds made from the same tree in the same run, with the same SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH. Left to its default, SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH is the newest modification time of files in src/, debian/, build/labwc-ospite/ and the two licence files, and a fresh checkout gives files new modification times. Two builds from two checkouts therefore differ unless the caller fixes SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH (for example to the commit time).

    18.7 · Version and release

    The version of the product exists only as package metadata. I found no version constant in src/ (no source file or header carries the number), and the page and the protocol have their own versions that are not the package's.

    Building the release package
    $ RX_VERSION=1.2.0 RX_REVISION=1 build/build-deb-vm.sh 1.2.0
$ TWICE=1 RX_VERSION=1.2.0 build/build-deb-vm.sh 1.2.0-twice     # also R23

    Without RX_VERSION a build is a development build, remotix_1.2.0~dev-1+ubuntu26.04_amd64.deb. The Debian 13 product has its own manual and its own file name, with a +deb13 suffix; the two packages are not interchangeable.

    What "release" means in this tree

    The tree has no release script, no signing step, no repository and no publication tool: the old packaging and site folders were not carried over (docs/INVENTARIO-non-debian.md lists what was left behind). A release is the output of build-deb-vm.sh with RX_VERSION=1.2.0: the .deb, the .buildinfo, the check files, and the source archive of the guest labwc with its checksum. The package is built unsigned (-us -uc). docs/STORIA-ubuntu-26.04.md leaves publication, the site and public repositories to the owner's decision, so none of them is described as existing.

    i
    A release has two files to publish. The guest labwc is GPL-2 software that the package ships in binary form. A release must therefore publish remotix-<version>-labwc-source.tar.gz (and its .sha256) next to the .deb: this is stated in debian/copyright and in section 8 of LICENSE.md, and it is why the build makes the archive and checks that it holds the two tarballs, the patch and the recipe. Whether the publication has been made is outside this tree and is not claimed here.

    18.8 · Generated and vendored inputs

    Four kinds of file in the product come from outside the package build. Their results are committed, except the tarballs of labwc and wlroots, which are fetched by the build script and checked by hash.

    +
    Tip. A change to vulkanvideo_rgb_nv12.comp needs a tool chain (glslang or similar) that no script in the tree provides. See ch. 20 “Extending REMOTIX and porting to another distribution” for how to add a codec.
    Chapter 19

    Performance and capacity

    19.1 · How to read the numbers of this chapter

    A number in this chapter is one of three kinds, and each is labelled. Measured on Ubuntu 26.04: printed by a check of prove/ in the round of 19 November 2026 (the log folder vm-gnome-unione10, package unione10, GNOME, one virtual machine). Recorded: written in docs/DECISIONS.md or in the problem register from an earlier campaign or a hand test; it is quoted with its date and is NOT a measurement of this tree on a controlled bench. Coded: a constant or default in the source, cited by name; it is a limit or a target, not an observation.

    Nothing here was measured while writing the manual, and no figure is derived or extrapolated. The figures are those of the round of 19 November 2026 (package unione10, before 1.2.0), on GNOME only: none was measured again on 1.2.0. The rounds of 1.2.0 on the four virtual machines of 17.8 “The VM bench” (GNOME 125 PASS and one known FAIL, KDE, XFCE and LXQt 126 PASS) were made for their verdicts, and no timing of them is quoted here, so no timing in this chapter holds for Kubuntu, Xubuntu or Lubuntu. A figure that was measured on Debian 13 and not repeated here is marked measured on Debian 13 only or left out. Where a figure that a reader would expect does not exist, the section says so (19.7 “Where no measurement exists”).

    i
    Note. A measurement made by a check that drives a browser through its debugging interface includes the check's own cost. The tool's limits are given in ch. 17 “Testing”. The figures below are evidence that a property holds under the stated conditions, not a benchmark of the product.

    19.2 · The test machine and the conditions of the measurements

    The figures come from one virtual machine on the dev server and from the conditions of the check suite. The bench is the virtual-machine bench of Ubuntu 26.04 (17.8 “The VM bench”), not the container bench of Debian 13.

    • Machine. A QEMU/KVM virtual machine with UEFI, installed from the Ubuntu 26.04 desktop image like a user would install it, with CPUS=8 MEM=12G DISKSZ=40G (server/vm-radeon.sh). The server's AMD Radeon is passed through to the machine by vfio-pci (PCI address 0000:03:00.0); the machine sees that card and no other, and only one machine at a time can hold it. The model of the card is not printed by the logs of the round (docs/SPECS.md §11.4 names an RX 6800 for the dev server; not verified for this machine). The time to power such a machine on or off is a property of the bench, not of the product, and is not reported.
    • Bench switches. RX_BANCO=vm selects the virtual-machine bench; RX_TEMPO=2 (the default of that bench) doubles every deadline of the checks. A figure that the product itself prints (for example "client told after 0 s") is not changed by it; a deadline that the check waits for is doubled. The checks reach the machine through the user-mode network of QEMU, so every client appears to the server as the address 10.0.2.2 (17.8 “The VM bench”).
    • Client. A real browser on the dev server driven by its debugging interface, in a headless compositor: Chrome 156.0.8078.79 and Firefox 153.7.0 as printed in the logs. The path to the machine is the virtual network of the host: nothing here says anything about bandwidth, loss or delay of a real link, except the single hand measurement of the problem register (19.7 “Where no measurement exists”).
    • Size. The canvas of the media check was 1344x768 with Chrome (coded sizes 1344x770 and 1344x768 in the log) and 1392x800 with Firefox. No figure below holds for another size. The load average of the host at the time is printed by the check: 1.80 (picture and frame rate) and 1.26 (two sessions).
    • Codec. Both browsers negotiated H.264 (avc1.640033, 8 bit). The log says the server's H.264 encoder at start-up was HARDWARE on /dev/dri/renderD128 (the session's process had that node open). HEVC did not reach the pixel on the test browsers (the page's capability probe answered no to every HEVC string), as on Debian 13. The route (Vulkan Video or VA-API) is not printed in the lines read; the history of the work on Ubuntu records that in the virtual machines the video went through Vulkan on the Radeon and on a real machine through VA-API on the card of that machine (docs/STORIA-ubuntu-26.04.md, 19 Nov 2026, hand test of the live image).

    19.3 · Picture, frame rate and sound measured on 19 November 2026

    From check-media.py (screen-updates, video, codec, two-sessions-budget), GNOME on Ubuntu 26.04, in the round vm-gnome-unione10. All four checks were PASS. The figures are those of Chrome; the log prints Firefox only for the codec check.

    How to read the table

    • Timing figures carry the tool's uncertainty. The browser is screenshotted: one screenshot takes about 50 ms, and the capture instant is somewhere inside it. The log itself gives the age of a picture as a range (median -12 ms if the capture is at the start of the screenshot, 40 ms if at its end, 13 ms taking the middle; 90th percentile 26 ms, maximum 39 ms). These are not glass-to-glass latency figures; the specification promises none, only 50 ms for the server's own piece.
    • Sound lags the picture by a constant 276 to 346 ms. This is the audio cushion AUDIO_BUFFER_MS = 250 in page.html, a declared price (the comment in the page explains why 60 ms produced gaps). The check's own limits, in its code, are a median of at most 400 ms and a drift of at most 150 ms over the ten pairs; the log prints the lag as "by design" and leaves lip-sync judgement to the owner. The docstring of check-media.py says 250 ms for the median; the code says 400 ms.
    • The two-session figure is a regression test, not a capacity test. The budget knob is off in this run (--budget-mpixel-s 0.0 (OFF) --session-cap 10 --reserve 0.50 in the journal of the run); the rule being tested is that whoever is inside is not degraded (the first user lost 0 percent).
    • Debian 13 only. The Debian 13 round of 17 Nov 2026 measured four desktops in containers (XFCE, LXQt and KDE at 58 to 62 frames per second painted, GNOME at 39 frames per second). Those figures were taken on another machine, with another compositor version and another card, and are not repeated here: on Ubuntu 26.04 only the GNOME row above exists, and it shows 60.0. Neither log says why the two GNOME figures differ, and the difference must not be attributed to the distribution (the bench, the card and the compositor version all changed).

    KDE: the lost frame, a property of the code

    No picture figure was measured on Kubuntu with these checks. The code, however, has a mechanism that bears on the picture of KDE, described here only as a coded limit: capture_watch_sequence() and capture_frame_lost() in capture.c watch the numbering of the buffers that KWin delivers; a gap forces a frame marked "all changed" and, after LOST_QUIET_MS = 200 ms without an image, a poke through kwin_poke(), at most LOST_POKES_MAX = 10 times in a row, with a window of SEQ_WINDOW = 600 buffer numbers (the mechanism is explained in 6.5 “The lost frame (KWin)”). The comments of the code record measurements on a Kubuntu machine (a window left halfway through an animation for 18 to 26 s; 68 pokes on a still desktop, all answered by frames with empty damage that are not sent); they are comments, not a run of this manual.

    19.4 · Session and login timings measured on 19 November 2026

    From check-lifecycle.py, check-resilience.py, check-ban.py and check-multiuser.py in the same round, GNOME only. They are measured, with the tools' resolution of one second.

    • The refusal time is the floor REJECT_FLOOR = 2500 ms in rcp.c plus the page's reaction; it is constant by design so that a wrong password and an unknown user are indistinguishable (the two medians above are equal).
    • On Ubuntu the child may tell the clients "the session is over" before it dismantles its stage (session_over_early() in child.c, only on a certain death and never on KDE), so the "client told" time of a Log Out is not comparable with a Debian 13 figure. The Debian 13 figures (0 s on XFCE and LXQt, 5 s on GNOME, 4 s on KDE, round of 17 Nov 2026) were measured on Debian 13 only and are not carried over. A process of the child can wait up to 25 s for RealtimeKit where that service is installed and does not answer (a property of the container boxes, the older bench; entry B2 of the register), which is why the child tells the clients first.
    • After a restart of the service the log of the round says that the client was told after 0 s, that the old desktop was gone and that the next login took one try (the desktops are closed with the service, DECISIONS-11 §11.56).
    • The values of clocks are from a run with the clocks shortened by a drop-in (30 s, 30 s, 90 s). At the defaults the service prints 30 s (fixed) for client silence, 1800 s for user inactivity and 3600 s for session abandonment; the defaults were not run to expiry.
    • The "login to a working session in 6 s" of two-users and three-users is the harness's polling steps as much as the product's; it shows an upper bound, not a typical time.
    • Local login on KDE (hand test, not a check). With the real login screen of a Kubuntu live image, the owner logged in locally while the remote desktop was open: the login was held in PAM, the client was sent away with 0x04 and the child closed the remote desktop in 10.9 s; on the GNOME live image the same step took 0.85 s (docs/STORIA-ubuntu-26.04.md, 19 Nov 2026). The difference is the closing time of KDE described in the register (section D); it is a figure of one run on one machine, not a repeated measurement.

    19.5 · Capacity: the recorded measurements and what they do not cover

    The question "how many users can one machine serve" has no measured answer for this tree. What exists is (a) the recorded capacity campaign of August 2026, made on an earlier build and on Intel hardware, and (b) the most users any check attaches at once on Ubuntu.

    Recorded: phase 10, 24 Aug 2026, on the earlier build

    Source: docs/DECISIONS.md §4.6-septies and §4.6-nonies. The campaign predates the 30 September 2026 change in which ffmpeg left the product and encoding moved to libva and Vulkan Video directly (comment of src/Makefile, DECISIONS §10.25), so the numbers are those of another encoder path. The hardware was the Intel integrated card of the dev server; §4.6-septies calls it a UHD 730, a name that DECISIONS-11 §11.21 corrected to UHD 770. The campaign is independent of the distribution and of the package, and was not repeated on Ubuntu 26.04.

    !
    Warning. These figures say where the limit comes from (the compositor's composition work, not the encoder), which is why the budget of ch. 8 “Quality, degradation and budget” counts composed pixels. They must not be quoted as the capacity of REMOTIX for Ubuntu, and a figure without its hardware must not be quoted at all (DECISIONS §4.6-septies).

    Recorded: bandwidth and audio traffic, phase 9

    • DECISIONS §3.1-ter: the worst case on the real path (a client over a throttled link) asked for 21.5 to 23.1 Mbit/s and was held with all 7,125 frames delivered and painted, one keyframe, no abandonment.
    • DECISIONS §3.1-septies: audio silence suppression cut the traffic of a still screen by 102 times (557.6 to 5.5 kbit/s).
    • Both are on an earlier build and an earlier page; they are context, not a specification of the current version.

    Measured on Ubuntu 26.04: the most users tried at once

    The widest multi-user check attaches three users together (three-users, GNOME, PASS: each canvas its own colour, no input crossing); two-users and same-user also pass. check-media.py runs two users animating at 60 Hz at once (60.0 frames per second each). check-desktop.py session-cap runs with the cap lowered to 2 and passes: the third user gets the farewell 0x0E and the two inside keep painting. Every other check runs with the default cap of RCP_SESSION_CAP = 10 sessions in force, but none fills it. The same checks were not run on the virtual machines of Kubuntu, Xubuntu and Lubuntu.

    19.6 · Limits fixed in the code

    These are properties of the source, not observations. Each names its definition. The constants were read again in this tree.

    The decision of 17 Nov 2026, recorded in the plan of the Debian tree, that the address ban stays at 20 failed attempts in 5 minutes matches the second row of the ban counters. The constants of the first twelve rows are the same as on Debian 13 (the diff of rcp.h and budget.h does not touch them, and the lines of rcp.c that define them are unchanged); the last four rows are specific to this tree.

    19.7 · Where no measurement exists

    This list is deliberate: a manual that stays silent about a missing measurement invites a reader to invent one.

    A real phone as client: small stutters in the video (register E4)

    The owner reported small stutters when playing a video (1440p and Full HD) in the remote GNOME session from Chrome on an Android phone, on the virtual machine of Ubuntu on 19 Nov 2026; from the tablet (Chrome on Linux) he did not notice them. The server was measured during 40 s of video towards the phone (docs/REGISTRO-problemi.md, entry E4; the raw logs of this measurement were not found on the dev server, and the figures are quoted from the register):

    The cause was not isolated: the phone (Wi-Fi and the Android decoder), the video player inside the virtual machine, the frame cadence of a virtual machine and the encoding path on the Radeon are all still possible. It is an open, non-blocking case (24.10 “Ubuntu: open points”), not a benchmark.

    +
    Suggestion. A measurement worth adding first, if capacity matters: check-multiuser.py style runs at 4, 6, 8 and 10 users with the budget off, on one named card, recording the composition delay of BUDGET_STRAIN_DELAY_MS. To settle the Android case: the same video towards the tablet with the same measurement on the server, and the same test on a real machine. These are suggestions, not plans recorded anywhere.
    Chapter 20

    Extending REMOTIX and porting to another distribution

    20.1 · The one-distribution rule

    REMOTIX 1.2.0 exists twice: for Debian 13 (trixie), in the folder debian13/, and for Ubuntu 26.04 (resolute) with its four flavours (Ubuntu with GNOME, Kubuntu with KDE Plasma, Xubuntu with XFCE, Lubuntu with LXQt), in this tree. The second tree is a separate copy of the first, with its own packaging, its own build VM, its own test bench and its own manual: the rule that a port is a copy and not a new if in the old tree has been followed once, and this chapter is written from what that port needed.

    Most of the code does not depend on the distribution at all: the transport, the RCP/1 protocol, capture, encoding, the budget, input, audio, clipboard, the page. Its dependencies are on the Linux kernel (DRM nodes, libei, PipeWire), on systemd and logind, on PAM and polkit, on the four desktops, and on a handful of facts about the distribution that the next section lists. The port from Debian to Ubuntu changed about fifty source files; the diff is dominated by src/session.c (the desktop sessions) and by the packaging.

    The product does not detect the distribution to choose a behaviour of its own. It does read, from the machine, what the machine offers: the session names that the display manager lists, the session that carries the distribution's name in /etc/os-release (gnome_session()), the markers of the installed desktops on the PATH. That is the criterion that let the same code serve the four Ubuntu flavours (ch. 12 “The four desktops”).

    !
    Removed code comes back. A decision of the first port is no longer true to the letter. The Debian tree removed the code that only another distribution needed (the Ubuntu session names, the GNOME 50 unit shape, the session-folder discovery of a local login) because it could not be reached on trixie. Ubuntu needs exactly that code, so it came back (20.3 “What the clean-up removed, kept and risked”). A third port must expect the same: removing code that is dead on one distribution is a loan, not a deletion.
    i
    Where the history is. The history of the clean-up is in two documents of docs/: docs/INVENTARIO-non-debian.md lists what existed only for another distribution, with a verdict per item; docs/PULIZIA-tranche1.md records what tranche 1 removed on 17 Nov 2026 on the Debian tree, with the proof that each item was unreachable on trixie. Both describe the Debian tree; in this tree part of that code is live again. Line numbers in the inventory are those of the tree before tranche 1 and no longer point to the right lines.

    20.2 · Where the code depends on the distribution

    The table lists what a porter must look at, area by area, for the two distributions the tree has been ported to. The Debian column describes the folder debian13/ and is quoted from the Debian 13 manual; the Ubuntu column was read in the code of this tree. Names are files and functions, not line numbers.

    The state of each item on the Debian tree (removed, left, or to be removed later) is in docs/INVENTARIO-non-debian.md, section "Status after tranche 1".

    20.3 · What the clean-up removed, kept and risked

    The Debian tree removed, on 17 Nov 2026, the code that could not be reached on trixie (docs/PULIZIA-tranche1.md). The Ubuntu port is the proof that a porter meets each of those problems again: the table says, item by item, what came back in this tree.

    What stays and why

    • The /usr/lib/pam.d lookup and the other distributions' texts in the PAM messages: /usr/lib/pam.d is a real PAM vendor directory, so the lookup is not provably dead. Only text.
    • The pam_selinux lines of remotix.pam: the module ships with the PAM modules of both distributions and the lines mirror sshd.
    • The lightdm and sddm readers and declared_desktop(): on Ubuntu the flavours use them (Xubuntu and Kubuntu set their session there).
    • The KWin workarounds: runtime probes, not version tests.
    • wheel and admin in the polkit rule: logic, kept (Ubuntu names admin).
    • The --no-split run-time option and TWIN and fingerprints in the Makefile.
    • Several header comments that mention other distributions, and the Ubuntu name in the page's font stack.

    Risks recorded by tranche 1, and where they stand

    • The session-folder lookup that imitated a local login (D-153) relied on x11-common not shipping 60x11-common_xdg_path: on Ubuntu it ships, the risk is realised and the code is back.
    • An administrator who installs SELinux finds no SELinux handling in REMOTIX, on either tree.
    • A build against libei older than 1.3.901 fails at make deps by design.
    • On apt remove (not purge) the certificates and ban list stay in net/ instead of moving back to the 1.0 location; a check that looks for the 1.0 location will not find them.

    What tranche 2 listed as still to do (the remaining Ubuntu and Xubuntu detection in session.c, the emulation of a local login's XDG_* variables) is live code in this tree and is described in ch. 12 “The four desktops”, not left as work. Comments naming other distributions, and the other cosmetic items, are in ch. 24 “Appendix C — Known issues and open points”.

    20.4 · Porting from Debian to Ubuntu: what changed in practice

    This section is the experience of the second port, taken from the problem register (docs/REGISTRO-problemi.md, the line "on a new distribution" of each entry) and from the code. It lists what had to change on the way from Debian 13 to Ubuntu 26.04, and what the second port found that the first had not.

    What a second port found that the first did not

    Most of these lessons were learned only because the second target had a real system around the product. None could have come from the Debian container bench; each cost a failure on a real machine or in front of the owner.

    i
    A class of programs. The programs that read the settings themselves are a class, not a case: any program that reads dconf without the library (or from inside a confinement) bypasses what the product puts in the environment of the session. A third port to a distribution with Flatpak or snap applications should expect the same.

    20.5 · A checklist for porting to another distribution

    The tree is not a template for a port, but the porting questions are now known from two ports. The list below is derived from the table above and from the register; it has been exercised once, for Ubuntu 26.04, and is the order in which that port met its problems.

    1. Start from a copy, not from a branch of an existing tree: the Ubuntu tree is a copy of the Debian one with its own debian/, build/, prove/ and manuals/.
    2. Check the library minimums in src/Makefile (MINIMI): OpenSSL 3.5 or newer, GLib 2.80, libei 1.3.901, PipeWire, libva, Vulkan loader 1.3.274. The QUIC libraries are built from source in the image whatever the distribution carries (Ubuntu's are too old, too).
    3. Rewrite the package for the new format: dependency names, install paths, maintainer scripts. Keep the guards of debian/rules (R13, R24) and the checks of build/build-deb-vm.sh (R4, R13, R14, R23) as requirements, however they are implemented. On Ubuntu they also cover our labwc: no libwlroots among its dependencies, and the corresponding source archive is built reproducibly.
    4. Write the PAM service file for that distribution's stack. Without the file, Linux-PAM falls back to the service other, and what other does depends on the distribution (on some it is a hard deny, so every right password is refused). The program checks the file at start-up (main.c). Look at where the session's PATH comes from.
    5. Check polkit. The rules directory; the groups that polkit calls administrator; whether a default privilege table overrides the rules; and the implications of the policy files of that systemd version (run power-implied; the list of forbidden actions is 19 in this tree; the same correction was made for Debian on 20 Nov 2026 (rule with 19 actions in debian13/; the rebuilt Debian package is not yet published), and the test from the seat of the local user with the corrected Debian package was done on the owner's tablet on 20 Nov 2026: all refused, and on any new distribution it must be derived again).
    6. Check the display manager and the session names the desktops register, against desktop_session(), gnome_session() and the readers in session.c. Check the order of the substring tests: a name that contains another (xubuntu, ubuntu) must be asked first.
    7. Check mandatory access control on a real or virtual machine. If SELinux is on, the removed handling of child.c and walls.c is needed. For AppArmor, adapt the profile, write every deny with its operations, and expect that the path that the profile sees is the resolved one (the XKB data are behind a symbolic link on Ubuntu). The profile is still shipped in complain mode: check-apparmor.py reads the kernel journal of every round and fails on any line of the profile, so adapt it until a round shows none; the enforce mode was not proven on either distribution (24.2 “What is unverified”).
    8. Check the programs that read the settings themselves (snap, Flutter, Flatpak): open them in a remote session and read the log of the session for settings errors (register C5).
    9. Check the compositor at the version the distribution carries, and the four desktops' versions, in particular the GNOME session unit shape (a template with instances from GNOME 50), the KWin version and whether the labwc of the distribution hosts KWin correctly: on Ubuntu it did not, and a labwc of our own is built into the package.
    10. Make the bench. Containers are good for speed and bad for the real login screen, the security module and the confined programs. Use virtual machines installed from the desktop images (17.8 “The VM bench”), the ports and names in banco-vm/box.sh and lib.py, and run the whole of prove/all.sh on each desktop (ch. 17 “Testing”). On a new distribution or desktop also try by hand, on a real machine started from a live USB stick, the local login with programs open in the remote desktop (17.10 “Testing the real machine from a live USB”).
    11. Run the package check (check-package.py): install, first start, remove, purge, reinstall. On Ubuntu it is not in the VM bench; it has to be run on a bench that can be reset, or by hand.
    12. Write the manual from the code of the new distribution, not by adapting the old one (register B5); and search for personal data in the finished package before publishing (register C3).
    !
    Warning. Do not add a branch for the new distribution to an existing tree. If code is shared, move it first; the trees must not need each other.

    20.6 · Adding a message to RCP/1

    RCP/1 is closed by design: a receiver that does not understand a message must close with the reason RCP_PROTOCOL_ERROR (0x0B), and a capability used without having been negotiated is the same error (ch. 5 “The RCP/1 protocol”). So adding a message is a protocol change, with the page and the server changed together. The places to touch, in order:

    1. Specify it first in docs/RCP.md (the message list of §7, the byte layout of §6, the version rules of §9) and in docs/SPECS.md if it adds a promise. Decide whether it needs a capability in HELLO and HERE_I_AM.
    2. The type number in the right enumeration of src/rcp.c: the control channel (low byte, e.g. T_TERMINATE_SESSION = 0x0011), input (high byte 0x01), clipboard (0x02), video (0x03) or the audio datagram (0x0401). The same constant goes into the TYPE table of src/page.html.
    3. The body length check. measure_fields() in rcp.c reads the fields of a body before the message is acted on. A type missing from it falls into the default and the check after the switch sends the client away after the action (the comment above measure_fields() records what that order cost with HELLO, ATTACH and CREDENTIALS). For a fixed-size input message also update the lengths in the comment block of the input enum.
    4. The handler in the dispatch switch of the channel (the control handler holds case T_HELLO to case T_TERMINATE_SESSION). If it needs the host (the transport or a session), add a hook to the struct of function pointers in src/rcp.h, with its comment, and connect it in webtransport.c or main.c. A function that is not a hook, like rcp_admitted_waiting(), needs no wiring.
    5. The rate class. Messages that a client can send in a flood have a class in src/msgrate.h (MC_POINTER ... MC_FIT_CANVAS, with a rate and a burst) and a mapping in control_class() or lww_index() in rcp.c. A new message needs a decision: its own class, or one that is never dropped.
    6. The page, both directions: how it encodes or decodes the message, and what it does on an unexpected type. A server message the page does not know ends the session with PROTOCOL_ERROR.
    7. A farewell that must reach a client in every state goes through wt_dismiss_user_session_over() in webtransport.c: it says the farewell at once to a client that is logged in, keeps it until the fixed second for a client that was already admitted, and skips a connection that is still waiting for PAM, so that a stranger trying passwords under that name learns nothing and nobody receives a false RCP_SESSION_TERMINATED. It is the model of the farewells of this tree that end a session (RCP_SESSION_UNSERVABLE when a stage is refused, RCP_SESSION_TERMINATED at a Log Out).
    8. Log lines follow ch. 21 “Conventions” (the mark at the head of a body sets the journal priority).
    9. A check: a new name in an existing check, or a new check file (below). The test is the page driven by a real browser, so the page and the server are tested together.
    i
    No protocol-level tests. There is no unit-test harness for rcp.c in this tree: the twin comparison and the benches that exercised the protocol alone were not carried over (ch. 18 “Build and release”). A protocol change is covered only by what the checks of prove/ exercise.

    20.7 · Adding a desktop

    The product knows four desktops, by the enumeration DesktopSession in src/session.h. A fifth is a larger change than it looks, because the desktop appears in places beyond session.c. The order that the code and its comments suggest:

    1. Classify the family. Capture, input, clipboard and remount talk to the compositor, not the desktop. XFCE and LXQt share labwc, a wlroots compositor, and session_on_wlroots() answers "is it the wlroots family"; GNOME uses Mutter, and KDE uses KWin nested in our own labwc. A new desktop that runs on labwc reuses the whole wlroots path.
    2. The enumeration. Add the value to DesktopSession at the END: the value travels as a uint32_t between the parent and the child, and renumbering the existing ones would break that boundary.
    3. Detection. desktop_session() in session.c chooses by markers on the PATH, in a stated order (the comment lists the branches and why the order is not free), and desktop_of_session_name() maps session names, including those of the Ubuntu flavours, where the order of the tests matters (a name that contains another is asked first). Add the marker and the name, and decide what happens when two desktops are installed (the code picks one and says so in the log).
    4. The names of the desktop's session as macros in session.h (for XFCE, SESSION_PRIMARY_XFCE and SESSION_BUS_XFCE), and its Log Out command.
    5. The places that branch on the desktop. In child.c, the birth of the session and the stage (the XFCE and LXQt wording and the KDE branch), and the close; in main.c, the switch that names the desktop in the log; in session.c, the branches that are specific to one desktop (for example the GNOME-only ones). Search for SESSION_DESKTOP_ to find all of them.
    6. Packaging. Recommends in debian/control if the desktop needs a compositor package. If the compositor can be missing (a Recommends is not a Depends), make session_missing_component() return its name: main.c then answers 0x0E with the package's name before it spawns a child, and the postinst warns when the desktop is installed alone.
    7. The bench. Add the desktop to the dictionaries that give the bench its ports: PORTS in lib.py (8841 to 8844 for the virtual machines chosen by RX_BANCO=vm; 8821 to 8824 belong to the older containers), box.sh of prove/banco-vm/box.sh, and a new virtual machine in server/vm-radeon.sh.
    8. Tests. Add the desktop to the dictionaries of the checks: PANEL and LOGOUT in deskkit.py, PORTS and SHELL_UP in lib.py, TERMINAL and FILEMGR in check-desktop.py (on Ubuntu GNOME the terminal is ptyxis), the desktop list in all.sh and matrix.sh (fresh.sh takes the desktop as its argument). Then run the full suite on it.

    The four existing desktops are described in ch. 12 “The four desktops”. The comments in session.h record what each addition cost: for example that, before LXQt, five places wrote the XFCE test directly, so the fifth value would have fallen into the GNOME and KDE branch silently.

    20.8 · Adding a video codec

    The chain is: card capability, encoder route, codec number in RCP, the offer in HERE_I_AM, the page's decoder. Video encoding is described in ch. 7 “Video encoding”; for an addition:

    1. Encoder. Routes are chosen by capability when each encoder opens (h264_card and hevc_card in src/encoder.c: Vulkan first, VA-API where Vulkan is not there). A codec needs an implementation on each route that can carry it (vadirect.c for VA-API, vulkanvideo.c for Vulkan) and an entry in the capability probe.
    2. The measurement at start-up. child_video_capabilities() measures what the card encodes and the result becomes the offer: rcp_video_codec_set(). With an empty list every HELLO ends in RCP_NOTHING_IN_COMMON.
    3. The number in RCP. Codec numbers are never reused: 1 is HEVC, 2 stays AV1 even though AV1 left the product, 3 is H.264 (the comment in page.html gives the reason: an old client hearing a reused number would paint garbage without an error). RCP_CODEC_VIDEO_MAX in rcp.h bounds the list.
    4. The page. The tables CODEC_RCP and CODEC_NAME, the preference list PREFERENCE, and the capability probe (the page asks the browser whether it can decode the codec string) in src/page.html. The server decides in the end; the page's list is a preference.
    5. The keyframe rules of RCP §5.2 apply to every codec: the first frame after SESSION, after a canvas change, and on request.
    6. Tests. The codec check of check-media.py reports the negotiated codec per browser and that it is hardware; a new codec needs its own expectation there and in the sharpness judge.
    i
    State of HEVC. HEVC is offered by the server but did not reach the pixel on the test browsers in the round of 19 Nov 2026 on Ubuntu (the page's probe refused every HEVC string, on Chrome and on Firefox: log media.out of vm-gnome-unione10, check codec), as it did not on Debian 13 on 17 Nov 2026. Every recorded run negotiated H.264. HEVC decoding in a browser is therefore not demonstrated by the logs of either distribution. On a real machine of the owner the server logged "HEVC: yes via vaapi" (docs/STORIA-ubuntu-26.04.md), which is the server's side only.

    20.9 · Adding a check to prove/

    A check is cheap to write and expensive to trust. The conventions below are what the existing checks do (thirteen check-*.py files; all.sh runs fifteen steps of them, check-package.py is run apart); a new check should do the same.

    1. One file, one docstring. Put the check in prove/check-<name>.py. The docstring says what it proves, how to run it, the users it makes, and the verdict names. Define a NAMES tuple.
    2. Use the kit. Build on lib.py: Results for verdict lines (attempt turns an exception into FAIL or BLOCKED; sequence runs the checks in order under a deadline), Rig for compositor, browser, user and login, deskkit.py to run things in the user's session.
    3. FAIL is the product, BLOCKED is the tool. Raise Fail when the product did not do it; let a tool error surface as ToolError. On the VM bench a check may also be reported as SKIP (it cannot be done there: the real login screen, other source addresses, the package check) or NOTE; neither is ever a PASS, and the runner's closing rule is that no check produced a pass by being left out.
    4. Use a user prefix of its own and add it to the pattern of lib.sweep() so that sessions are ended at the end of all.sh (the pattern lists the prefixes of every check).
    5. Judge from inside the box. Log what the application received (a test window), not what the browser was told to send. If a new window is needed, add it next to window.py. Where the window itself may lose events (the GTK 4.22 case of register B3-bis), read the raw events.
    6. Print evidence on the line. The format is PASS|FAIL|BLOCKED <name> - evidence, one line per name. A check that reads the journal must not write the string it looks for into the journal: the VM bench enters the machine as root by key and not with sudo, because sudo logs each command line and the typed secret of a check (the false red of typed-names-not-logged in the first full round on Ubuntu).
    7. Register it in all.sh with a time limit: run <label> <seconds> python3 check-<name>.py --box "$DE". A check that changes the box in a way that other checks must not see (like check-ban.py and check-package.py) goes last or outside. Use all.sh --only label,label to repeat a part (the run says "PARTIAL RUN" and exits with 3 when everything passed but not everything ran).
    8. Prove that it can say red. A check that cannot fail is a net with no fish. The existing checks keep a --selftest for the picture judge (base-check.py) and report numbers in their evidence so that a pass can be read.
    9. Record a limit honestly. If the check is an emulation (the phone) or has a declared tool limit (AltGr), write it in the docstring.

    Running order and limits are in ch. 17 “Testing”.

    Chapter 21

    Conventions

    21.1 · The written rules and what the tree does with them

    The rules that are written are in CLAUDE.md, about a dozen lines of them. In this tree the file is the one of the Debian tree carried over and not rewritten: its title, its first paragraph and its build lines are Debian's, and they are not repeated here as facts of this tree (they are listed in ch. 24 “Appendix C — Known issues and open points”). Everything else in this chapter is observed in the tree and said as an observation: where the code does not follow a rule, the chapter says so.

    21.2 · Names, language and the Italian that remains

    The text of the product is English: comments, log lines, messages and the page. Italian survives in names, and in the working documents of the project; the manual cites those names as code because they are the real ones.

    Italian that remains in identifiers

    The comments were translated; some names were not. They are real names in the source, and the manual quotes them in code. The counts are of this tree.

    • registro_dice() is the macro every module calls to write a log line (the string registro_dice( occurs 1,261 times in src/*.c and src/*.h, the definition included, counted with grep -o on 20 Nov 2026); the function behind it is log_says_in().
    • In src/Makefile: SORGENTI (sources), OGGETTI (objects), PROTOCOLLI (protocols), GEMELLATI (twinned files), MINIMI (minimum versions), AVVERTIMENTI (warnings), deps's variable stato, and the generated GENERATI.
    • In rcp.c: short variables such as lung (length), and comments that name handlers tratta_*() that no function of that name implements any more.
    • wt_chi in the WebTransport module and codificatore_chiedi_chiave in the encoder code.
    • In the build and server scripts, output and folder names: costruzione.log, immagine.log, controlli.txt, elenco.txt, pacchetti/, prove/, prepara-server.sh. fanwatch.py is English.
    • New in this tree, all Italian names quoted as they are: the VM scripts server/vm-radeon.sh (commands crea create, accendi switch on, spegni switch off, ssh, stato state, istantanea snapshot, ripristina restore, prova-avvio start-up test), server/vm-radeon-aggiorna.sh (update), server/vm-radeon-controllo.sh (check), server/vm-radeon-installa.sh (install), server/live-installa.sh (installer for a live image); the folder of our labwc, build/labwc-ospite/ (ospite = guest, the labwc that hosts KWin); the bench variables RX_BANCO (banco = bench), RX_TEMPO (tempo = time factor), RX_BAN_ADDR, PACCHETTO (package) and UTENTI (users); the name of a test package such as unione10 (unione = union: the build that merged the fixes; a round is a giro); and the folders /media/REMOTIX-UBUNTU/albero (tree), pacchetti (packages), prove (checks), vm, log, lavoro (work) and vm-radeon on the dev server.
    • In the document headings: docs/DECISIONS.md opens as "DECISIONI" and docs/SPECS.md as "SPECIFICHE"; DECISIONS.md refers to LEZIONI.md (the file is LESSONS.md here).
    i
    Renaming. Do not rename an Italian identifier as a side effect of another change. A name is public if a log line, a message, an option or a file name carries it; those are recorded in the documents as they are.

    21.3 · Comments, marks and references

    The comments are long on purpose. A block comment states why a thing is the way it is, with the date, the source and the failure it prevents. The code is short next to its comments (105,799 lines of C and headers in src/ plus a page of 14,258 lines, most of it in a few large files: child.c 12,671 lines, rcp.c 10,485, webtransport.c 9,618, session.c 8,829; counted with wc -l in this tree on 20 Nov 2026).

    • The marks of evidence come from CODER.md §5 (cited by docs/SPECS.md and docs/DECISIONS.md; that file is not in this repository). A line in the specification without a mark is a product decision, not a technical fact.
    • References are by section: DECISIONS.md §x, RCP.md §x, SPECS.md §x. Audit findings are cited by identifier (for example R12.3). Citing a section that has moved is the usual way a comment goes stale.
    • The decision register uses three marks for certainty: decided, derived and open (the header of docs/DECISIONS.md). A derived entry is corrected without discussion if wrong; a decided one is reopened only by a measurement that contradicts it.
    • Measurements carry a date and a machine. In this tree the [M] marks added on 18 and 19 Nov 2026 name where the figure was taken (for example a Ubuntu 26.04 virtual machine with its snaps, or the KDE test machine rx-kde); a mark without a machine is not a figure to quote.
    • Comments are not always right. The manual follows the rule that the code wins when the two disagree; the places where they were found to disagree are listed in ch. 24 “Appendix C — Known issues and open points”.
    • Dead references. Many comments cite files that are not in this repository: CODER.md, REVIEWER.md, STUDIES.md, the phases/ folder, benches/ and PHASES.md. They are history, not instructions.

    21.4 · Errors, fallbacks and invariants

    The product is written to fail closed and to say so. The rules below are visible in the sources again and again; each names an example.

    The invariants I1 to I7 are named in the comments and documents; their formal list is in CODER.md, which is not in this tree. The ones whose wording is in files of the tree are the ones quoted here; do not assume the others from their number alone.

    21.5 · Logging conventions for a writer of code

    Logging has one funnel, src/log.c, so that rules about what is written can be checked in one place (ch. 16 “Logging and diagnostics” describes the mechanism). The conventions a writer of code has to follow:

    • Always through the macros. registro_dice(area, fmt, ...) for lines that are always written; log_detail(area, fmt, ...) for chatter, written only with --verbose. Never fprintf(stderr, ...). The macros add __FILE__ and __LINE__, which go to the journal as CODE_FILE and CODE_LINE.
    • The first characters of a body set the severity. In the journal, a body that starts with the prohibition mark is priority 3 (error), with the warning mark priority 4, anything else priority 6, and chatter 7 (log.c, log.h). Choose the mark deliberately: an expected event written with the error mark appears in journalctl -p err. docs/REGISTRO-priorita.md records the 17 Nov 2026 pass that moved routine lines down (33 patterns observed: 5 to info, 24 to warning, 4 left as errors).
    • The area is part of the call. Use one of the areas declared in log.h (LOG_STARTUP, REG_QUIC, REG_WT, REG_RCP, LOG_PAGE, REG_CERT, LOG_SESSION, REG_VIDEO, REG_BUDGET); a new subject that is read as its own column gets its own area. The prefixes of these macro names are not uniform (LOG_ and REG_).
    • Whose line it is. A process that serves one session sets its identity once with log_identity(); the process that serves all of them passes the identity with the line through log_says_of(). A line with no known owner goes out without brackets, never with an empty or a guessed name. The bracket is cut at LOG_IDENTITY_MAX = 48.
    • Never log a secret or a keystroke. Passwords appear in no line (the funnel exists so that this can be checked). Keys are logged as "key" with an evdev code, except the modifiers, decided by log_speakable_key(). A typed user name is not logged before the verdict (tested by typed-names-not-logged).
    • Rate-limit what a client can trigger. Lines that a hostile or broken client can cause repeatedly are written with a counter and an interval (see the burst line of webtransport.c in the priority register).
    • Say what, not "error". A line names the thing that was not understood or that failed and, where there is one, the reason code. Two lines of this tree show it: the verdict that names the missing labwc package in delivery_verdict(), and the line of stage_refused_by_child() that says the stage was refused for the scale and how many clients were sent away.

    21.6 · The layout of the tree and the habits around it

    The tree has a few fixed places and a few habits that follow from where a thing runs.

    • Temporary files never go to /tmp on the dev server: its root file system is in RAM. The build script makes its small staging folder under TMPDIR (the compiling is done in the build VM) and the checks run from a folder on the persistent disk (/media/REMOTIX-UBUNTU).
    • Nothing is deleted, moved or overwritten without the owner asking. This binds the scripts too: the build script copies the tree and never edits the working tree, and the header of server/vm-radeon.sh says what the only thing it removes is (its own temporary image) and that a disk is never touched twice.
    • Scripts print one status line per step (OK or FAIL) and keep going where the next step is independent; destructive operations are named in the header (check-package.py resets the box, check-ban.py bans an address and always unblocks, fresh-vm.sh removes the test users).
    • Generated files are marked. vulkanvideo_rgb_nv12_spv.h says in its first line that it is generated and not to be edited by hand.
    • The manual checks itself against the tree. python3 manuals/sources/build.py --check verifies that every function, file and REMOTIX_* variable cited in code form exists, and flags Italian sentences.

    21.7 · Conventions of the Ubuntu tree

    A few conventions are new in this tree. They were not needed on Debian 13, and each comes from a failure of the Ubuntu port.

    Chapter 22

    Appendix A — Data structures and messages

    22.1 · The main C structures

    The central data structures of the server, with the file that defines them and the chapter that explains them. They are the contracts that run through REMOTIX. Structures private to one file are listed only when a maintainer will meet them while following a login, a child or a desktop found again.

    22.2 · The root-side protocol, message by message

    Every packet is one SOCK_SEQPACKET message of exactly the size of its struct, starting with struct rxr_head: magic (RXR_MAGIC, 0x31525852, “RXR1” little-endian, u32), version (RXR_VERSION = 3, u16), kind (u16) and request (u64, chosen by the network side and echoed in the answer; 0 in events). The sizes below were obtained by compiling rootside_proto.h alone with gcc on x86-64; the file asserts only two of them (rxr_verdict = 296 and rxr_spawn_refused = 24).

    Constants. RXR_FOUND_MAX = 256 (the most desktops found again, equal to MAX_FOUND_AGAIN in main.c), RXR_GRANT_BYTES = 16, RXR_AUTH_IN_FLIGHT_MAX = 16, RXR_AUTH_PER_S = 3, RXR_AUTH_BURST = 8, RXR_GRANT_LIFE_MS = 30 000. The root side's other bounds are in rootside.h: ROOTSIDE_LOGIN_PAIR_LIMIT = 5, ROOTSIDE_LOGIN_HOST_LIMIT = 20, ROOTSIDE_LOGIN_USER_LIMIT = 15, ROOTSIDE_LOGIN_WINDOW_MS = 300 000, ROOTSIDE_LOGIN_USER_PAUSE_MS = 900 000, ROOTSIDE_LOGIN_FORGET_MS = 86 400 000, ROOTSIDE_ORPHAN_PER_S = 2, ROOTSIDE_ORPHAN_BURST = 5, ROOTSIDE_ORPHAN_UID_MS = 30 000, ROOTSIDE_ABANDON_S_MAX = 31 536 000 (one year).

    !
    Header comments. Three comments in the headers disagree with the code. rootside_proto.h says the child's socket is “the only fd that ever crosses” the channel, but birth() in rootside.c sends two (the socket and a pidfd, chan_try2()). Its long comment gives the AUTH rate as “10 per second with a burst of 20”, while the constants, and the later paragraph of the same comment, say 3 and 8. And its list of root-to-network kinds omits RXR_CODEC. The code is described in this manual.

    22.3 · The PAM helper's packets

    The packets between the root side (or, in the single-process mode, the server) and the PAM dispatcher are one SOCK_SEQPACKET pair; the dispatcher's socket is descriptor 3.

    22.4 · Messages between the network side and a child

    The header is the same for all (ch. 2 “Overall architecture”): magic FIG1, kind u16, version u16 (CHILD_VERSION = 1), serial u64, declared_uid u32, byte u32. The longest message is MAX_ENVELOPE (a head, a struct body_frame and MAX_PIECE = 32 768 bytes). A frame is at most FRAME_MAX = 16 MiB; the clipboard text at most RCP_CLIPBOARD_CAP = 1 000 000 bytes.

    22.5 · The unblock command socket

    The only text protocol on a local socket is the bench's unblock command in command.c. It exists only if the server is started with --command-socket <path>; the packaged unit does not pass it, and the owner decided on 17 November 2026 that the administrator has no command to lift a ban (the plan of the Debian tree; prove/check-ban.py check “unblock-shipped” reports that the packaged unit has no such option and that there is no command-line tool; as written it cannot fail). When given, the socket is created mode 0600, one line is read per connection (with a short timeout, so that a silent client holds the loop for two tenths of a second at most) and one line is answered:

    i
    A bench tool. With the network side behind its walls the socket would live in /run/remotix/net (the only writable run folder, noexec). The file says it cannot tell whether the ban file was rewritten: it reports that the rewrite was requested.

    22.6 · Index of RCP/1 messages and farewell reasons

    All RCP/1 message types by number. The bodies are in docs/RCP.md at the section given; the constants are the T_* enumerations at the top of rcp.c. The protocol itself is explained in ch. 5 “The RCP/1 protocol”.

    Numbers carried in bodies. Video codec: 1 HEVC, 2 AV1 (never reused, no longer negotiated), 3 H.264 (RCP_CODEC_VIDEO_MAX = 3). Audio codec: 1 Opus, 2 PCM; these are not the video numbers. Framing: the largest message is MAX_MESSAGE = 1 MiB, framing included; a video frame at most 16 MiB; a cursor at most 256×256. Elementary types are big-endian and unaligned (RCP.md §6.0).

    Chapter 24

    Appendix C — Known issues and open points

    24.1 · How to read this appendix

    This appendix lists what is known to be open, unverified or inconsistent in REMOTIX 1.2.0 for Ubuntu 26.04, area by area. It is meant to be complete rather than flattering. An item is here because a source file, a check, the problem register (docs/REGISTRO-problemi.md) or docs/STORIA-ubuntu-26.04.md (the history of the work) says so; where something was read only in a comment and not observed, it is said. Two sections are specific to this tree: what real machines showed that the container boxes did not, and the open points of the Ubuntu port. The last section lists the places where code, comments and documents disagree: in every case the code was taken as the truth and the chapters describe the code.

    i
    Scope. The package is checked with prove/all.sh on virtual machines, one per desktop (Ubuntu, Kubuntu, Xubuntu, Lubuntu), with the Radeon passed through (register G). The round of 1.2.0 (26 and 27 Nov 2026) gave GNOME 125 PASS and one known FAIL (desktop/users-shell-and-environment, below) and 126 PASS on KDE, XFCE and LXQt; P7 and P9 of prove/check-prelocal.py (the local login with programs open in the remote desktop) ran on all four desktops and P8 on KDE and XFCE (it is BLOCKED by construction on GNOME and LXQt); the update from 1.0.1 and the removal were clean on the four. The owner then tried the four virtual machines and, on a real machine, the four live images of 26.04.1: all OK (27 Nov 2026). The older round on GNOME (19 Nov 2026, package numbered 1.0.0, build unione10) is in the chapter on testing. Nothing in this appendix is a failure of those rounds unless it is stated so.

    Chapter 25

    Glossary

    25.1 · Terms used in this manual

    AppArmor
    Linux security module; the profile remotix_network confines the network side (complain mode). On Ubuntu 26.04 it also mediates unix sockets, so the profile's deny lines name their operations.
    Ban
    Block of an address or a user after wrong passwords: 15 minutes, then 1 hour, then 12 hours.
    Child
    The per-user process, running as that user, that holds the desktop stage, capture, encoder, input and audio.
    Compositor
    The Wayland program that draws the desktop: the distribution's labwc for XFCE and LXQt, Mutter for GNOME, and for KDE KWin nested in our own labwc.
    Declared fallback
    A different behaviour taken when the intended one is not available, announced by a line of the log that names the decision (for example DECLARED FALLBACK, D-015 for the dconf model) so that it can be told from an accident.
    Detach, reattach
    The browser leaves and the desktop stays alive; a later login finds it again.
    Fixed second
    The rule that a login's answer is not given before a fixed time after the credentials (one second; 2.5 s for a refusal), so that the time says nothing about the account; a farewell for an admitted client is held until it has passed. RCP.md §4.4-bis.
    Flutter program
    A program of Ubuntu written with the Flutter toolkit (the installer of the live image, Firmware Updater, Security Center). It has its own dconf reader that knows only the user and system databases; this is why the settings of a remote session are a system database and not a profile with other layers.
    Found again
    A desktop with no child whose user returns within the few seconds before the root side ends it ("no orphan desktops"); after an orderly stop there is none. rediscover.c.
    HTTP/3
    HTTP over QUIC; carries the page and WebTransport.
    Local excludes remote
    A user with a local graphical session cannot start a remote one.
    Local-login hold
    The pause of a local graphical login, made by the PAM hook remotix-local-login, until the user's remote desktop is closed.
    Log Out
    The user's request to end the desktop session; it closes the logind session on every desktop.
    Lost frame, poke
    A frame that KWin did not deliver: a gap in the numbering of its buffers (capture_watch_sequence(), capture_frame_lost()). The cure is a poke, a request to KWin for a new frame (kwin_poke()), at most every 200 ms and never on a still desktop.
    Needrestart drop-in
    The file /etc/needrestart/conf.d/remotix.conf, which tells needrestart never to restart remotix.service by itself, because a restart closes every remote desktop; the service is only listed for a manual restart.
    Network side
    The part of the server that runs as user remotix with no capability and holds the sockets.
    No orphan desktops
    The rule that a REMOTIX desktop with no child of ours must not stay: the root side ends it.
    Opus
    Audio codec; decoded in the page by a WebAssembly build.
    Our labwc (guest labwc)
    The labwc inside the package, /usr/libexec/remotix/labwc: labwc 0.9.3 with a patched wlroots 0.19.2, linked statically (recipe in build/labwc-ospite/, ospite meaning guest). It hosts the nested KWin of the KDE desktop, because the distribution's labwc leaves KWin 6.5 and later on its first frame. Its corresponding source is published with each release.
    PAM
    Pluggable Authentication Modules; the login password is checked through the service remotix.
    PipeWire
    Media server used to capture the screen and the sound of the session.
    QUIC
    Encrypted transport over UDP (library ngtcp2, linked statically).
    RCP/1
    REMOTIX's own protocol, specified in docs/RCP.md.
    remotix-pam-hook
    The script /usr/libexec/remotix/remotix-pam-hook that the unit runs before every start (ExecStartPre): it checks that the line of the local-login hook is in /etc/pam.d/common-session and puts it back through pam-auth-update if it is not.
    Root side
    The part of the server that stays root: PAM, session birth, start of the network side; it answers a closed list of requests.
    Runtime dconf profile
    The file $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/dconf/profile, which the session writes and dconf reads when the variable DCONF_PROFILE is absent: the base profile's first line, system-db:remotix, user-db:remotix, then the rest of the base profile. Removed, or rewritten with the base profile alone, at the end of the session.
    Sentinel
    The module (sentinel.c) that asks logind whether a user has a local graphical session; its answer is behind the farewells 0x04 and 0x05. It also asks whether power-off, reboot, suspend and hibernate are forbidden, and accepts "no" or "not available".
    Session life
    The answer to "is the desktop alive" with three values, SESSION_LIFE_ALIVE, SESSION_LIFE_DEAD and SESSION_LIFE_UNKNOWN (session_life()): dead only when the bus answered and the compositor's name has no owner; unknown when the question could not be asked.
    Snap
    Ubuntu's confined package format. A confined snap has its own runtime folder and cannot open the paths of the session's run folder, which is why the dconf profile moved to a system database and the runtime folder.
    Stage
    What a desktop draws on: the compositor and its virtual monitor, with capture and input attached.
    sudo-rs, rust-coreutils
    The Rust reimplementations of sudo and of the core utilities that Ubuntu 26.04 installs. The checks of the Ubuntu tree expect the messages of sudo-rs, and the scripts of the package must run on the Rust utilities.
    System dconf database
    /etc/dconf/db/remotix: the locked settings of the remote GNOME session, compiled with dconf compile by the package's postinst (and by the service at start, if it is missing or different) from key files that the build generates with remotix --dconf-keyfiles from the table DCONF_KEYS of session.c.
    Unione
    The Italian word (union) in the names of the test packages of the Ubuntu work, such as unione10: a build that merges the fixes made so far. A "round" of the checks is called a giro in the log folders.
    Vulkan Video
    Hardware video encoding through Vulkan; tried first, where the card's driver offers it.
    VA-API
    Video Acceleration API; the way to encode on the card where Vulkan Video is missing.
    VM bench
    The test bench of the Ubuntu release: four QEMU virtual machines installed from the desktop images, with the server's Radeon passed through to one at a time by vfio-pci (server/vm-radeon.sh, prove/banco-vm/, RX_BANCO=vm, deadlines doubled by RX_TEMPO=2). It has a real login screen, AppArmor and snap, which the container boxes did not. Before every start with the Radeon the script checks that the guest has amdgpu.runpm=0 and refuses to hand the card over if not (server/VM-BANCO.md); a fifth machine, costruzione, builds the package and never gets the card.
    Walls
    The ordered list of restrictions put on the network side before it starts (walls.c, applied as root just before the exec): identity, capabilities, mounts, seccomp, Landlock.
    WebTransport
    Streams and datagrams over HTTP/3, used by the page to speak RCP/1.
